Arrays, Bits & Recursion

Bit Magic

Bit manipulation treats an integer as a row of 0/1 switches. A handful of operators (& | ^ ~ << >>) and a dozen tricks turn O(n) counting problems into O(1) formulas, cancel paired elements with XOR, and enumerate every subset of a set with a counter.

Bit magic — solving problems by operating directly on the binary representation of integers — testing, setting, clearing and counting bits, and using XOR's cancelling property — instead of on their decimal value.

Binary representation and two's complement

An n-bit integer has n positions; bit 0 is the least significant bit (LSB, rightmost, worth 1) and bit n-1 the most significant bit (MSB, leftmost). Unsigned numbers use all bits for magnitude; signed numbers use two's complement, where the MSB acts as the sign and the representable range is -2^(n-1) … 2^(n-1) - 1.

1
Write the positive number
3 in 4 bits is 0011.
2
Invert every bit
0011 → 1100 (this is the one's complement).
3
Add 1
1100 + 1 → 1101. That is -3 in 4-bit two's complement.
two's complement of x in n bits = 2^n − x (4 bits: 16 − 3 = 13 = 1101)
Every 4-bit pattern is used exactly once; there is only one zero
4-bit two's complement (range -8 … 7)

 bits   value         bits   value
 0000     0           1000    -8   ← MSB set ⇒ negative
 0001     1           1001    -7
 0010     2           1010    -6
 0011     3           1011    -5
 0100     4           1100    -4
 0101     5           1101    -3
 0110     6           1110    -2
 0111     7           1111    -1

Why two's complement rather than a separate sign bit? Three reasons that make hardware simpler:

  • One zero. A sign-magnitude scheme has +0 and -0; two's complement has a single 0000.
  • Addition just works. The same adder handles positive and negative operands: 3 + (-3) = 0011 + 1101 = 1 0000, and dropping the carry gives 0000. Subtraction is addition of the complement, which is where the name 0 − x comes from.
  • The leading bit is the sign. MSB 1 ⇒ negative, so a sign test is a single bit check.
Python
def bits(x, n):
    # the low n bits of x, most significant first ((x >> i) & 1 picks bit i)
    return "".join("1" if (x >> i) & 1 else "0" for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1))

for x in (3, 7, -1, -3, -8):
    print(x, "in 4 bits:", bits(x, 4))
print("2^4 - 3 =", (1 << 4) - 3, "->", bits((1 << 4) - 3, 4))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

string bits(int x, int n) {
    string s;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)        // (x >> i) & 1 picks bit i
        s += ((x >> i) & 1) ? '1' : '0';
    return s;
}

int main() {
    for (int x : {3, 7, -1, -3, -8})
        cout << x << " in 4 bits: " << bits(x, 4) << "\n";
    cout << "2^4 - 3 = " << ((1 << 4) - 3) << " -> " << bits((1 << 4) - 3, 4) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static String bits(int x, int n) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)    // (x >> i) & 1 picks bit i
            sb.append((x >> i) & 1);
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int x : new int[]{3, 7, -1, -3, -8})
            System.out.println(x + " in 4 bits: " + bits(x, 4));
        System.out.println("2^4 - 3 = " + ((1 << 4) - 3) + " -> " + bits((1 << 4) - 3, 4));
    }
}
JavaScript
function bits(x, n) {
    let s = "";
    for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)        // (x >> i) & 1 picks bit i
        s += (x >> i) & 1;
    return s;
}

for (const x of [3, 7, -1, -3, -8])
    console.log(x, "in 4 bits:", bits(x, 4));
console.log("2^4 - 3 =", (1 << 4) - 3, "->", bits((1 << 4) - 3, 4));
Output
3 in 4 bits: 0011
7 in 4 bits: 0111
-1 in 4 bits: 1111
-3 in 4 bits: 1101
-8 in 4 bits: 1000
2^4 - 3 = 13 -> 1101
Key point

Masking with (x >> i) & 1 works for negative numbers too, because every language above shifts a negative int arithmetically (the sign bit is copied in). Python has no fixed width, so -3 is conceptually …11111101 with infinitely many leading ones — taking the low 4 bits still gives 1101.

Bitwise operators
OperatorNameRule per bit12 (1100) with 10 (1010)
a & bAND1 only if both bits are 11000 = 8
a | bOR1 if either bit is 11110 = 14
a ^ bXOR1 if the bits differ0110 = 6
~aNOTflips every bit; equals -a - 1 in two's complement~12 = -13
a << kleft shiftshift left, zeros enter on the right; multiplies by 2^k12 << 2 = 48
a >> kright shiftshift right, drops the low bits; divides by 2^k (floor)12 >> 2 = 3
Python
def bits(x, n):
    return "".join("1" if (x >> i) & 1 else "0" for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1))

def show(label, v):
    print(f"{label} = {v} -> {bits(v, 8)}")

a, b = 12, 10
show("a", a)
show("b", b)
show("a & b", a & b)
show("a | b", a | b)
show("a ^ b", a ^ b)
show("~a", ~a)            # -13: Python prints the signed value, low 8 bits are 11110011
show("a << 2", a << 2)
show("a >> 2", a >> 2)

Language differences you must know
PythonC++ / JavaJavaScript
Width of an intunbounded — 1 << 100 is fine, ~x is always -x-132-bit int, 64-bit long/long long; overflow wraps (Java) or is undefined for signed (C++)numbers are doubles, but every bitwise operator converts to a 32-bit signed int first — 1 << 31 is -2147483648
>> on negativesarithmetic (floor division by 2^k)arithmetic; C++ guarantees it since C++20arithmetic
Logical (zero-fill) shiftnot needed — mask first: (x & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> kJava: x >>> k. C++: cast to unsigned firstx >>> k
Shift by ≥ widthfine (just a bigger number)undefined in C++, taken mod 32/64 in Javataken mod 32
Popcount built-inn.bit_count() (3.10+) or bin(n).count('1')std::popcount (<bit>, unsigned) / __builtin_popcount; Integer.bitCount(n)none — n.toString(2).split('1').length - 1
Python
x = -16
print("-16 >> 2 =", x >> 2)                       # arithmetic: sign bit copied in
print("-16 >>> 2 =", (x & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 2)       # emulate a 32-bit logical shift
print("1 << 10 =", 1 << 10)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int x = -16;
    cout << "-16 >> 2 = " << (x >> 2) << "\n";                        // arithmetic shift
    cout << "-16 >>> 2 = " << (static_cast<unsigned>(x) >> 2) << "\n"; // logical: shift as unsigned
    cout << "1 << 10 = " << (1 << 10) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = -16;
        System.out.println("-16 >> 2 = " + (x >> 2));     // arithmetic shift
        System.out.println("-16 >>> 2 = " + (x >>> 2));   // logical shift fills with zeros
        System.out.println("1 << 10 = " + (1 << 10));
    }
}
JavaScript
const x = -16;
console.log("-16 >> 2 =", x >> 2);        // arithmetic shift
console.log("-16 >>> 2 =", x >>> 2);      // logical shift; result is an unsigned 32-bit value
console.log("1 << 10 =", 1 << 10);
Output
-16 >> 2 = -4
-16 >>> 2 = 1073741820
1 << 10 = 1024
Pitfall

In JavaScript 2 ** 40 | 0 silently truncates to 32 bits, and in C++ 1 << 31 on an int and any shift by 32 or more are undefined behaviour. When you need 64 bits use 1n << 40n (BigInt) in JS and 1LL << 40 / 1L << 40 in C++/Java.

The classic tricks
ExpressionWhat it doesWhy
n & 11 if n is oddthe LSB is the only odd place value
n << 1, n >> 1n * 2, n / 2 (floor)shifting moves every bit to the next place value
1 << k2^k, a mask with only bit k set1 moved k places left
n & (1 << k)non-zero iff bit k is setAND keeps only that bit
n | (1 << k)set bit kOR with the mask forces a 1
n & ~(1 << k)clear bit kAND with every bit except k set
n ^ (1 << k)toggle bit kXOR with 1 flips, with 0 keeps
n & (n - 1)clear the rightmost set bitsubtracting 1 flips that bit and the zeros after it
n & -n (= n & ~(n - 1))isolate the rightmost set bit-n agrees with n only at that bit
n & (n - 1) == 0n is a power of two (for n > 0)a power of two has exactly one set bit
x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = xXOR cancels pairsthe basis of the odd-occurrence problems below
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= bswap without a temporarya ^ b ^ b = a
Decimal to binary and back

Repeated division by 2 produces the bits from the right: the remainder is the next bit, the quotient is what is left. Reading a binary string left to right is the reverse: value = value * 2 + bit. Both loops are O(number of bits) = O(log n).

Python
def to_binary(n):
    if n == 0:
        return "0"
    s = ""
    while n > 0:
        s = str(n % 2) + s      # remainder = next bit from the right
        n //= 2
    return s

def to_decimal(b):
    v = 0
    for ch in b:
        v = v * 2 + (1 if ch == '1' else 0)   # shift what we have, add the new bit
    return v

print(37, "->", to_binary(37))
print("100101", "->", to_decimal("100101"))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

string toBinary(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return "0";
    string s;
    while (n > 0) {
        s = char('0' + n % 2) + s;     // remainder = next bit from the right
        n /= 2;
    }
    return s;
}

int toDecimal(const string& b) {
    int v = 0;
    for (char ch : b) v = v * 2 + (ch == '1' ? 1 : 0);   // shift what we have, add the new bit
    return v;
}

int main() {
    cout << 37 << " -> " << toBinary(37) << "\n";
    cout << "100101" << " -> " << toDecimal("100101") << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static String toBinary(int n) {
        if (n == 0) return "0";
        StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder();
        while (n > 0) {
            s.insert(0, n % 2);        // remainder = next bit from the right
            n /= 2;
        }
        return s.toString();
    }

    static int toDecimal(String b) {
        int v = 0;
        for (char ch : b.toCharArray()) v = v * 2 + (ch == '1' ? 1 : 0);   // shift, add the new bit
        return v;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(37 + " -> " + toBinary(37));
        System.out.println("100101" + " -> " + toDecimal("100101"));
    }
}
JavaScript
function toBinary(n) {
    if (n === 0) return "0";
    let s = "";
    while (n > 0) {
        s = (n % 2) + s;              // remainder = next bit from the right
        n = Math.floor(n / 2);
    }
    return s;
}

function toDecimal(b) {
    let v = 0;
    for (const ch of b) v = v * 2 + (ch === '1' ? 1 : 0);   // shift what we have, add the new bit
    return v;
}

console.log(37, "->", toBinary(37));
console.log("100101", "->", toDecimal("100101"));
Output
37 -> 100101
100101 -> 37
Key point

The built-ins do the same: Python bin(37) / int('100101', 2), C++ bitset<8>(37) / stoi(s, nullptr, 2), Java Integer.toBinaryString(37) / Integer.parseInt(s, 2), JavaScript (37).toString(2) / parseInt(s, 2).

Check whether the kth bit is set
Example

Input: n = 5, k = 1
Output: Yes
Input: n = 5, k = 2
Output: No
Input: n = 5, k = 3
Output: Yes

Bits are counted from the right, so the kth bit (1-based) is the mask 1 << (k - 1); k must not exceed the width of n. Two equivalent ways:

Idea

Move the mask to the bit: n & (1 << (k-1)) keeps only bit k; the result is non-zero exactly when that bit is 1. Or move the bit to the mask: (n >> (k-1)) & 1 drags bit k down to position 0 and reads it as 0 or 1.

Both methods look at the same bit
n = 5 = 0 1 0 1          k = 3 → mask 1 << 2 = 0 1 0 0
        k=4 3 2 1
n & mask = 0 1 0 0  ≠ 0  → bit 3 is set
n >> 2   = 0 0 0 1  & 1 = 1 → the same answer, read at position 0
Python
def is_kth_set_mask(n, k):
    return (n & (1 << (k - 1))) != 0     # way 1: move the mask to the bit

def is_kth_set_shift(n, k):
    return ((n >> (k - 1)) & 1) == 1     # way 2: move the bit to position 0

n = 5
print("n =", n, "->", format(n, "04b"))
for k in range(1, 5):
    print(f"k = {k}:", "Yes" if is_kth_set_mask(n, k) else "No",
          "Yes" if is_kth_set_shift(n, k) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <bitset>
using namespace std;

bool isKthSetMask(int n, int k) {
    return (n & (1 << (k - 1))) != 0;    // way 1: move the mask to the bit
}

bool isKthSetShift(int n, int k) {
    return ((n >> (k - 1)) & 1) == 1;    // way 2: move the bit to position 0
}

int main() {
    int n = 5;
    cout << "n = " << n << " -> " << bitset<4>(n) << "\n";
    for (int k = 1; k <= 4; k++)
        cout << "k = " << k << ": " << (isKthSetMask(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No")
             << " " << (isKthSetShift(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static boolean isKthSetMask(int n, int k) {
        return (n & (1 << (k - 1))) != 0;    // way 1: move the mask to the bit
    }

    static boolean isKthSetShift(int n, int k) {
        return ((n >> (k - 1)) & 1) == 1;    // way 2: move the bit to position 0
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 5;
        String b = String.format("%4s", Integer.toBinaryString(n)).replace(' ', '0');
        System.out.println("n = " + n + " -> " + b);
        for (int k = 1; k <= 4; k++)
            System.out.println("k = " + k + ": " + (isKthSetMask(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No")
                               + " " + (isKthSetShift(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
function isKthSetMask(n, k) {
    return (n & (1 << (k - 1))) !== 0;   // way 1: move the mask to the bit
}

function isKthSetShift(n, k) {
    return ((n >> (k - 1)) & 1) === 1;   // way 2: move the bit to position 0
}

const n = 5;
console.log("n =", n, "->", n.toString(2).padStart(4, "0"));
for (let k = 1; k <= 4; k++)
    console.log(`k = ${k}:`, isKthSetMask(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No", isKthSetShift(n, k) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output
n = 5 -> 0101
k = 1: Yes Yes
k = 2: No No
k = 3: Yes Yes
k = 4: No No
Time O(1)Space O(1)
Key point

Way 2 is the one to use when you want the bit's value (0/1) rather than a yes/no — e.g. when reading a number bit by bit. Both are a single AND plus a shift.

Pitfall

if n & (1 << (k-1)) == 1 is wrong for k > 1: the AND leaves the bit in place, so the result is 4 for k = 3, not 1. Compare with != 0 (or use the shift form). Also, in C++ 1 << 31 overflows a signed int — use 1u << k or 1LL << k for high bits.

Count set bits
Example

Input: n = 5
Output: 2
Input: n = 13
Output: 3
Input: n = 255
Output: 8

The number of 1 bits is also called the population count or Hamming weight. There are four standard ways, from obvious to fastest.

Naive: walk the bits from LSB to MSB — n % 2 (or n & 1) reads the lowest bit, n // 2 (or n >> 1) drops it. Runs once per bit, set or not.

Python
def count_bits(n):
    res = 0
    while n:
        res += n & 1          # 1 if the lowest bit is set
        n >>= 1               # drop it
    return res

for n in (9, 13, 255, 1023):
    print(n, "->", count_bits(n))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int countBits(int n) {
    int res = 0;
    while (n) {
        res += n & 1;         // 1 if the lowest bit is set
        n >>= 1;              // drop it
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    for (int n : {9, 13, 255, 1023}) cout << n << " -> " << countBits(n) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int countBits(int n) {
        int res = 0;
        while (n != 0) {
            res += n & 1;     // 1 if the lowest bit is set
            n >>>= 1;         // logical shift so a negative n also terminates
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int n : new int[]{9, 13, 255, 1023}) System.out.println(n + " -> " + countBits(n));
    }
}
JavaScript
function countBits(n) {
    let res = 0;
    while (n !== 0) {
        res += n & 1;         // 1 if the lowest bit is set
        n >>>= 1;             // logical shift so a negative n also terminates
    }
    return res;
}

for (const n of [9, 13, 255, 1023]) console.log(n, "->", countBits(n));
Output
9 -> 2
13 -> 3
255 -> 8
1023 -> 10
Time O(number of bits) = O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

With an arithmetic shift (>>) a negative n never reaches zero — -1 >> 1 is still -1 — so the loop runs forever. Use the logical shift (>>> in Java/JS, cast to unsigned in C++) or loop a fixed 32 times. Python's n >>= 1 on a negative number has the same problem.

Brian Kernighan's algorithm: n & (n - 1) clears the rightmost set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position. For a sparse number it is much faster.

Subtracting 1 flips the rightmost 1 and every 0 after it; AND-ing keeps everything to its left
n = 13:   1101
1101 & 1100 = 1100   (12)   rightmost 1 cleared → count 1
1100 & 1011 = 1000   ( 8)                       → count 2
1000 & 0111 = 0000   ( 0)                       → count 3, stop
Python
def count_bits(n):
    res = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1            # clears the rightmost set bit
        res += 1
    return res

for n in (9, 13, 255, 1023):
    print(n, "->", count_bits(n))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int countBits(int n) {
    int res = 0;
    while (n) {
        n &= n - 1;           // clears the rightmost set bit
        res++;
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    for (int n : {9, 13, 255, 1023}) cout << n << " -> " << countBits(n) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int countBits(int n) {
        int res = 0;
        while (n != 0) {
            n &= n - 1;       // clears the rightmost set bit
            res++;
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int n : new int[]{9, 13, 255, 1023}) System.out.println(n + " -> " + countBits(n));
    }
}
JavaScript
function countBits(n) {
    let res = 0;
    while (n !== 0) {
        n &= n - 1;           // clears the rightmost set bit
        res++;
    }
    return res;
}

for (const n of [9, 13, 255, 1023]) console.log(n, "->", countBits(n));
Output
9 -> 2
13 -> 3
255 -> 8
1023 -> 10
Time O(number of set bits)Space O(1)

Lookup table: precompute the count for every byte value 0…255 once (O(1), it is a constant 256 entries), then a 32-bit number is just four table reads. Each entry is built from a smaller one: tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1].

Python
tbl = [0] * 256
for i in range(1, 256):
    tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1]      # lowest bit + count of the rest

def count_bits(n):                      # 32-bit n: four bytes
    return (tbl[n & 0xff] + tbl[(n >> 8) & 0xff]
            + tbl[(n >> 16) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >> 24) & 0xff])

for n in (9, 13, 255, 1023):
    print(n, "->", count_bits(n))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int tbl[256];

void initialize() {
    for (int i = 1; i < 256; i++) tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1];   // lowest bit + count of the rest
}

int countBits(unsigned n) {             // unsigned: >> never drags a sign bit in
    return tbl[n & 0xff] + tbl[(n >> 8) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >> 16) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >> 24) & 0xff];
}

int main() {
    initialize();
    for (int n : {9, 13, 255, 1023}) cout << n << " -> " << countBits(n) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int[] tbl = new int[256];

    static void initialize() {
        for (int i = 1; i < 256; i++) tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1];   // lowest bit + count of the rest
    }

    static int countBits(int n) {       // >>> so a negative n gives the right 32-bit answer
        return tbl[n & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 8) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 16) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 24) & 0xff];
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        initialize();
        for (int n : new int[]{9, 13, 255, 1023}) System.out.println(n + " -> " + countBits(n));
    }
}
JavaScript
const tbl = new Array(256).fill(0);
for (let i = 1; i < 256; i++) tbl[i] = (i & 1) + tbl[i >> 1];   // lowest bit + count of the rest

function countBits(n) {                 // >>> so a negative n gives the right 32-bit answer
    return tbl[n & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 8) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 16) & 0xff] + tbl[(n >>> 24) & 0xff];
}

for (const n of [9, 13, 255, 1023]) console.log(n, "->", countBits(n));
Output
9 -> 2
13 -> 3
255 -> 8
1023 -> 10
Time O(1) — four lookupsSpace O(1) — a fixed 256-entry table

Built-ins: in production code use the library — it compiles to a single popcnt instruction where the CPU has one.

Python
for n in (9, 13, 255, 1023):
    print(n, "->", n.bit_count())        # Python 3.10+; older: bin(n).count("1")

int main() {
    for (int n : {9, 13, 255, 1023})
        cout << n << " -> " << popcount(static_cast<unsigned>(n)) << "\n";   // C++20; or __builtin_popcount(n)
}
Java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int n : new int[]{9, 13, 255, 1023})
            System.out.println(n + " -> " + Integer.bitCount(n));          // Long.bitCount for long
    }

for (const n of [9, 13, 255, 1023])
    console.log(n, "->", n.toString(2).split("1").length - 1);   // no popcount in JS: count '1's in the binary string

255 -> 8

Is n a power of 2?
Example

Input: n = 4
Output: Yes
Input: n = 6
Output: No
Input: n = 0
Output: No

Naive: keep halving while n is even; it is a power of two if you end at exactly 1. O(log n).

Python
def is_power_of_two(n):
    if n == 0:
        return False
    while n != 1:
        if n % 2 != 0:          # an odd number above 1 cannot be a power of two
            return False
        n //= 2
    return True

for n in (4, 0, 1, 6, 1024):
    print(n, "->", "Yes" if is_power_of_two(n) else "No")
Output
4 -> Yes
0 -> No
1 -> Yes
6 -> No
1024 -> Yes
Idea

A power of two has exactly one set bit (1, 10, 100, 1000…). n & (n - 1) clears the rightmost set bit, so for a power of two it leaves 0; any other positive number still has a bit left. n = 0 has no set bit at all and must be rejected separately — 0 & (0 - 1) is also 0.

Python
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n != 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0     # exactly one set bit

for n in (4, 0, 1, 6, 1024):
    print(n, "->", "Yes" if is_power_of_two(n) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

bool isPowerOfTwo(int n) {
    return n != 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;      // exactly one set bit
}

int main() {
    for (int n : {4, 0, 1, 6, 1024})
        cout << n << " -> " << (isPowerOfTwo(n) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static boolean isPowerOfTwo(int n) {
        return n != 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;  // exactly one set bit
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int n : new int[]{4, 0, 1, 6, 1024})
            System.out.println(n + " -> " + (isPowerOfTwo(n) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
function isPowerOfTwo(n) {
    return n !== 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0;    // exactly one set bit
}

for (const n of [4, 0, 1, 6, 1024])
    console.log(n, "->", isPowerOfTwo(n) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output
4 -> Yes
0 -> No
1 -> Yes
6 -> No
1024 -> Yes
Time O(1)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Two edge cases: n = 0 passes the n & (n-1) == 0 test but is not a power of two, and a negative n such as -2147483648 (INT_MIN, a single set bit in 32 bits) also passes. Write n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 when negatives are possible.

Find the one odd-occurring element
Example

Input: arr = [10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20]
Output: 20
Input: arr = [4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]
Output: 3

Every element appears an even number of times except one. Naive: for each element count its occurrences with a second loop and return the first with an odd count — O(n²).

Python
def find_odd(arr):
    for x in arr:
        count = 0
        for y in arr:               # O(n) count for each of the n elements
            if x == y:
                count += 1
        if count % 2 == 1:
            return x
    return -1

print(find_odd([10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20]))
print(find_odd([4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]))
Output
20
3
Idea

XOR is commutative and associative, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. XOR-ing the whole array therefore lets every pair cancel itself regardless of order, and the only thing left standing is the element that had no partner.

Pairs cancel to 0; 0 is the XOR identity
  10 ^ 30 ^ 30 ^ 10 ^ 30 ^ 30 ^ 20
= (10 ^ 10) ^ (30 ^ 30) ^ (30 ^ 30) ^ 20      reorder: XOR is commutative
=    0      ^    0      ^    0      ^ 20
= 20
Python
def find_odd(arr):
    res = 0
    for x in arr:
        res ^= x              # pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
    return res

for arr in ([10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20], [4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]):
    print(" ".join(map(str, arr)), "->", find_odd(arr))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int findOdd(const vector<int>& arr) {
    int res = 0;
    for (int x : arr) res ^= x;      // pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> tests = {{10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20}, {4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5}};
    for (const auto& arr : tests) {
        for (int x : arr) cout << x << " ";
        cout << "-> " << findOdd(arr) << "\n";
    }
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int findOdd(int[] arr) {
        int res = 0;
        for (int x : arr) res ^= x;  // pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20}, {4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5}};
        for (int[] arr : tests) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int x : arr) sb.append(x).append(' ');
            System.out.println(sb + "-> " + findOdd(arr));
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function findOdd(arr) {
    let res = 0;
    for (const x of arr) res ^= x;   // pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
    return res;
}

for (const arr of [[10, 30, 30, 10, 30, 30, 20], [4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]])
    console.log(arr.join(" "), "->", findOdd(arr));
Output
10 30 30 10 30 30 20 -> 20
4 3 4 4 4 5 5 -> 3
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

The same trick solves missing number (XOR 1…n with the array — the missing value survives) and find the element that appears once while the rest appear twice. It fails when more than one element is odd-occurring — the result is the XOR of all of them — which is exactly the next problem.

Find the two odd-occurring elements
Example

Input: arr = [3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7]
Output: 5 6
Input: arr = [20, 15, 20, 16]
Output: 15 16

Now exactly two elements, x and y, occur an odd number of times. XOR-ing everything gives x ^ y, which is not enough on its own — we need to separate them.

Idea

x ^ y has a 1 exactly where x and y differ. Take its rightmost set bit, sn = xors & -xors. Partition the array into elements that have that bit set and elements that do not: x lands in one group and y in the other, and every paired element lands in the same group as its partner. XOR each group separately and the pairs cancel again, leaving x in one group and y in the other.

The rightmost differing bit splits the two odd elements into different groups
arr = 3 4 3 4 5 4 4 6 7 7
XOR of all      = 5 ^ 6 = 101 ^ 110 = 011          (every pair cancels)
rightmost 1 bit = 011 & -011 = 001                 (5 and 6 differ in bit 0)

bit 0 set   : 3 3 5 7 7   → XOR = 5
bit 0 clear : 4 4 4 4 6   → XOR = 6
Python
def two_odd(arr):
    xors = 0
    for x in arr:
        xors ^= x                 # = x ^ y
    sn = xors & -xors             # rightmost set bit (same as xors & ~(xors - 1))
    res1 = res2 = 0
    for x in arr:
        if x & sn:
            res1 ^= x             # group with the bit set
        else:
            res2 ^= x             # group with the bit clear
    return min(res1, res2), max(res1, res2)

for arr in ([3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7], [20, 15, 20, 16]):
    a, b = two_odd(arr)
    print(" ".join(map(str, arr)), "->", a, b)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

pair<int, int> twoOdd(const vector<int>& arr) {
    int xors = 0;
    for (int x : arr) xors ^= x;        // = x ^ y
    int sn = xors & -xors;              // rightmost set bit (same as xors & ~(xors - 1))
    int res1 = 0, res2 = 0;
    for (int x : arr) {
        if (x & sn) res1 ^= x;          // group with the bit set
        else        res2 ^= x;          // group with the bit clear
    }
    return {min(res1, res2), max(res1, res2)};
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> tests = {{3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7}, {20, 15, 20, 16}};
    for (const auto& arr : tests) {
        for (int x : arr) cout << x << " ";
        auto [a, b] = twoOdd(arr);
        cout << "-> " << a << " " << b << "\n";
    }
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int[] twoOdd(int[] arr) {
        int xors = 0;
        for (int x : arr) xors ^= x;    // = x ^ y
        int sn = xors & -xors;          // rightmost set bit (same as xors & ~(xors - 1))
        int res1 = 0, res2 = 0;
        for (int x : arr) {
            if ((x & sn) != 0) res1 ^= x;   // group with the bit set
            else               res2 ^= x;   // group with the bit clear
        }
        return new int[]{Math.min(res1, res2), Math.max(res1, res2)};
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7}, {20, 15, 20, 16}};
        for (int[] arr : tests) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int x : arr) sb.append(x).append(' ');
            int[] r = twoOdd(arr);
            System.out.println(sb + "-> " + r[0] + " " + r[1]);
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function twoOdd(arr) {
    let xors = 0;
    for (const x of arr) xors ^= x;     // = x ^ y
    const sn = xors & -xors;            // rightmost set bit (same as xors & ~(xors - 1))
    let res1 = 0, res2 = 0;
    for (const x of arr) {
        if (x & sn) res1 ^= x;          // group with the bit set
        else        res2 ^= x;          // group with the bit clear
    }
    return [Math.min(res1, res2), Math.max(res1, res2)];
}

for (const arr of [[3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7], [20, 15, 20, 16]]) {
    const [a, b] = twoOdd(arr);
    console.log(arr.join(" "), "->", a, b);
}
Output
3 4 3 4 5 4 4 6 7 7 -> 5 6
20 15 20 16 -> 15 16
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The two results come out in group order, not sorted — which group holds the smaller value depends on the bit chosen. Sort the pair (as above) or the output will look random. xors & -xors relies on two's complement: -xors is ~xors + 1, which agrees with xors only at the rightmost set bit.

Power set using bitmasks
Example

Input: s = "abc"
Output: {} {a} {b} {a,b} {c} {a,c} {b,c} {a,b,c}

Idea

A set of n elements has 2^n subsets, and there are exactly 2^n integers from 0 to 2^n - 1. Read each counter as a mask: bit j set means include s[j]. Looping the counter enumerates every subset exactly once, with no recursion.

The counter's bits choose the elements
s = "abc", n = 3, masks 0 … 7       (bit 0 ↔ a, bit 1 ↔ b, bit 2 ↔ c)

i    c b a    subset
0    0 0 0    {}
1    0 0 1    {a}
2    0 1 0    {b}
3    0 1 1    {a,b}
4    1 0 0    {c}
5    1 0 1    {a,c}
6    1 1 0    {b,c}
7    1 1 1    {a,b,c}
Python
def power_set(s):
    n = len(s)
    for i in range(1 << n):                      # 2^n masks
        chosen = [s[j] for j in range(n) if i & (1 << j)]   # bit j set → take s[j]
        print(format(i, f"0{n}b"), "-> {" + ",".join(chosen) + "}")

power_set("abc")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

void powerSet(const string& s) {
    int n = s.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < (1 << n); i++) {        // 2^n masks
        string mask, chosen;
        for (int j = n - 1; j >= 0; j--) mask += ((i >> j) & 1) ? '1' : '0';
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
            if (i & (1 << j)) {                  // bit j set → take s[j]
                if (!chosen.empty()) chosen += ',';
                chosen += s[j];
            }
        cout << mask << " -> {" << chosen << "}\n";
    }
}

int main() { powerSet("abc"); }
Java
public class Main {
    static void powerSet(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        for (int i = 0; i < (1 << n); i++) {    // 2^n masks
            StringBuilder mask = new StringBuilder(), chosen = new StringBuilder();
            for (int j = n - 1; j >= 0; j--) mask.append((i >> j) & 1);
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
                if ((i & (1 << j)) != 0) {       // bit j set → take s[j]
                    if (chosen.length() > 0) chosen.append(',');
                    chosen.append(s.charAt(j));
                }
            System.out.println(mask + " -> {" + chosen + "}");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { powerSet("abc"); }
}
JavaScript
function powerSet(s) {
    const n = s.length;
    for (let i = 0; i < (1 << n); i++) {        // 2^n masks
        const chosen = [];
        for (let j = 0; j < n; j++)
            if (i & (1 << j)) chosen.push(s[j]); // bit j set → take s[j]
        console.log(i.toString(2).padStart(n, "0"), "-> {" + chosen.join(",") + "}");
    }
}

powerSet("abc");
Output
000 -> {}
001 -> {a}
010 -> {b}
011 -> {a,b}
100 -> {c}
101 -> {a,c}
110 -> {b,c}
111 -> {a,b,c}
Time O(2^n · n)Space O(n) for the current subset
Key point

Bitmasks are the standard way to iterate over subsets in bitmask DP (travelling salesman, assignment problems): the mask is the state, mask | (1 << j) adds an element, mask & ~(1 << j) removes one, and __builtin_popcount(mask) tells how many are chosen. The recursive include/exclude version of this problem is in the Recursion topic.

Interview Q&A
Why does n & (n - 1) clear the rightmost set bit?

Subtracting 1 borrows from the rightmost 1: that bit becomes 0 and every 0 to its right becomes 1; the bits to its left are untouched. AND-ing with n keeps the untouched left part and zeroes everything from that bit rightwards. Example: 12 = 1100, 11 = 1011, 12 & 11 = 1000.

How do you check if two integers have opposite signs without comparing them?

(x ^ y) < 0. The sign bit of the XOR is 1 exactly when the sign bits differ. Related: x and y have the same parity iff ((x ^ y) & 1) == 0.

What is the difference between >> and >>>?

>> is an arithmetic shift: the sign bit is copied into the vacated positions, so -16 >> 2 = -4 (floor division). >>> (Java, JavaScript) is a logical shift that fills with zeros, so -16 >>> 2 is 1073741820 — the number reinterpreted as unsigned. C++ gets the logical behaviour by casting to unsigned; Python has unbounded ints, so mask to a width first.

Every element appears three times except one. Does XOR still work?

Plain XOR does not, because x ^ x ^ x = x — triples do not cancel. Count the set bits per position: each of the 32 positions has a count that is a multiple of 3 plus the lone element's bit, so count % 3 rebuilds the answer in O(32·n). Alternatively use two accumulators (ones, twos) that act as a mod-3 counter per bit.

How would you find the missing number in 1…n with one slot missing, without extra space?

XOR all numbers 1…n and XOR all array elements; everything present cancels and the missing number remains. The sum formula n(n+1)/2 − sum(arr) also works but can overflow a 32-bit int for large n, which XOR never does.

When is the lookup-table popcount actually better than Kernighan's loop?

When numbers are dense (many set bits) and you count millions of them: the table is a constant four array reads with no data-dependent branch, whereas Kernighan does one iteration per set bit (up to 32). For a few calls, or sparse numbers, the loop is simpler and just as fast. In real code use the built-in — it maps to the hardware popcnt instruction.

Arrays, Bits & Recursion

Recursion

Recursion solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance and trusting that call's answer. The problems here — rope cutting, subsets, Tower of Hanoi, Josephus, subset sum and permutations — are the templates for backtracking and dynamic programming later in the course.

Recursion — a function that calls itself with an input strictly closer to a base case, which is answered directly. Each active call lives in its own stack frame, so the maximum depth of the recursion is also the auxiliary space.

How a recursive call runs

Every call pushes a frame (parameters, locals, return address) on the call stack; the frame is popped when the call returns. Work written before the recursive call happens on the way down, work after it happens on the way up — the trace below shows both.

Python
def trace(n):
    if n == 0:                    # base case: answered without another call
        print("base case reached")
        return
    print("enter", n)             # on the way down
    trace(n - 1)                  # smaller instance
    print("exit", n)              # on the way up, after the sub-call finished

trace(3)
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void trace(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {                 // base case: answered without another call
        cout << "base case reached\n";
        return;
    }
    cout << "enter " << n << "\n";    // on the way down
    trace(n - 1);                     // smaller instance
    cout << "exit " << n << "\n";     // on the way up, after the sub-call finished
}

int main() { trace(3); }
Java
public class Main {
    static void trace(int n) {
        if (n == 0) {             // base case: answered without another call
            System.out.println("base case reached");
            return;
        }
        System.out.println("enter " + n);   // on the way down
        trace(n - 1);                       // smaller instance
        System.out.println("exit " + n);    // on the way up, after the sub-call finished
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { trace(3); }
}
JavaScript
function trace(n) {
    if (n === 0) {                // base case: answered without another call
        console.log("base case reached");
        return;
    }
    console.log("enter", n);      // on the way down
    trace(n - 1);                 // smaller instance
    console.log("exit", n);       // on the way up, after the sub-call finished
}

trace(3);
Output
enter 3
enter 2
enter 1
base case reached
exit 1
exit 2
exit 3
Depth 4 = O(n) auxiliary space, even though the function declares no arrays
trace(3)                         call stack (top is the running call)
 └ trace(2)                      ┌──────────┐
    └ trace(1)                   │ trace(0) │ ← base case, 4 frames deep
       └ trace(0)  base case     │ trace(1) │
                                 │ trace(2) │
                                 │ trace(3) │
                                 └──────────┘

Base case first

Without it the recursion never stops: Python raises RecursionError at ~1000 frames, C++/Java crash with a stack overflow.

Make progress

Every call must move strictly towards the base case (n-1, i+1, a shorter string).

Trust the sub-call

Assume f(n-1) is correct and only write how to build f(n) from it — the recursive leap of faith.

Count the tree

Time ≈ number of nodes in the recursion tree (branching^depth); space = its height.

Rope cutting problem
Example

Input: n = 5, a = 2, b = 5, c = 1
Output: 5
Input: n = 23, a = 12, b = 9, c = 11
Output: 2
Input: n = 5, a = 4, b = 2, c = 6
Output: -1

Cut a rope of length n into the maximum number of pieces, each of length a, b or c; return -1 if no exact division exists. For n = 23 the best is 12 + 11 (2 pieces); for n = 5 with c = 1 it is five unit pieces.

Idea

The first cut is a, b or c. Whichever it is, the rest of the rope is a smaller rope with the same question — so maxPieces(n) = 1 + max(maxPieces(n-a), maxPieces(n-b), maxPieces(n-c)). A rope of length 0 needs 0 more cuts (base case); a negative length means that cut overshoots and is reported as -1, which the max discards unless all three branches fail.

Three branches per node; a negative length is a dead branch (-1)
maxPieces(5)  a=2 b=5 c=1
├── maxPieces(3)   (cut 2)
│   ├── maxPieces(1)  → ├ (-1) → -1   ├ (-4) → -1   ├ (0) → 0     ⇒ 1
│   ├── maxPieces(-2) → -1
│   └── maxPieces(2)  → … ⇒ 2
│                                          ⇒ 1 + max(1, -1, 2) = 3
├── maxPieces(0)   (cut 5)  → 0            ⇒ 0 + 1 = 1
└── maxPieces(4)   (cut 1)  → … ⇒ 4        ⇒ 5
                                           answer = max(3, 1, 5) = 5
Python
def max_pieces(n, a, b, c):
    if n == 0:
        return 0                      # nothing left to cut: 0 more pieces
    if n < 0:
        return -1                     # this cut overshot the rope: invalid
    res = max(max_pieces(n - a, a, b, c),
              max_pieces(n - b, a, b, c),
              max_pieces(n - c, a, b, c))
    if res == -1:
        return -1                     # none of the three cuts can finish the rope
    return res + 1                    # +1 for the piece cut here

for n, a, b, c in ((5, 2, 5, 1), (23, 12, 9, 11), (5, 4, 2, 6)):
    print(f"n={n} a={a} b={b} c={c} ->", max_pieces(n, a, b, c))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int maxPieces(int n, int a, int b, int c) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;                 // nothing left to cut: 0 more pieces
    if (n < 0) return -1;                 // this cut overshot the rope: invalid
    int res = max({maxPieces(n - a, a, b, c),
                   maxPieces(n - b, a, b, c),
                   maxPieces(n - c, a, b, c)});
    if (res == -1) return -1;             // none of the three cuts can finish the rope
    return res + 1;                       // +1 for the piece cut here
}

int main() {
    int tests[3][4] = {{5, 2, 5, 1}, {23, 12, 9, 11}, {5, 4, 2, 6}};
    for (auto& t : tests)
        cout << "n=" << t[0] << " a=" << t[1] << " b=" << t[2] << " c=" << t[3]
             << " -> " << maxPieces(t[0], t[1], t[2], t[3]) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int maxPieces(int n, int a, int b, int c) {
        if (n == 0) return 0;             // nothing left to cut: 0 more pieces
        if (n < 0) return -1;             // this cut overshot the rope: invalid
        int res = Math.max(maxPieces(n - a, a, b, c),
                  Math.max(maxPieces(n - b, a, b, c), maxPieces(n - c, a, b, c)));
        if (res == -1) return -1;         // none of the three cuts can finish the rope
        return res + 1;                   // +1 for the piece cut here
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{5, 2, 5, 1}, {23, 12, 9, 11}, {5, 4, 2, 6}};
        for (int[] t : tests)
            System.out.println("n=" + t[0] + " a=" + t[1] + " b=" + t[2] + " c=" + t[3]
                               + " -> " + maxPieces(t[0], t[1], t[2], t[3]));
    }
}
JavaScript
function maxPieces(n, a, b, c) {
    if (n === 0) return 0;                // nothing left to cut: 0 more pieces
    if (n < 0) return -1;                 // this cut overshot the rope: invalid
    const res = Math.max(maxPieces(n - a, a, b, c),
                         maxPieces(n - b, a, b, c),
                         maxPieces(n - c, a, b, c));
    if (res === -1) return -1;            // none of the three cuts can finish the rope
    return res + 1;                       // +1 for the piece cut here
}

for (const [n, a, b, c] of [[5, 2, 5, 1], [23, 12, 9, 11], [5, 4, 2, 6]])
    console.log(`n=${n} a=${a} b=${b} c=${c} ->`, maxPieces(n, a, b, c));
Output
n=5 a=2 b=5 c=1 -> 5
n=23 a=12 b=9 c=11 -> 2
n=5 a=4 b=2 c=6 -> -1
Time O(3^n)Space O(n) recursion depth
Pitfall

Returning 0 for a negative length (instead of -1) silently counts an impossible cut as valid and over-reports the answer. Also note the massive overlap in the tree — maxPieces(2) is computed many times. Memoising on n turns this into the O(n) dynamic-programming solution in the DP topic.

Subsets of a string
Example

Input: s = "AB"
Output: "" B A AB
Input: s = "ABC"
Output: "" C B BC A AC AB ABC

Generate all 2^n subsets (subsequences keeping the original order) of a string of distinct characters.

Idea

Walk the string one index at a time. For s[i] there are exactly two choices — leave it out or put it in — and the rest of the string is the same problem. When the index reaches the end, the accumulated curr is one finished subset. Two choices at each of n levels gives 2^n leaves.

Depth n, 2^n leaves — one per subset. Exclude first, so the empty string is printed first
sub("", 0)                                       s = "ABC"
├── exclude A → sub("", 1)
│   ├── exclude B → sub("", 2)
│   │   ├── exclude C → ""      ✔
│   │   └── include C → "C"     ✔
│   └── include B → sub("B", 2)
│       ├── "B"  ✔     └── "BC" ✔
└── include A → sub("A", 1)
    ├── sub("A", 2)  → "A" ✔, "AC" ✔
    └── sub("AB", 2) → "AB" ✔, "ABC" ✔
Python
def subsets(s, curr, i, out):
    if i == len(s):
        out.append(curr if curr else '""')    # a finished subset
        return
    subsets(s, curr, i + 1, out)              # exclude s[i]
    subsets(s, curr + s[i], i + 1, out)       # include s[i]

for s in ("AB", "ABC"):
    out = []
    subsets(s, "", 0, out)
    print(s, "->", " ".join(out), f"({len(out)} subsets)")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void subsets(const string& s, string curr, int i, vector<string>& out) {
    if (i == (int)s.size()) {
        out.push_back(curr.empty() ? "\"\"" : curr);   // a finished subset
        return;
    }
    subsets(s, curr, i + 1, out);             // exclude s[i]
    subsets(s, curr + s[i], i + 1, out);      // include s[i]
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"AB", "ABC"}) {
        vector<string> out;
        subsets(s, "", 0, out);
        cout << s << " ->";
        for (const string& x : out) cout << " " << x;
        cout << " (" << out.size() << " subsets)\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static void subsets(String s, String curr, int i, List<String> out) {
        if (i == s.length()) {
            out.add(curr.isEmpty() ? "\"\"" : curr);  // a finished subset
            return;
        }
        subsets(s, curr, i + 1, out);                 // exclude s[i]
        subsets(s, curr + s.charAt(i), i + 1, out);   // include s[i]
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"AB", "ABC"}) {
            List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
            subsets(s, "", 0, out);
            System.out.println(s + " -> " + String.join(" ", out) + " (" + out.size() + " subsets)");
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function subsets(s, curr, i, out) {
    if (i === s.length) {
        out.push(curr === "" ? '""' : curr);  // a finished subset
        return;
    }
    subsets(s, curr, i + 1, out);             // exclude s[i]
    subsets(s, curr + s[i], i + 1, out);      // include s[i]
}

for (const s of ["AB", "ABC"]) {
    const out = [];
    subsets(s, "", 0, out);
    console.log(s, "->", out.join(" "), `(${out.length} subsets)`);
}
Output
AB -> "" B A AB (4 subsets)
ABC -> "" C B BC A AC AB ABC (8 subsets)
Time O(2^n · n)Space O(n) recursion depth (plus the output)
Key point

Swapping the two recursive calls (include first) lists ABC AB AC A BC B C "" instead — the set of subsets is the same, only the order changes. The iterative bitmask version of this problem is in Bit Magic → Power set using bitmasks. With repeated characters this prints duplicate subsets; sort the string and skip equal neighbours to avoid that.

Tower of Hanoi
Example

Input: n = 1
Output: Move disc 1 from A to C
Input: n = 2
Output: Move disc 1 from A to B / Move disc 2 from A to C / Move disc 1 from B to C

Move n discs from peg A (source) to peg C (destination) using peg B (auxiliary), under three rules:

  1. Only one disc moves at a time.
  2. A larger disc may never sit on a smaller one.
  3. Only the top disc of a peg can be moved.
n = 3: the whole tower must end on C in the same order
    A          B          C                 A          B          C
    |          |          |                 |          |          |
   ═╪═         |          |      →          |          |         ═╪═
  ══╪══        |          |                 |          |        ══╪══
 ═══╪═══       |          |                 |          |       ═══╪═══
────┴──────────┴──────────┴──          ────┴──────────┴──────────┴──
Idea

To move n discs A → C, the biggest disc n can only move when the other n-1 discs are out of the way on B. So: move n-1 discs A → B (using C as spare), move disc n A → C, then move the n-1 discs B → C (using A as spare). The recursion is the same problem with the pegs relabelled — that is why the function takes the three pegs as parameters.

1
TOH(n-1, A, C, B)
Park the top n-1 discs on the auxiliary peg B, using C as the spare.
2
Move disc n from A to C
The largest disc makes its single move onto the empty destination.
3
TOH(n-1, B, A, C)
Bring the n-1 discs from B onto C, using A as the spare.
moves(n) = 2 · moves(n−1) + 1 = 2^n − 1 (3 discs → 7, 10 discs → 1023, 64 discs → 1.8 × 10^19)
Python
def toh(n, src, aux, dst):
    if n == 0:
        return 0                              # no discs: no moves
    moves = toh(n - 1, src, dst, aux)         # park n-1 discs on the auxiliary peg
    print(f"Move disc {n} from {src} to {dst}")
    moves += 1 + toh(n - 1, aux, src, dst)    # bring them onto the destination
    return moves

for n in (2, 3):
    print("n =", n)
    print("moves:", toh(n, "A", "B", "C"))
C++

    int moves = toh(n - 1, src, dst, aux);        // park n-1 discs on the auxiliary peg
    cout << "Move disc " << n << " from " << src << " to " << dst << "\n";
    moves += 1 + toh(n - 1, aux, src, dst);       // bring them onto the destination
    return moves;
}

        cout << "n = " << n << "\n";

}

Time O(2^n) movesSpace O(n) recursion depth
Pitfall

The classic slip is the peg order in the two recursive calls. With the signature TOH(n, source, auxiliary, destination) the first call is TOH(n-1, A, C, B) (destination becomes the spare) and the second is TOH(n-1, B, A, C) (source becomes the spare). Using n == 1 as the base case also works; n == 0 avoids a special-cased print.

Josephus problem (elimination game)
Example

Input: n = 7, k = 3
Output: 3
Input: n = 8, k = 2
Output: 0

n people stand in a circle numbered 0 … n-1. Starting at 0, every kth person is eliminated and the count restarts from the next person. Which position survives?

Idea

After the first elimination (k-1 is removed), the circle has n-1 people and the count restarts at position k. If we renumber so that position k becomes 0, the remaining game is exactly josephus(n-1, k). Its survivor j in the renumbered circle sits at (j + k) % n in the original one — hence jos(n, k) = (jos(n-1, k) + k) % n, with jos(1, k) = 0.

Unwinding the recursion from the base case up
jos(1,3) = 0
jos(2,3) = (0 + 3) % 2 = 1
jos(3,3) = (1 + 3) % 3 = 1
jos(4,3) = (1 + 3) % 4 = 0
jos(5,3) = (0 + 3) % 5 = 3
jos(6,3) = (3 + 3) % 6 = 0
jos(7,3) = (0 + 3) % 7 = 3     ← survivor for n = 7, k = 3
Python
def josephus(n, k):
    if n == 1:
        return 0                          # one person left: position 0 survives
    return (josephus(n - 1, k) + k) % n   # shift the smaller game's answer back by k

for n, k in ((7, 3), (8, 2), (5, 2)):
    print(f"n={n} k={k} ->", josephus(n, k))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int josephus(int n, int k) {
    if (n == 1) return 0;                     // one person left: position 0 survives
    return (josephus(n - 1, k) + k) % n;      // shift the smaller game's answer back by k
}

int main() {
    int tests[3][2] = {{7, 3}, {8, 2}, {5, 2}};
    for (auto& t : tests)
        cout << "n=" << t[0] << " k=" << t[1] << " -> " << josephus(t[0], t[1]) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {

        if (n == 1) return 0;                 // one person left: position 0 survives
        return (josephus(n - 1, k) + k) % n;  // shift the smaller game's answer back by k
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{7, 3}, {8, 2}, {5, 2}};
        for (int[] t : tests)
            System.out.println("n=" + t[0] + " k=" + t[1] + " -> " + josephus(t[0], t[1]));
    }
}

    if (n === 1) return 0;                    // one person left: position 0 survives
    return (josephus(n - 1, k) + k) % n;      // shift the smaller game's answer back by k
}

for (const [n, k] of [[7, 3], [8, 2], [5, 2]])
    console.log(`n=${n} k=${k} ->`, josephus(n, k));
Output
n=7 k=3 -> 3
n=8 k=2 -> 0
n=5 k=2 -> 2
Time O(n)Space O(n) recursion depth — or O(1) with a loop

To see the eliminations, simulate the circle with a list: the next victim is (idx + k - 1) % size and the count resumes at that index.

Python
def simulate(n, k):
    people = list(range(n))
    idx = 0
    while len(people) > 1:
        idx = (idx + k - 1) % len(people)     # count k people from idx, wrapping around
        removed = people.pop(idx)             # the next person now sits at idx
        print("remove", removed, "-> left:", " ".join(map(str, people)))
    print("survivor:", people[0])

simulate(7, 3)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void simulate(int n, int k) {
    vector<int> people;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) people.push_back(i);
    int idx = 0;
    while (people.size() > 1) {
        int size = people.size();
        idx = (idx + k - 1) % size;               // count k people from idx, wrapping around
        int removed = people[idx];
        people.erase(people.begin() + idx);       // the next person now sits at idx
        cout << "remove " << removed << " -> left:";
        for (int x : people) cout << " " << x;
        cout << "\n";
    }
    cout << "survivor: " << people[0] << "\n";
}

int main() { simulate(7, 3); }
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static void simulate(int n, int k) {
        List<Integer> people = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) people.add(i);
        int idx = 0;
        while (people.size() > 1) {
            idx = (idx + k - 1) % people.size();  // count k people from idx, wrapping around
            int removed = people.remove(idx);     // the next person now sits at idx
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int x : people) sb.append(' ').append(x);
            System.out.println("remove " + removed + " -> left:" + sb);
        }
        System.out.println("survivor: " + people.get(0));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { simulate(7, 3); }
}
JavaScript
function simulate(n, k) {
    const people = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
    let idx = 0;
    while (people.length > 1) {
        idx = (idx + k - 1) % people.length;      // count k people from idx, wrapping around
        const [removed] = people.splice(idx, 1);  // the next person now sits at idx
        console.log("remove", removed, "-> left:", people.join(" "));
    }
    console.log("survivor:", people[0]);
}

simulate(7, 3);
Output
remove 2 -> left: 0 1 3 4 5 6
remove 5 -> left: 0 1 3 4 6
remove 1 -> left: 0 3 4 6
remove 6 -> left: 0 3 4
remove 4 -> left: 0 3
remove 0 -> left: 3
survivor: 3
Time O(n²) with list deletion, O(n · k) with a linked circleSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Mixing up 0-based and 1-based numbering. The formula above returns a 0-based position; if the people are numbered 1 … n the survivor is jos(n, k) + 1 (for n = 7, k = 3 that is 4). Also people.remove(idx) in Java must receive an int, not an Integer — remove(Integer) removes by value.

Subset sum (count the subsets)
Example

Input: arr = [10, 5, 2, 3, 6], sum = 8
Output: 2
Input: arr = [10, 20, 15], sum = 0
Output: 1

Count the subsets of arr whose elements add up to sum. For {10, 5, 2, 3, 6} and 8 there are two: {5, 3} and {2, 6}. For sum = 0 the empty subset always counts, so the answer is at least 1.

Idea

Look at the last element arr[n-1]. Either it is left out — count the subsets of the first n-1 elements that reach sum — or it is taken — count those that reach sum - arr[n-1]. Add the two. With no elements left (n == 0) there is exactly one subset, the empty one, and it works only if the remaining sum is 0.

Each leaf with sum 0 is one valid subset
count(n=3, sum=3)   arr = {1, 2, 3}
├── exclude 3 → count(2, 3)
│   ├── exclude 2 → count(1, 3) → count(0,3)=0, count(0,2)=0          ⇒ 0
│   └── include 2 → count(1, 1) → count(0,1)=0, count(0,0)=1  {1,2}  ⇒ 1
└── include 3 → count(2, 0)
    ├── exclude 2 → count(1, 0) → count(0,0)=1  {3}, count(0,-1)=0   ⇒ 1
    └── include 2 → count(1,-2) → 0                                   ⇒ 0
                                                               total = 2
Python
def count_subsets(arr, n, target):
    if n == 0:
        return 1 if target == 0 else 0            # empty subset: valid only if nothing is left to reach
    return (count_subsets(arr, n - 1, target)                 # exclude arr[n-1]
            + count_subsets(arr, n - 1, target - arr[n - 1]))  # include arr[n-1]

for arr, target in (([10, 5, 2, 3, 6], 8), ([10, 20, 15], 0), ([1, 2, 3], 3)):
    print(" ".join(map(str, arr)), "| sum", target, "->", count_subsets(arr, len(arr), target))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int countSubsets(const vector<int>& arr, int n, int target) {
    if (n == 0) return target == 0 ? 1 : 0;       // empty subset: valid only if nothing is left to reach
    return countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target)                   // exclude arr[n-1]
         + countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target - arr[n - 1]);     // include arr[n-1]
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<vector<int>, int>> tests = {{{10, 5, 2, 3, 6}, 8}, {{10, 20, 15}, 0}, {{1, 2, 3}, 3}};
    for (auto& [arr, target] : tests) {
        for (int x : arr) cout << x << " ";
        cout << "| sum " << target << " -> " << countSubsets(arr, arr.size(), target) << "\n";
    }
}

public class Main {
    static int countSubsets(int[] arr, int n, int target) {
        if (n == 0) return target == 0 ? 1 : 0;   // empty subset: valid only if nothing is left to reach
        return countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target)               // exclude arr[n-1]
             + countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target - arr[n - 1]); // include arr[n-1]
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] arrays = {{10, 5, 2, 3, 6}, {10, 20, 15}, {1, 2, 3}};
        int[] targets = {8, 0, 3};
        for (int t = 0; t < arrays.length; t++) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int x : arrays[t]) sb.append(x).append(' ');
            System.out.println(sb + "| sum " + targets[t] + " -> "
                               + countSubsets(arrays[t], arrays[t].length, targets[t]));
        }

}
JavaScript
function countSubsets(arr, n, target) {
    if (n === 0) return target === 0 ? 1 : 0;     // empty subset: valid only if nothing is left to reach
    return countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target)                   // exclude arr[n-1]
         + countSubsets(arr, n - 1, target - arr[n - 1]);     // include arr[n-1]
}

for (const [arr, target] of [[[10, 5, 2, 3, 6], 8], [[10, 20, 15], 0], [[1, 2, 3], 3]])
    console.log(arr.join(" "), "| sum", target, "->", countSubsets(arr, arr.length, target));
Output
10 5 2 3 6 | sum 8 -> 2
10 20 15 | sum 0 -> 1
1 2 3 | sum 3 -> 2
Time O(2^n)Space O(n) recursion depth
Key point

Pruning target < 0 (return 0 early) is safe only when all elements are non-negative. The same recurrence, memoised on (n, target), is the O(n · sum) subset-sum DP; replacing + with or answers the decision version (does any subset reach the sum?).

Print all permutations of a string
Example

Input: s = "AB"
Output: AB BA
Input: s = "ABC"
Output: ABC ACB BAC BCA CBA CAB

Print every arrangement of the characters of s — there are n! of them for n distinct characters.

Idea

Fix position i by trying every character from i to the end in that slot (swap it in), recursively permute the rest i+1 … n-1, then swap it back so the next candidate starts from the original arrangement. The swap-back is what makes this backtracking: the shared array is restored after every choice.

n choices at level 0, n−1 at level 1, … → n! leaves. Note the order is not alphabetical
permute(ABC, i=0)
├── swap(0,0) → A|BC  permute(i=1)
│                ├── swap(1,1) → AB|C → ABC ✔
│                └── swap(1,2) → AC|B → ACB ✔   (swap back → ABC)
├── swap(0,1) → B|AC  permute(i=1)
│                ├── BAC ✔
│                └── BCA ✔                       (swap back → ABC)
└── swap(0,2) → C|BA  permute(i=1)
                 ├── CBA ✔
                 └── CAB ✔                       (swap back → ABC)
Python
def permute(chars, i, out):
    n = len(chars)
    if i == n - 1:
        out.append("".join(chars))            # every position fixed: one permutation
        return
    for j in range(i, n):
        chars[i], chars[j] = chars[j], chars[i]   # choose chars[j] for position i
        permute(chars, i + 1, out)
        chars[i], chars[j] = chars[j], chars[i]   # backtrack: undo the swap

for s in ("AB", "ABC"):
    out = []
    permute(list(s), 0, out)
    print(s, "->", " ".join(out))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

void permute(string& s, int i, vector<string>& out) {
    int n = s.size();
    if (i == n - 1) {
        out.push_back(s);                     // every position fixed: one permutation
        return;
    }
    for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
        swap(s[i], s[j]);                     // choose s[j] for position i
        permute(s, i + 1, out);
        swap(s[i], s[j]);                     // backtrack: undo the swap
    }
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"AB", "ABC"}) {
        vector<string> out;
        string work = s;
        permute(work, 0, out);
        cout << s << " ->";
        for (const string& p : out) cout << " " << p;
        cout << "\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static void permute(char[] s, int i, List<String> out) {
        int n = s.length;
        if (i == n - 1) {
            out.add(new String(s));           // every position fixed: one permutation
            return;
        }
        for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
            char t = s[i]; s[i] = s[j]; s[j] = t;   // choose s[j] for position i
            permute(s, i + 1, out);
            t = s[i]; s[i] = s[j]; s[j] = t;        // backtrack: undo the swap
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"AB", "ABC"}) {
            List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
            permute(s.toCharArray(), 0, out);
            System.out.println(s + " -> " + String.join(" ", out));
        }
    }
}
JavaScript
function permute(chars, i, out) {
    const n = chars.length;
    if (i === n - 1) {
        out.push(chars.join(""));             // every position fixed: one permutation
        return;
    }
    for (let j = i; j < n; j++) {
        [chars[i], chars[j]] = [chars[j], chars[i]];   // choose chars[j] for position i
        permute(chars, i + 1, out);
        [chars[i], chars[j]] = [chars[j], chars[i]];   // backtrack: undo the swap
    }
}

for (const s of ["AB", "ABC"]) {
    const out = [];
    permute([...s], 0, out);
    console.log(s, "->", out.join(" "));
}
Output
AB -> AB BA
ABC -> ABC ACB BAC BCA CBA CAB
Time O(n! · n)Space O(n) recursion depth, swapping in place
Pitfall

Forgetting the second swap corrupts the array for the next j and produces duplicates and missing permutations. The in-place swap uses no extra array, but the auxiliary space is still O(n) because of the recursion depth — not O(1). With repeated characters ("AAB") this prints duplicates; skip a j whose character was already tried at this position, or use a frequency map.

Recursion trees at a glance

The cost of a recursive solution is read off its tree: time is roughly the number of nodes (branching factor to the power of the depth), auxiliary space is the height. Overlapping subproblems (the same node appearing many times) are the signal to memoise.

ProblemBranchingDepthTimeAux spaceOverlap?
Rope cutting3n / min(a,b,c)O(3^n)O(n)yes → DP O(n)
Subsets of a string2nO(2^n · n)O(n)no — every leaf is a distinct answer
Tower of Hanoi2nO(2^n)O(n)no — every move is output
Josephus1nO(n)O(n) (loop: O(1))—
Subset sum count2nO(2^n)O(n)yes → DP O(n · sum)
Permutationsn, n-1, …, 1nO(n! · n)O(n)no — every leaf is a distinct answer
Depth limits

Each language limits recursion depth: Python stops at about 1000 frames (sys.setrecursionlimit raises it, but the C stack still overflows around tens of thousands), Java and C++ overflow their thread stack at roughly 10^4–10^5 frames depending on frame size, Node around 10^4. A linear recursion over n = 10^5 elements must be rewritten as a loop or use an explicit stack.

Interview Q&A
What are the two things every recursive function needs?

A base case that returns without recursing, and a recursive case whose argument is strictly closer to the base case. Missing or unreachable base cases give infinite recursion; a recursive case that does not shrink the input (e.g. f(n) calling f(n)) does the same.

What is tail recursion, and does it help?

A call is tail-recursive when the recursive call is the very last action, with nothing left to do after it returns — jos above is not, because it still adds k and takes % n after the call returns. C++ compilers optimise tail calls at -O2; Python and Java never do, JavaScript engines in practice do not either. So in those languages tail recursion is a style, not a space saving — convert to a loop when depth matters.

Why is Tower of Hanoi O(2^n) and not O(n)? There is only one print per call.

Because there are 2^n − 1 calls that print: moves(n) = 2·moves(n−1) + 1. The recursion tree is a full binary tree of height n, and every node does O(1) work, so the total is the number of nodes. A single print per call does not mean a linear number of calls.

How do you turn an exponential recursion into a fast one?

Check whether the same subproblem appears many times in the tree (rope cutting: maxPieces(2) is recomputed; subset sum: (n, target) repeats). If so, store each result the first time it is computed — memoisation (top-down DP) — or fill a table from the base cases up (bottom-up DP). If every leaf is a distinct required answer (subsets, permutations, Hanoi) the output itself is exponential and no algorithm can be faster.

Recursion vs iteration — when to pick which?

Recursion wins when the problem is naturally a tree of choices (subsets, permutations, Hanoi, tree traversals): the call stack keeps the partial state for you and the code mirrors the definition. Iteration wins for linear problems (sum, factorial, Josephus) where recursion only adds O(n) stack and the risk of overflow. Any recursion can be made iterative with an explicit stack; it is just more code.

What does the Josephus formula (jos(n-1, k) + k) % n actually mean?

After the first kill the circle is one person smaller and the count restarts at position k (0-based). Renumber that person as 0 and the rest is a smaller instance of the game. Its survivor j corresponds to j + k in the original numbering — the % n wraps around the circle. Unwinding from jos(1) = 0 gives the answer in O(n) with no simulation.

Arrays, Bits & Recursion

List

A list (Python's dynamic array) is the input of most interview problems. These notes collect the classic array problems and the handful of patterns — running minimum, prefix sums, two pointers, sliding window, Kadane's running best, difference arrays, majority voting — that turn the obvious O(n²) double loop into a single O(n) pass.

Array / list — a contiguous block of elements addressed by index. arr[i] costs O(1); appending at the end is amortised O(1); inserting or deleting anywhere else shifts everything after it — O(n).

Vocabulary: a *subarray* is contiguous; a *subsequence* keeps order but may skip
index:   0    1    2    3    4    5    6
       ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
arr:   │ 2  │ 3  │ 10 │ 6  │ 4  │ 8  │ 1  │     n = 7
       └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
subarray arr[2..4] = 10 6 4   (contiguous)      subsequence 2 10 1 (not contiguous)
The patterns behind every solution

Almost every naive solution below fixes a left end i and scans every right end j — n(n-1)/2 pairs, hence O(n²). The efficient solution replaces the inner scan with something that is already known when we reach j: the minimum so far, a prefix sum, the best subarray ending here. One pass, O(n).

PatternWhat you carry while scanningProblems
Running min / maxThe best arr[i] seen so far — the inner loop over i < j disappearsMaximum difference, trapping rain water
Greedy local stepsAdd every upward step; the sum of steps equals the best transaction setStock buy and sell
Kadane (running best ending here)maxEnding = max(maxEnding + x, x) — extend or restartMaximum subarray sum, circular sum, even-odd subarray
Sliding windowThe sum of the last k elements: add the new one, drop the old oneMax sum of k consecutive
Two pointersA window [s, i] that grows at the right and shrinks at the leftSubarray with given sum
Prefix sumpsum[i] = sum of arr[0..i], so any range sum is one subtractionRange sum queries, equilibrium point
Difference array+1 at left, -1 at right+1; a prefix sum turns it into countsMaximum appearing element in ranges
Boyer–Moore votingA candidate and a counter; every mismatch cancels one voteMajority element
ReversalThree reversals rotate in placeLeft rotate by d
Left rotate by d places
Example

Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], d = 2
Output: 3 4 5 1 2
Input: arr = [10, 20, 30], d = 1
Output: 20 30 10

Python can do this in one line with slicing or deque.rotate, both O(n) but using O(n) extra space. Popping from the front d times is O(n · d) because every pop(0) shifts the whole list.

Python
from collections import deque

l = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
d = 2
print(*(l[d:] + l[:d]))        # slicing: new list, O(n) space

dq = deque(l)
dq.rotate(-d)                  # negative = left rotation
print(*dq)

def left_rotate_slow(l, d):    # O(n * d): pop(0) shifts every element
    for _ in range(d):
        l.append(l.pop(0))
left_rotate_slow(l, d)
print(*l)
Output
30 40 50 10 20
30 40 50 10 20
30 40 50 10 20
Idea

Reversal algorithm. Reverse the first d elements, reverse the remaining n-d, then reverse the whole array. Each element is touched a constant number of times and nothing is copied: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Three reversals rotate left by d
1 2 3 4 5     d = 2
2 1 | 3 4 5   reverse arr[0..d-1]
2 1 | 5 4 3   reverse arr[d..n-1]
3 4 5 1 2     reverse arr[0..n-1]
Python
def reverse_range(arr, b, e):
    while b < e:
        arr[b], arr[e] = arr[e], arr[b]
        b += 1
        e -= 1

def left_rotate(arr, d):
    n = len(arr)
    d %= n                        # rotating by n is a no-op
    reverse_range(arr, 0, d - 1)  # 2 1 | 3 4 5
    reverse_range(arr, d, n - 1)  # 2 1 | 5 4 3
    reverse_range(arr, 0, n - 1)  # 3 4 5 1 2

for arr, d in (([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2), ([10, 20, 30], 1)):
    left_rotate(arr, d)
    print(*arr)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

void reverseRange(vector<int>& arr, int b, int e) {
    while (b < e) swap(arr[b++], arr[e--]);
}

void leftRotate(vector<int>& arr, int d) {
    int n = arr.size();
    d %= n;                        // rotating by n is a no-op
    reverseRange(arr, 0, d - 1);   // 2 1 | 3 4 5
    reverseRange(arr, d, n - 1);   // 2 1 | 5 4 3
    reverseRange(arr, 0, n - 1);   // 3 4 5 1 2
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, b = {10, 20, 30};
    leftRotate(a, 2);
    leftRotate(b, 1);
    for (int x : a) cout << x << " ";
    cout << "\n";
    for (int x : b) cout << x << " ";
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static void reverseRange(int[] arr, int b, int e) {
        while (b < e) { int t = arr[b]; arr[b] = arr[e]; arr[e] = t; b++; e--; }
    }

    static void leftRotate(int[] arr, int d) {
        int n = arr.length;
        d %= n;                        // rotating by n is a no-op
        reverseRange(arr, 0, d - 1);   // 2 1 | 3 4 5
        reverseRange(arr, d, n - 1);   // 2 1 | 5 4 3
        reverseRange(arr, 0, n - 1);   // 3 4 5 1 2
    }

    static void print(int[] arr) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int x : arr) sb.append(x).append(' ');
        System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, b = {10, 20, 30};
        leftRotate(a, 2);
        leftRotate(b, 1);
        print(a);
        print(b);
    }
}
JavaScript
function reverseRange(arr, b, e) {
    while (b < e) { [arr[b], arr[e]] = [arr[e], arr[b]]; b++; e--; }
}

function leftRotate(arr, d) {
    const n = arr.length;
    d %= n;                        // rotating by n is a no-op
    reverseRange(arr, 0, d - 1);   // 2 1 | 3 4 5
    reverseRange(arr, d, n - 1);   // 2 1 | 5 4 3
    reverseRange(arr, 0, n - 1);   // 3 4 5 1 2
}

for (const [arr, d] of [[[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2], [[10, 20, 30], 1]]) {
    leftRotate(arr, d);
    console.log(arr.join(" "));
}
Output
3 4 5 1 2
20 30 10
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

A right rotation by d is a left rotation by n - d. Always reduce d % n first — d may be larger than n.

Maximum difference

Find the maximum value of arr[j] - arr[i] with i < j (buy once, sell once later).

Example

Input: arr = [2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1]
Output: 8
Input: arr = [7, 9, 5, 6, 3, 2]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [30, 20, 10]
Output: -10

The naive solution tries every pair (i, j) — O(n²):

Python
def max_diff_naive(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    res = arr[1] - arr[0]
    for i in range(n - 1):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):          # every pair i < j
            res = max(res, arr[j] - arr[i])
    return res

print(max_diff_naive([2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1]))
Output
8
Idea

For a fixed j, the best i is simply the minimum element before j. Carry that minimum while scanning left to right: at each j compute arr[j] - minSoFar, then update the minimum. The inner loop collapses into one variable.

Python
def max_diff(arr):
    res = arr[1] - arr[0]
    min_val = arr[0]                     # smallest element before j
    for j in range(1, len(arr)):
        res = max(res, arr[j] - min_val)
        min_val = min(min_val, arr[j])   # update AFTER using it (i must be < j)
    return res

for arr in ([2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1], [7, 9, 5, 6, 3, 2], [30, 20, 10]):
    print(max_diff(arr))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int maxDiff(const vector<int>& arr) {
    int n = arr.size();
    int res = arr[1] - arr[0];
    int minVal = arr[0];                     // smallest element before j
    for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
        res = max(res, arr[j] - minVal);
        minVal = min(minVal, arr[j]);        // update AFTER using it (i must be < j)
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> tests = {{2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1}, {7, 9, 5, 6, 3, 2}, {30, 20, 10}};
    for (auto& arr : tests) cout << maxDiff(arr) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int maxDiff(int[] arr) {
        int res = arr[1] - arr[0];
        int minVal = arr[0];                     // smallest element before j
        for (int j = 1; j < arr.length; j++) {
            res = Math.max(res, arr[j] - minVal);
            minVal = Math.min(minVal, arr[j]);   // update AFTER using it (i must be < j)
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1}, {7, 9, 5, 6, 3, 2}, {30, 20, 10}};
        for (int[] arr : tests) System.out.println(maxDiff(arr));
    }
}
JavaScript
function maxDiff(arr) {
    let res = arr[1] - arr[0];
    let minVal = arr[0];                     // smallest element before j
    for (let j = 1; j < arr.length; j++) {
        res = Math.max(res, arr[j] - minVal);
        minVal = Math.min(minVal, arr[j]);   // update AFTER using it (i must be < j)
    }
    return res;
}

for (const arr of [[2, 3, 10, 6, 4, 8, 1], [7, 9, 5, 6, 3, 2], [30, 20, 10]])
    console.log(maxDiff(arr));
Output
8
2
-10
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Initialise res with arr[1] - arr[0], not 0 — for a strictly decreasing array the answer is negative. Also update min_val after computing the difference, or you allow i == j.

Stock buy and sell

Given daily prices, buy and sell any number of times (one share at a time, sell before buying again). Maximise the total profit.

Example

Input: price = [1, 5, 3, 8, 12]
Output: 13
Input: price = [30, 20, 10]
Output: 0
Input: price = [1, 2, 3, 4]
Output: 3

The naive idea considers every pair (i, j) with price[j] > price[i] as one transaction and recurses on both sides: profit = (price[j] - price[i]) + maxProfit(0, i-1) + maxProfit(j+1, n-1). For [1, 5, 3, 8, 12] the pair (1, 5) gives 4 + 0 + 9 = 13. It is exponential.

Python
def max_profit_naive(price, b, e):
    if e <= b:
        return 0
    res = 0
    for i in range(b, e):
        for j in range(i + 1, e + 1):
            if price[j] > price[i]:
                curr = (price[j] - price[i]
                        + max_profit_naive(price, b, i - 1)
                        + max_profit_naive(price, j + 1, e))
                res = max(res, curr)
    return res

print(max_profit_naive([1, 5, 3, 8, 12], 0, 4))
Output
13
Idea

Every rise price[i] > price[i-1] can be collected on its own: buying at the bottom and selling at the top of a rising run equals the sum of its daily rises. So just add every positive day-to-day difference — a greedy one-pass solution.

Local rises sum to the optimal profit
price:  1   5   3   8   12
rises:   +4  -2  +5  +4        collect the rises: 4 + 5 + 4 = 13
Python
def max_profit(price):
    profit = 0
    for i in range(1, len(price)):
        if price[i] > price[i - 1]:          # a rise: buy yesterday, sell today
            profit += price[i] - price[i - 1]
    return profit

for price in ([1, 5, 3, 8, 12], [30, 20, 10], [1, 2, 3, 4]):
    print(max_profit(price))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int maxProfit(const vector<int>& price) {
    int n = price.size();
    int profit = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++)
        if (price[i] > price[i - 1])             // a rise: buy yesterday, sell today
            profit += price[i] - price[i - 1];
    return profit;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> tests = {{1, 5, 3, 8, 12}, {30, 20, 10}, {1, 2, 3, 4}};
    for (auto& price : tests) cout << maxProfit(price) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static int maxProfit(int[] price) {
        int profit = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < price.length; i++)
            if (price[i] > price[i - 1])             // a rise: buy yesterday, sell today
                profit += price[i] - price[i - 1];
        return profit;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] tests = {{1, 5, 3, 8, 12}, {30, 20, 10}, {1, 2, 3, 4}};
        for (int[] price : tests) System.out.println(maxProfit(price));
    }
}

function maxProfit(price) {
    let profit = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i < price.length; i++)
        if (price[i] > price[i - 1])             // a rise: buy yesterday, sell today
            profit += price[i] - price[i - 1];

for (const price of [[1, 5, 3, 8, 12], [30, 20, 10], [1, 2, 3, 4]])
    console.log(maxProfit(price));

0
