5
11
Time O(R · log C · log(max − min))Space O(1)
Pitfall

The original notes ran this on the 4 × 4 matrix 1..16 and claimed the output 20 — an even count has no single middle element and 20 is not even in the matrix. For an even R × C, run the search twice for ranks RC/2 and RC/2 + 1 and average the two values.

Key point

upper_bound (count of elements ≤ mid) is what makes duplicates work: with bisect_left / lower_bound the count would exclude copies of mid itself and the search could overshoot.

Interview Q&A
How do you rotate a square matrix 90° in place?

Transpose it (swap mat[i][j] with mat[j][i] for j > i), then reverse the row order for an anticlockwise rotation or reverse each row for a clockwise one. Both steps are O(N²) time and O(1) extra space. A non-square matrix changes shape, so it needs a new C × R array.

Why does the staircase search start at the top-right (or bottom-left) corner?

At the top-right corner the two possible moves point in opposite directions in terms of value: left is smaller, down is larger. One comparison therefore discards a whole row or column. At the top-left corner both right and down are larger, so a comparison cannot eliminate anything.

What is the time complexity of the staircase search and why?

O(R + C). Every step moves either one column left or one row down, and neither pointer ever reverses, so there are at most C left moves and R down moves.

How does binary search on the answer find the median of a row-wise sorted matrix?

The predicate 'at least (RC+1)/2 elements are ≤ m' is false for small m and true for large m, so binary search over the value range [min, max] finds the smallest m that satisfies it — the median. Each probe costs O(R log C) using upper_bound on every row, giving O(R · log C · log(max − min)) overall with O(1) extra space.

What goes wrong with [[0] * cols] * rows in Python?

The outer * copies the reference to a single inner list, so all rows alias the same object and mat[0][0] = 1 changes column 0 of every row. Use a comprehension, [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)], which creates a fresh list per row. JavaScript's Array(rows).fill([]) has the same bug.

How would you print a matrix in spiral order without the boundary-crossing bugs?

Keep top, bottom, left, right. Print the top row and right column unconditionally, then print the bottom row only if top <= bottom and the left column only if left <= right. Those two guards prevent re-printing the middle row or column of a non-square matrix on its last ring.

Searching, Sorting & Hashing

Searching

Advanced searching is rarely “find x in a sorted array”. It is recognising that a problem has a monotone structure — an index range that can be halved, an answer range that can be halved, or two ends that can be walked inwards — and then applying binary search or two pointers to it.

Binary search (general form) — given a predicate that is false for a prefix of the search space and true for the rest, find the boundary in O(log n) probes. Searching for a value in a sorted array is just the special case arr[i] >= x.

The four patterns in this topic

Binary search on an index

The array is sorted, or piecewise sorted (rotated, bitonic). Decide in O(1) which half can contain the answer and discard the other.

Binary search on the answer

The array is not sorted, but the answer is a number and “is ans feasible?” is monotone. Binary search over the answer range, checking feasibility in O(n).

Two pointers

One pointer at each end of a sorted array; the sum tells you which pointer to move. Pair / triplet with a given sum.

Cycle detection on indices

Treat i → arr[i] as a linked list. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds the repeated value in O(n) time and O(1) space without touching the array.

ProblemPatternTimeExtra space
Search in an infinite sorted arraydoubling + binary searchO(log p) (p = position)O(1)
Search in a sorted rotated arraybinary search with a sorted-half testO(log n)O(1)
Find a peak elementbinary search towards the rising sideO(log n)O(1)
Pair with given sum (sorted)two pointersO(n)O(1)
Triplet with given sum (sorted)fix one + two pointersO(n²)O(1)
Median of two sorted arraysbinary search on a partitionO(log min(n1, n2))O(1)
Repeating elementFloyd's cycle detectionO(n)O(1)
Allocate minimum pagesbinary search on the answerO(n log S)O(1)
Key point

Every solution below uses the same loop skeleton: while low <= high: mid = low + (high - low) // 2 … with low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1. Writing low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2 avoids integer overflow in C++ and Java when low + high exceeds 2³¹ - 1.

Search in an infinite sorted array
Example

Input: arr = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120, …], x = 100
Output: 7
Input: arr = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120, …], x = 50
Output: -1

The array has no known size (think of a stream, a file, or an API that returns elements by index), so high = n - 1 is unavailable. A linear scan is O(p) where p is the position of x. We can do better: find a bracket around x first.

Idea

Double the index until arr[i] >= x: probe 1, 2, 4, 8, …. After O(log p) probes we know x lies in (i/2, i], a range of size i/2. One binary search on that range finds it in another O(log p) steps.

1
Check index 0
If arr[0] == x return 0.
2
Gallop
Start at i = 1; while arr[i] < x set i = 2i. Stop when arr[i] >= x (or we have overshot into values larger than x).
3
Binary search
Search for x in [i/2 + 1, i] — every index below i/2 + 1 was already seen to be < x.
Python
# Naive: scan until we pass x — O(p) probes
def search(arr, x):
    i = 0
    while True:
        if arr[i] == x:
            return i
        if arr[i] > x:      # sorted, so x cannot appear later
            return -1
        i += 1

arr = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120]
print(search(arr, 100))
print(search(arr, 50))
Output
7
-1

The efficient version only needs at(i) — a way to read the element at position i. The demo below models the infinite array with a function that returns a very large value beyond the data we actually have, which is exactly how a real stream would look (“everything further out is bigger than anything we are searching for”).

Python
INF = 10**9
data = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120]

def at(i):                      # the "infinite" array: beyond our data everything is huge
    return data[i] if i < len(data) else INF

def binary_search(low, high, x):
    while low <= high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        if at(mid) == x:
            return mid
        if at(mid) < x:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1

def search(x):
    if at(0) == x:
        return 0
    i = 1
    while at(i) < x:            # gallop: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
        i *= 2
    if at(i) == x:
        return i
    return binary_search(i // 2 + 1, i - 1, x)

for x in (100, 50, 40):
    print(f"x = {x} → {search(x)}")

    return i < (int)arr.size() ? arr[i] : INF;
}

int binarySearch(int low, int high, int x) {
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (at(mid) == x) return mid;
        if (at(mid) < x) low = mid + 1;
        else high = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

int search(int x) {
    if (at(0) == x) return 0;
    int i = 1;
    while (at(i) < x) i *= 2;    // gallop: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
    if (at(i) == x) return i;
    return binarySearch(i / 2 + 1, i - 1, x);
}

        cout << "x = " << x << " → " << search(x) << "\n";

const INF = 1e9;
const data = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120];

const at = (i) => (i < data.length ? data[i] : INF);   // the "infinite" array

function binarySearch(low, high, x) {
    while (low <= high) {
        const mid = low + Math.floor((high - low) / 2);
        if (at(mid) === x) return mid;
        if (at(mid) < x) low = mid + 1;
        else high = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

function search(x) {
    if (at(0) === x) return 0;
    let i = 1;
    while (at(i) < x) i *= 2;       // gallop: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
    if (at(i) === x) return i;

for (const x of [100, 50, 40]) console.log(`x = ${x} → ${search(x)}`);
Output
x = 100 → 7
x = 50 → -1
x = 40 → 3
Time O(log p)Space O(1)
Key point

p is the position of x, not the (unknown) array size. The same “gallop then binary search” trick is exponential search; Timsort uses it to merge runs of very different lengths.

Search in a sorted rotated array
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 8, 9], x = 30
Output: 2
Input: arr = [100, 200, 300, 10, 20], x = 40
Output: -1

A sorted array rotated by some unknown amount consists of two sorted runs, with the second run entirely smaller than the first. Plain binary search fails because arr[mid] < x no longer tells you which side x is on.

Whichever half contains mid's boundary, the other half is always a plain sorted run
index:   0   1   2   3   4   5   6
value:  10  20  30  40  50   8   9
        └─── sorted run 1 ────┘ └ run 2 ┘
         mid = 3 → arr[low]=10 < arr[mid]=40, so [0..3] is sorted
Idea

At every step one of the two halves is sorted — if arr[low] < arr[mid] the left half is, otherwise the right half is. Check whether x lies inside the sorted half (a simple range test); if yes, search there, otherwise search the other half. Each step still discards half the array.

Python
def search_rotated(arr, x):
    low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        if arr[mid] == x:
            return mid
        if arr[low] <= arr[mid]:                 # left half [low..mid] is sorted
            if arr[low] <= x < arr[mid]:
                high = mid - 1
            else:
                low = mid + 1
        else:                                    # right half [mid..high] is sorted
            if arr[mid] < x <= arr[high]:
                low = mid + 1
            else:
                high = mid - 1
    return -1

a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 8, 9]
print("x = 30 →", search_rotated(a, 30))
print("x = 8 →", search_rotated(a, 8))
print("x = 40 →", search_rotated([100, 200, 300, 10, 20], 40))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int searchRotated(const vector<int>& arr, int x) {
    int low = 0, high = (int)arr.size() - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (arr[mid] == x) return mid;
        if (arr[low] <= arr[mid]) {              // left half [low..mid] is sorted
            if (arr[low] <= x && x < arr[mid]) high = mid - 1;
            else low = mid + 1;
        } else {                                 // right half [mid..high] is sorted
            if (arr[mid] < x && x <= arr[high]) low = mid + 1;
            else high = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 8, 9};
    cout << "x = 30 → " << searchRotated(a, 30) << "\n";
    cout << "x = 8 → " << searchRotated(a, 8) << "\n";
    cout << "x = 40 → " << searchRotated({100, 200, 300, 10, 20}, 40) << "\n";
}

    while (low <= high) {

        if (arr[mid] === x) return mid;
        if (arr[low] <= arr[mid]) {              // left half [low..mid] is sorted
            if (arr[low] <= x && x < arr[mid]) high = mid - 1;
            else low = mid + 1;
        } else {                                 // right half [mid..high] is sorted

const a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 8, 9];
console.log("x = 30 →", searchRotated(a, 30));
console.log("x = 8 →", searchRotated(a, 8));

Output
x = 30 → 2
x = 8 → 5
x = 40 → -1
Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Use arr[low] <= arr[mid] (not <) so that a two-element window like [8, 9] with mid == low is classified as “left half sorted”. The original notes used <, which sends x = 8 the wrong way in such windows. With duplicates ([3, 1, 3, 3, 3]) neither half can be identified and the worst case degrades to O(n).

Find a peak element
Example

Input: arr = [5, 10, 20, 15, 7]
Output: 20
Input: arr = [10, 20, 15, 5, 23, 90, 67]
Output: 20 (90 is also a valid answer)

A peak is an element that is not smaller than its neighbours (the ends only have one neighbour). Every array has at least one peak — the maximum is always one — but we only need any peak, which is what makes O(log n) possible.

Idea

Look at mid. If it is a peak, done. If its left neighbour is bigger, the left half must contain a peak: walking left along rising values must eventually stop, either at a local maximum or at index 0 — both are peaks. Symmetrically, if the right neighbour is bigger, go right.

Binary search follows the rising side; it never needs the global maximum
10  20  15   5  23  90  67
 0   1   2   3   4   5   6
             ↑ mid=3: arr[2]=15 > 5 → a peak exists on the left
     ↑ mid=1: 10 ≤ 20 ≥ 15 → peak = 20
Python
# Naive: check every element against its neighbours — O(n)
def get_peak(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        left_ok = i == 0 or arr[i - 1] <= arr[i]
        right_ok = i == n - 1 or arr[i + 1] <= arr[i]
        if left_ok and right_ok:
            return arr[i]

print(get_peak([5, 10, 20, 15, 7]))
print(get_peak([10, 20, 15, 5, 23, 90, 67]))
Output
20
20
Python
def get_peak(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    low, high = 0, n - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        left_ok = mid == 0 or arr[mid - 1] <= arr[mid]
        right_ok = mid == n - 1 or arr[mid + 1] <= arr[mid]
        if left_ok and right_ok:
            return arr[mid]                # mid is a peak
        if mid > 0 and arr[mid - 1] > arr[mid]:
            high = mid - 1                 # rising towards the left → peak there
        else:
            low = mid + 1                  # rising towards the right
    return -1

print(get_peak([5, 10, 20, 15, 7]))
print(get_peak([10, 20, 15, 5, 23, 90, 67]))
print(get_peak([1, 2, 3]))
print(get_peak([7]))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int getPeak(const vector<int>& arr) {
    int n = arr.size();
    int low = 0, high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        bool leftOk = mid == 0 || arr[mid - 1] <= arr[mid];
        bool rightOk = mid == n - 1 || arr[mid + 1] <= arr[mid];
        if (leftOk && rightOk) return arr[mid];          // mid is a peak
        if (mid > 0 && arr[mid - 1] > arr[mid]) high = mid - 1;   // rising to the left
        else low = mid + 1;                                       // rising to the right
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    cout << getPeak({5, 10, 20, 15, 7}) << "\n";
    cout << getPeak({10, 20, 15, 5, 23, 90, 67}) << "\n";
    cout << getPeak({1, 2, 3}) << "\n";
    cout << getPeak({7}) << "\n";
}

Key point

The array is not sorted here — binary search works because the predicate “a peak exists in this half” can be decided from mid and one neighbour. The same reasoning finds the maximum of a bitonic array (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing).

Two-pointer approach: pair with a given sum
Example

Input: arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 30], x = 17
Output: true
Input: arr = [3, 8, 13, 18], x = 14
Output: false

Given a sorted array, is there a pair whose sum is x? The brute force tries all n(n-1)/2 pairs.

Python
# Naive: every pair — O(n²)
def has_pair(arr, x):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if arr[i] + arr[j] == x:
                return True
    return False

print("true" if has_pair([2, 5, 8, 12, 30], 17) else "false")
print("true" if has_pair([3, 8, 13, 18], 14) else "false")
Output
true
false
Idea

Put i at the start and j at the end. If arr[i] + arr[j] < x the sum must grow — only moving i right can do that (every pair with this i and a smaller j is even smaller, so i is finished). If the sum is too large, move j left. Each step retires one index, so at most n steps.

Python
def has_pair(arr, x):
    i, j = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while i < j:
        s = arr[i] + arr[j]
        if s == x:
            return True
        if s < x:
            i += 1          # need a bigger sum
        else:
            j -= 1          # need a smaller sum
    return False

print("[2, 5, 8, 12, 30] x=17 →", "true" if has_pair([2, 5, 8, 12, 30], 17) else "false")
print("[3, 8, 13, 18] x=14 →", "true" if has_pair([3, 8, 13, 18], 14) else "false")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

bool hasPair(const vector<int>& arr, int x) {
    int i = 0, j = (int)arr.size() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int s = arr[i] + arr[j];
        if (s == x) return true;
        if (s < x) i++;       // need a bigger sum
        else j--;             // need a smaller sum
    }
    return false;
}

int main() {
    cout << "[2, 5, 8, 12, 30] x=17 → " << (hasPair({2, 5, 8, 12, 30}, 17) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
    cout << "[3, 8, 13, 18] x=14 → " << (hasPair({3, 8, 13, 18}, 14) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
}

    static boolean hasPair(int[] arr, int x) {
        int i = 0, j = arr.length - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            int s = arr[i] + arr[j];
            if (s == x) return true;
            if (s < x) i++;   // need a bigger sum
            else j--;         // need a smaller sum
        }
        return false;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("[2, 5, 8, 12, 30] x=17 → " + hasPair(new int[]{2, 5, 8, 12, 30}, 17));
        System.out.println("[3, 8, 13, 18] x=14 → " + hasPair(new int[]{3, 8, 13, 18}, 14));

}
JavaScript
function hasPair(arr, x) {
    let i = 0, j = arr.length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        const s = arr[i] + arr[j];
        if (s === x) return true;

    }

}

console.log("[2, 5, 8, 12, 30] x=17 →", hasPair([2, 5, 8, 12, 30], 17));
console.log("[3, 8, 13, 18] x=14 →", hasPair([3, 8, 13, 18], 14));
Output
[2, 5, 8, 12, 30] x=17 → true
[3, 8, 13, 18] x=14 → false
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

If the array is not sorted, two pointers need an O(n log n) sort first; a hash set gives O(n) time with O(n) space instead (see Hashing). Two pointers win when the input is already sorted or when O(1) extra space is required.

Triplet in a sorted array
Example

Input: arr = [2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40], x = 32
Output: true
Input: arr = [1, 2, 5, 6], x = 14
Output: false

Idea

Fix the smallest element arr[i] of the triplet, then ask the two-pointer routine for a pair with sum x - arr[i] in the suffix arr[i+1..]. Searching only to the right avoids reusing arr[i] and avoids counting the same triplet three times. n fixes × O(n) pair search = O(n²), down from the O(n³) triple loop.

Python
def has_pair_from(arr, start, x):
    i, j = start, len(arr) - 1
    while i < j:
        s = arr[i] + arr[j]
        if s == x:
            return True
        if s < x:
            i += 1
        else:
            j -= 1
    return False

def has_triplet(arr, x):
    for i in range(len(arr) - 2):              # fix the smallest element
        if has_pair_from(arr, i + 1, x - arr[i]):
            return True
    return False

print("[2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40] x=32 →", "true" if has_triplet([2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40], 32) else "false")
print("[1, 2, 5, 6] x=14 →", "true" if has_triplet([1, 2, 5, 6], 14) else "false")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

bool hasPairFrom(const vector<int>& arr, int start, int x) {
    int i = start, j = (int)arr.size() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int s = arr[i] + arr[j];
        if (s == x) return true;
        if (s < x) i++; else j--;
    }
    return false;
}

bool hasTriplet(const vector<int>& arr, int x) {
    int n = arr.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++)                 // fix the smallest element
        if (hasPairFrom(arr, i + 1, x - arr[i])) return true;
    return false;
}

int main() {
    cout << "[2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40] x=32 → " << (hasTriplet({2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40}, 32) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
    cout << "[1, 2, 5, 6] x=14 → " << (hasTriplet({1, 2, 5, 6}, 14) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
}

    static boolean hasTriplet(int[] arr, int x) {
        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length - 2; i++)    // fix the smallest element

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println("[1, 2, 5, 6] x=14 → " + hasTriplet(new int[]{1, 2, 5, 6}, 14));

}
JavaScript
function hasPairFrom(arr, start, x) {
    let i = start, j = arr.length - 1;
    while (i < j) {

console.log("[2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40] x=32 →", hasTriplet([2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40], 32));

Output
[2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40] x=32 → true
[1, 2, 5, 6] x=14 → false
Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Key point

This is the standard 3-Sum technique. To list all distinct triplets instead of answering yes/no, skip over equal values after each move of i, j and the fixed index so duplicates are not reported twice.

Median of two sorted arrays
Example

Input: a1 = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], a2 = [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]
Output: 27.5
Input: a1 = [1, 2, 3], a2 = [4, 5, 6]
Output: 3.5
Input: a1 = [1, 3, 5], a2 = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
Output: 4.5

The median of the merged array is wanted, without merging. Merging takes O(n1 + n2) time and space; the target is O(log min(n1, n2)).

Python
# Naive: merge (like merge sort's merge step), then pick the middle — O(n1 + n2)
def median_by_merge(a1, a2):
    merged, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(a1) and j < len(a2):
        if a1[i] <= a2[j]:
            merged.append(a1[i]); i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(a2[j]); j += 1
    merged += a1[i:] + a2[j:]
    n = len(merged)
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return merged[n // 2]
    return (merged[n // 2 - 1] + merged[n // 2]) / 2

print(median_by_merge([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]))
print(median_by_merge([1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]))
Output
27.5
4.5
Idea

The median splits the n1 + n2 elements into a left half and a right half of (almost) equal size. Take i1 elements from a1 and i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1 from a2 to form the left half. The split is correct exactly when every left element is <= every right element: maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1. If maxLeft1 > minRight2, i1 is too big — binary search i1 over [0, n1].

A valid partition: five elements on the left, five on the right
a1 = 10 20 | 30 40 50       i1 = 2  →  maxLeft1 = 20, minRight1 = 30
a2 =  5 15 25 | 35 45       i2 = 3  →  maxLeft2 = 25, minRight2 = 35

left half  = {10, 20, 5, 15, 25}   max = 25
right half = {30, 40, 50, 35, 45}  min = 30
20 ≤ 35 and 25 ≤ 30 ✓  →  median = (25 + 30) / 2 = 27.5
1
Make a1 the shorter array
Swap if needed, so the search space is [0, n1] with n1 = min, and i2 always stays within [0, n2].
2
Binary search i1
i1 = (low + high) / 2, i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1. Use -∞ / +∞ when a side of a split is empty.
3
Check the partition
maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1 → found. If maxLeft1 > minRight2 move high = i1 - 1, else low = i1 + 1.
4
Read the median
Odd total: max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2). Even total: average of that and min(minRight1, minRight2).

To keep the four programs' output byte-identical the code computes twice the median as an integer (the sum of the two middle values) and prints it as k.0 or k.5 — the median of integers is always a whole or half number.

Python
INF = float("inf")

def median_x2(a1, a2):
    if len(a1) > len(a2):
        a1, a2 = a2, a1                     # binary search over the shorter array
    n1, n2 = len(a1), len(a2)
    low, high = 0, n1
    while low <= high:
        i1 = (low + high) // 2
        i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) // 2 - i1
        max_l1 = -INF if i1 == 0 else a1[i1 - 1]
        min_r1 = INF if i1 == n1 else a1[i1]
        max_l2 = -INF if i2 == 0 else a2[i2 - 1]
        min_r2 = INF if i2 == n2 else a2[i2]
        if max_l1 <= min_r2 and max_l2 <= min_r1:       # valid partition
            if (n1 + n2) % 2 == 1:
                return 2 * max(max_l1, max_l2)
            return max(max_l1, max_l2) + min(min_r1, min_r2)
        if max_l1 > min_r2:
            high = i1 - 1                    # took too many from a1
        else:
            low = i1 + 1                     # took too few from a1
    return 0

def show(a1, a2):
    m2 = int(median_x2(a1, a2))
    print(f"{m2 // 2}.{'5' if m2 % 2 else '0'}")

show([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], [5, 15, 25, 35, 45])
show([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])
show([1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6, 8, 10])
show([1, 2], [3])
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int medianX2(vector<int> a1, vector<int> a2) {
    if (a1.size() > a2.size()) swap(a1, a2);        // binary search over the shorter array
    int n1 = a1.size(), n2 = a2.size();
    int low = 0, high = n1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int i1 = (low + high) / 2;
        int i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1;
        int maxL1 = i1 == 0 ? INT_MIN : a1[i1 - 1];
        int minR1 = i1 == n1 ? INT_MAX : a1[i1];
        int maxL2 = i2 == 0 ? INT_MIN : a2[i2 - 1];
        int minR2 = i2 == n2 ? INT_MAX : a2[i2];
        if (maxL1 <= minR2 && maxL2 <= minR1) {        // valid partition
            if ((n1 + n2) % 2 == 1) return 2 * max(maxL1, maxL2);
            return max(maxL1, maxL2) + min(minR1, minR2);
        }
        if (maxL1 > minR2) high = i1 - 1;              // took too many from a1
        else low = i1 + 1;                             // took too few from a1
    }
    return 0;
}

void show(const vector<int>& a1, const vector<int>& a2) {
    int m2 = medianX2(a1, a2);
    cout << m2 / 2 << "." << (m2 % 2 ? "5" : "0") << "\n";
}

int main() {
    show({10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, {5, 15, 25, 35, 45});
    show({1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6});
    show({1, 3, 5}, {2, 4, 6, 8, 10});
    show({1, 2}, {3});
}

Pitfall

Three bugs in the original notes, all fixed above: maxLeft1 for an empty left part must be -∞, not +∞; a2[i2] and a2[i2 - 1] need the same empty-side guards as a1, otherwise i2 == n2 indexes out of range; and the solution assumed len(a1) <= len(a2) without enforcing it. Also the notes' answer for [1, 3, 5] and [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] was 4.0 — the merged array is 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 10, so the median is 4.5.

Repeating element

Constraints that make this problem interesting:

  • array size n >= 2
  • exactly one value repeats — any number of times
  • all values from 0 to max(arr) are present, so 0 <= max(arr) <= n - 2
Example

Input: arr = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]
Output: 3

ApproachTimeExtra spaceModifies array?
Compare every pairO(n²)O(1)no
Sort, then compare neighboursO(n log n)O(1)yes
Hash set of seen valuesO(n)O(n)no
Boolean visited array (values are < n)O(n)O(n)no
Floyd's cycle detection on i → arr[i]O(n)O(1)no
Python
# Sort-based: O(n log n), but the array is reordered
def repeating_by_sort(arr):
    arr = sorted(arr)
    for i in range(len(arr) - 1):
        if arr[i] == arr[i + 1]:
            return arr[i]
    return -1

# Set-based: O(n) time but O(n) extra space
def repeating_by_set(arr):
    seen = set()
    for x in arr:
        if x in seen:
            return x
        seen.add(x)
    return -1

print(repeating_by_sort([0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]), repeating_by_set([0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]))
print(repeating_by_sort([1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]), repeating_by_set([1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]))
Output
2 2
3 3

Because every value is smaller than n, a boolean array indexed by value replaces the hash set — same O(n) time, less constant overhead, no hashing.

Python
def repeating(arr):
    visited = [False] * len(arr)       # values lie in 0..n-2, so index by value
    for x in arr:
        if visited[x]:
            return x
        visited[x] = True
    return -1

print(repeating([0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]))
print(repeating([1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]))

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Repeating element in O(n) time, O(1) space, array unchanged
Example

Input: arr = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]
Output: 3
Input: arr = [0, 0]
Output: 0

Now the array may not be modified and no extra array is allowed. The trick is to stop looking at the values as data and treat them as pointers.

Idea

Define next(i) = arr[i] + 1. Index 0 is never anybody's next (values are >= 0, so next >= 1), and every index has exactly one outgoing edge — the structure is a linked list that ends in a cycle (a ρ shape), starting at 0. The repeated value is the node with two incoming edges, which is precisely where the cycle begins. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds that node in O(n) with two integer variables; subtract the +1 to recover the value.

Indices as a functional graph: the cycle entry has two in-edges, i.e. the repeated value
arr = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]        next(i) = arr[i] + 1

0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 3 → 4 → …        4 and 5 both point to 3
            ↑___|                 (arr[4] = arr[5] = 2)
        5 ──┘
cycle starts at node 3  →  value = 3 - 1 = 2
1
Phase 1 — meet inside the cycle
slow = next(slow), fast = next(next(fast)) from 0 until they are equal. They must meet because once both are on the cycle the gap shrinks by one every step.
2
Phase 2 — find the entry
Reset slow = 0; move both one step at a time. They meet exactly at the cycle entry (the distance from 0 to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry, modulo the cycle length).
3
Recover the value
The entry index is v + 1 for the repeated value v, so return entry - 1.
Python
def repeating(arr):
    nxt = lambda i: arr[i] + 1          # +1 so that index 0 is never a target
    slow = fast = 0
    while True:                         # phase 1: meet somewhere on the cycle
        slow = nxt(slow)
        fast = nxt(nxt(fast))
        if slow == fast:
            break
    slow = 0                            # phase 2: walk to the cycle entry
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nxt(slow)
        fast = nxt(fast)
    return slow - 1

print(repeating([0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]))
print(repeating([1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]))
print(repeating([0, 0]))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int repeating(const vector<int>& arr) {
    auto next = [&](int i) { return arr[i] + 1; };   // +1 so that index 0 is never a target
    int slow = 0, fast = 0;
    do {                                             // phase 1: meet somewhere on the cycle
        slow = next(slow);
        fast = next(next(fast));
    } while (slow != fast);
    slow = 0;                                        // phase 2: walk to the cycle entry
    while (slow != fast) {
        slow = next(slow);
        fast = next(fast);
    }
    return slow - 1;
}

int main() {
    cout << repeating({0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2}) << "\n";
    cout << repeating({1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3}) << "\n";
    cout << repeating({0, 0}) << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static int repeating(int[] arr) {
        int slow = 0, fast = 0;
        do {                                         // phase 1: meet somewhere on the cycle
            slow = arr[slow] + 1;                    // +1 so that index 0 is never a target
            fast = arr[arr[fast] + 1] + 1;
        } while (slow != fast);
        slow = 0;                                    // phase 2: walk to the cycle entry
        while (slow != fast) {
            slow = arr[slow] + 1;
            fast = arr[fast] + 1;
        }
        return slow - 1;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(repeating(new int[]{0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2}));
        System.out.println(repeating(new int[]{1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3}));
        System.out.println(repeating(new int[]{0, 0}));
    }
}

        slow = next(slow);
        fast = next(next(fast));
    } while (slow !== fast);
    slow = 0;                           // phase 2: walk to the cycle entry
    while (slow !== fast) {
        slow = next(slow);
        fast = next(fast);
    }
    return slow - 1;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The +1 shift matters. Without it, arr[0] == 0 makes index 0 point to itself and the “start” is already inside a cycle, so Floyd's phase 2 returns the wrong node. The popular variant Find the Duplicate Number (n + 1 values in 1..n) needs no shift because its values are already >= 1 — use next(i) = arr[i] and return the entry itself. The notes' example [1, 1] belongs to that variant (it violates max(arr) <= n - 2), so it was replaced by [0, 0].

Allocate minimum number of pages
Example

Input: pages = [10, 20, 30, 40], k = 2
Output: 60
Input: pages = [10, 20, 30], k = 1
Output: 60
Input: pages = [10, 20, 30, 40], k = 3
Output: 40

n books with pages[i] pages must be split among k students. Each student gets a contiguous run of books and every book goes to someone. Minimise the maximum number of pages any one student reads. For [10, 20, 30, 40] and k = 2 the best split is [10, 20, 30] | [40] → max(60, 40) = 60.

Python
# Naive: try every position for the last cut, recursively — exponential
def min_pages(pages, n, k):
    if k == 1:
        return sum(pages[:n])          # one student takes all remaining books
    if n == 1:
        return pages[0]
    best = float("inf")
    for i in range(1, n):              # last student gets pages[i..n-1]
        best = min(best, max(min_pages(pages, i, k - 1), sum(pages[i:n])))
    return best

print(min_pages([10, 20, 30, 40], 4, 2))
print(min_pages([10, 20, 30], 3, 1))
Output
60
60

The recursion explores C(n-1, k-1) ways of placing cuts. Memoising it gives an O(n² k) dynamic programme — still slow. The breakthrough is to search over the answer instead of over the cuts.

Idea

Ask the inverse question: “can every student stay within cap pages?” Greedily fill students left to right; start a new student whenever adding the next book would exceed cap. If at most k students were needed, cap is feasible. Feasibility is monotone — a larger cap is never harder — so binary search the smallest feasible cap between max(pages) (one book must fit) and sum(pages) (one student takes all).

1
Bounds
low = max(pages), high = sum(pages). The answer is always in this range.
2
Probe
mid = (low + high) / 2. Run the greedy isFeasible(mid) in O(n).
3
Shrink
Feasible → record mid, try smaller (high = mid - 1). Not feasible → low = mid + 1.
Python
def is_feasible(pages, k, cap):
    students, current = 1, 0
    for pg in pages:
        if pg > cap:
            return False
        if current + pg > cap:          # this book starts a new student's share
            students += 1
            current = pg
        else:
            current += pg
    return students <= k

def min_pages(pages, k):
    low, high = max(pages), sum(pages)
    result = high
    while low <= high:                  # binary search on the answer
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        if is_feasible(pages, k, mid):
            result = mid
            high = mid - 1              # try an even smaller cap
        else:
            low = mid + 1
    return result

print(min_pages([10, 20, 30, 40], 2))
print(min_pages([10, 20, 30], 1))
print(min_pages([10, 20, 30, 40], 3))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

bool isFeasible(const vector<int>& pages, int k, int cap) {
    int students = 1, current = 0;
    for (int pg : pages) {
        if (pg > cap) return false;
        if (current + pg > cap) {       // this book starts a new student's share
            students++;
            current = pg;
        } else {
            current += pg;
        }
    }
    return students <= k;
}

int minPages(const vector<int>& pages, int k) {
    int low = *max_element(pages.begin(), pages.end());
    int high = accumulate(pages.begin(), pages.end(), 0);
    int result = high;
    while (low <= high) {               // binary search on the answer
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (isFeasible(pages, k, mid)) { result = mid; high = mid - 1; }   // try smaller
        else low = mid + 1;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    cout << minPages({10, 20, 30, 40}, 2) << "\n";
    cout << minPages({10, 20, 30}, 1) << "\n";
    cout << minPages({10, 20, 30, 40}, 3) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static boolean isFeasible(int[] pages, int k, int cap) {
        int students = 1, current = 0;
        for (int pg : pages) {
            if (pg > cap) return false;
            if (current + pg > cap) {   // this book starts a new student's share
                students++;
                current = pg;
            } else {
                current += pg;
            }
        }
        return students <= k;
    }

    static int minPages(int[] pages, int k) {
        int low = 0, high = 0;
        for (int pg : pages) { low = Math.max(low, pg); high += pg; }
        int result = high;
        while (low <= high) {           // binary search on the answer
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (isFeasible(pages, k, mid)) { result = mid; high = mid - 1; }   // try smaller
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(minPages(new int[]{10, 20, 30, 40}, 2));
        System.out.println(minPages(new int[]{10, 20, 30}, 1));
        System.out.println(minPages(new int[]{10, 20, 30, 40}, 3));
    }
}

function isFeasible(pages, k, cap) {
    let students = 1, current = 0;
    for (const pg of pages) {
        if (pg > cap) return false;
        if (current + pg > cap) {       // this book starts a new student's share
            students++;
            current = pg;
        } else {
            current += pg;
        }
    }
    return students <= k;
}

function minPages(pages, k) {
    let low = Math.max(...pages), high = pages.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    let result = high;
    while (low <= high) {               // binary search on the answer
        const mid = low + Math.floor((high - low) / 2);
        if (isFeasible(pages, k, mid)) { result = mid; high = mid - 1; }   // try smaller
        else low = mid + 1;
    }
    return result;
}
