for (const [txt, pat] of [["abcdefg", "bcd"], ["aaaaab", "aaaa"], ["aaaaabaaaaac", "aaaa"]])
    console.log(pat, "in", txt, "→", kmpSearch(txt, pat).join(" "));
Output
bcd in abcdefg → 1
aaaa in aaaaab → 0 1
aaaa in aaaaabaaaaac → 0 1 6 7
Time O(n + m)Space O(m)
Pitfall

After a full match do not reset j = 0 — that misses overlapping occurrences (aaaa in aaaaab occurs at both 0 and 1). j = lps[m − 1] keeps the longest reusable overlap. And guard the mismatch branch with j != 0 before indexing lps[j − 1].

Anagram search
Example

Input: txt = "geeksforgeeks", pat = "forg"
Output: Yes (window "forg" at 5)
Input: txt = "geeksforgeeks", pat = "rseek"
Output: No

Does the text contain any permutation of the pattern as a substring? Order no longer matters, only the multiset of characters, so hashing by comparison fails and we count instead. Naive: for every window, count the pattern's characters up and the window's characters down and check that everything cancels.

Python — naive
CHAR = 256

def is_anagram_at(txt, pat, i):
    count = [0] * CHAR
    for j in range(len(pat)):
        count[ord(pat[j])] += 1
        count[ord(txt[i + j])] -= 1
    return all(c == 0 for c in count)

def contains_anagram(txt, pat):
    n, m = len(txt), len(pat)
    return any(is_anagram_at(txt, pat, i) for i in range(n - m + 1))

print("Yes" if contains_anagram("geeksforgeeks", "forg") else "No")
print("Yes" if contains_anagram("geeksforgeeks", "rseek") else "No")
Output
Yes
No
Time O((n − m + 1) · (m + CHAR))Space O(CHAR)
Idea

Sliding window of size m with two count arrays: cp for the pattern (fixed) and ct for the current window. Moving the window one step changes two counts in ct (one character in, one out) — O(1). After each move compare ct with cp; a window is an anagram exactly when the two arrays are equal.

Python
CHAR = 256

def contains_anagram(txt, pat):
    n, m = len(txt), len(pat)
    if m > n:
        return False
    ct, cp = [0] * CHAR, [0] * CHAR
    for i in range(m):                     # first window and the pattern
        ct[ord(txt[i])] += 1
        cp[ord(pat[i])] += 1
    for i in range(m, n):
        if ct == cp:
            return True
        ct[ord(txt[i])] += 1               # character entering the window
        ct[ord(txt[i - m])] -= 1           # character leaving the window
    return ct == cp                        # the last window

for txt, pat in [("geeksforgeeks", "forg"), ("geeksforgeeks", "rseek"), ("cbaebabacd", "abc")]:
    print(pat, "in", txt, "→", "Yes" if contains_anagram(txt, pat) else "No")
C++
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

const int CHAR = 256;

bool containsAnagram(const string& txt, const string& pat) {
    int n = txt.size(), m = pat.size();
    if (m > n) return false;
    array<int, CHAR> ct{}, cp{};
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {                      // first window and the pattern
        ct[(unsigned char)txt[i]]++;
        cp[(unsigned char)pat[i]]++;
    }
    for (int i = m; i < n; i++) {
        if (ct == cp) return true;
        ct[(unsigned char)txt[i]]++;                   // character entering the window
        ct[(unsigned char)txt[i - m]]--;               // character leaving the window
    }
    return ct == cp;                                   // the last window
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<string, string>> tests = {{"geeksforgeeks", "forg"}, {"geeksforgeeks", "rseek"}, {"cbaebabacd", "abc"}};
    for (auto& [txt, pat] : tests)
        cout << pat << " in " << txt << " → " << (containsAnagram(txt, pat) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static final int CHAR = 256;

    static boolean containsAnagram(String txt, String pat) {
        int n = txt.length(), m = pat.length();
        if (m > n) return false;
        int[] ct = new int[CHAR], cp = new int[CHAR];
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {                  // first window and the pattern
            ct[txt.charAt(i)]++;
            cp[pat.charAt(i)]++;
        }
        for (int i = m; i < n; i++) {
            if (Arrays.equals(ct, cp)) return true;
            ct[txt.charAt(i)]++;                       // character entering the window
            ct[txt.charAt(i - m)]--;                   // character leaving the window
        }
        return Arrays.equals(ct, cp);                  // the last window
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[][] tests = {{"geeksforgeeks", "forg"}, {"geeksforgeeks", "rseek"}, {"cbaebabacd", "abc"}};
        for (String[] t : tests)
            System.out.println(t[1] + " in " + t[0] + " → " + (containsAnagram(t[0], t[1]) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
const CHAR = 256;

function sameCounts(a, b) {
    for (let i = 0; i < CHAR; i++) if (a[i] !== b[i]) return false;
    return true;
}

function containsAnagram(txt, pat) {
    const n = txt.length, m = pat.length;
    if (m > n) return false;
    const ct = new Array(CHAR).fill(0), cp = new Array(CHAR).fill(0);
    for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {                      // first window and the pattern
        ct[txt.charCodeAt(i)]++;
        cp[pat.charCodeAt(i)]++;
    }
    for (let i = m; i < n; i++) {
        if (sameCounts(ct, cp)) return true;
        ct[txt.charCodeAt(i)]++;                       // character entering the window
        ct[txt.charCodeAt(i - m)]--;                   // character leaving the window
    }
    return sameCounts(ct, cp);                         // the last window
}

for (const [txt, pat] of [["geeksforgeeks", "forg"], ["geeksforgeeks", "rseek"], ["cbaebabacd", "abc"]])
    console.log(pat, "in", txt, "→", containsAnagram(txt, pat) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output
forg in geeksforgeeks → Yes
rseek in geeksforgeeks → No
abc in cbaebabacd → Yes
Time O(n · CHAR)Space O(CHAR)
Key point

CHAR is a constant, so this is linear — but comparing 256 counters per window is the dominant cost. The standard refinement keeps a single mismatches counter: when a count in ct changes, update whether that slot agrees with cp; the window is an anagram when mismatches == 0. That is O(n) with no array comparison at all.

Lexicographic rank of a string
Example

Input: s = "ABC"
Output: 1
Input: s = "BAC"
Output: 3
Input: s = "STRING"
Output: 598

Among all permutations of the string's characters listed in dictionary order, which position does the string itself hold (1-based)? For "ABC" the six permutations are:

RankPermutation
1ABC
2ACB
3BAC
4BCA
5CAB
6CBA

The pen-and-paper method generates every permutation and counts — O(n · n!):

Python — naive
from itertools import permutations

def rank_naive(s):
    perms = sorted(''.join(p) for p in permutations(s))     # n! strings, sorted
    return perms.index(s) + 1

print(rank_naive("ABC"), rank_naive("BAC"), rank_naive("STRING"))
Output
1 3 598
Idea

Count how many permutations come before s. Every permutation that starts with a character smaller than s[0] precedes s — there are (number of smaller characters) × (n − 1)! of them. Fix s[0] and repeat on the remainder: at position i, add (smaller unused characters to the right of i) × (n − i − 1)!. A cumulative count array count[c] = number of unused characters ≤ c answers “how many smaller” in O(1); after using s[i], decrement count[c] for every c ≥ s[i].

Rank of "BAC"
s = "BAC",  n = 3,  (n-1)! = 2

i = 0, 'B' : smaller unused chars = {A} → 1 × 2! = 2 permutations start with 'A'
i = 1, 'A' : smaller unused chars = {}  → 0 × 1! = 0
rank = 1 + 2 + 0 = 3
Python
CHAR = 256

def factorial(n):
    r = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        r *= i
    return r

def lex_rank(s):
    n = len(s)
    count = [0] * CHAR
    for ch in s:
        count[ord(ch)] += 1
    for c in range(1, CHAR):                 # cumulative: count[c] = #chars <= c
        count[c] += count[c - 1]
    rank = 1
    mul = factorial(n)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        mul //= n - i                        # (n - i - 1)!
        c = ord(s[i])
        rank += count[c - 1] * mul           # unused chars smaller than s[i]
        for j in range(c, CHAR):             # s[i] is used up now
            count[j] -= 1
    return rank

for s in ["ABC", "BAC", "CBA", "STRING"]:
    print(s, "→", lex_rank(s))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

const int CHAR = 256;

long long factorial(int n) {
    long long r = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) r *= i;
    return r;
}

long long lexRank(const string& s) {
    int n = s.size();
    int count[CHAR] = {0};
    for (char ch : s) count[(unsigned char)ch]++;
    for (int c = 1; c < CHAR; c++) count[c] += count[c - 1];   // cumulative: count[c] = #chars <= c
    long long rank = 1, mul = factorial(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        mul /= n - i;                                    // (n - i - 1)!
        int c = (unsigned char)s[i];
        rank += count[c - 1] * mul;                      // unused chars smaller than s[i]
        for (int j = c; j < CHAR; j++) count[j]--;       // s[i] is used up now
    }
    return rank;
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"ABC", "BAC", "CBA", "STRING"})
        cout << s << " → " << lexRank(s) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static final int CHAR = 256;

    static long factorial(int n) {
        long r = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) r *= i;
        return r;
    }

    static long lexRank(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[] count = new int[CHAR];
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) count[ch]++;
        for (int c = 1; c < CHAR; c++) count[c] += count[c - 1];   // cumulative: count[c] = #chars <= c
        long rank = 1, mul = factorial(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
            mul /= n - i;                                    // (n - i - 1)!
            int c = s.charAt(i);
            rank += count[c - 1] * mul;                      // unused chars smaller than s[i]
            for (int j = c; j < CHAR; j++) count[j]--;       // s[i] is used up now
        }
        return rank;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"ABC", "BAC", "CBA", "STRING"})
            System.out.println(s + " → " + lexRank(s));
    }
}
JavaScript
const CHAR = 256;

function factorial(n) {
    let r = 1;
    for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) r *= i;
    return r;
}

function lexRank(s) {
    const n = s.length;
    const count = new Array(CHAR).fill(0);
    for (const ch of s) count[ch.charCodeAt(0)]++;
    for (let c = 1; c < CHAR; c++) count[c] += count[c - 1];   // cumulative: count[c] = #chars <= c
    let rank = 1, mul = factorial(n);
    for (let i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        mul /= n - i;                                    // (n - i - 1)!  (exact: mul is a multiple)
        const c = s.charCodeAt(i);
        rank += count[c - 1] * mul;                      // unused chars smaller than s[i]
        for (let j = c; j < CHAR; j++) count[j]--;       // s[i] is used up now
    }
    return rank;
}

for (const s of ["ABC", "BAC", "CBA", "STRING"])
    console.log(s, "→", lexRank(s));
Output
ABC → 1
BAC → 3
CBA → 6
STRING → 598
Time O(n · CHAR)Space O(CHAR)
Pitfall

This formula assumes distinct characters. With repeats ("AAB") the count of permutations starting with a smaller character must be divided by the factorials of the repeated characters' counts. Also n! overflows a 32-bit int from n = 13 — use 64-bit integers (as above), which last until n = 20.

Longest substring with distinct characters
Example

Input: s = "abcdabc"
Output: 4 ("abcd")
Input: s = "aaa"
Output: 1
Input: s = "geeksforgeeks"
Output: 7 ("eksforg")

Find the length of the longest substring in which no character repeats. The naive version tests every substring; the better one notices that once a substring from i contains a repeat, no longer substring from i can be distinct — so it breaks out of the inner loop.

Python — naive O(n³) and better O(n²)
def longest_distinct_naive(s):                 # O(n^3): every (i, j), each checked in O(n)
    n, best = len(s), 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            if len(set(s[i:j + 1])) == j - i + 1:
                best = max(best, j - i + 1)
    return best

def longest_distinct_better(s):                # O(n^2): extend from i until the first repeat
    n, best = len(s), 0
    for i in range(n):
        seen = set()
        for j in range(i, n):
            if s[j] in seen:
                break
            seen.add(s[j])
            best = max(best, j - i + 1)
    return best

print(longest_distinct_naive("abcdabc"), longest_distinct_better("abcdabc"))
print(longest_distinct_naive("geeksforgeeks"), longest_distinct_better("geeksforgeeks"))
Output
4 4
7 7
Idea

Sliding window with a last-seen index per character. Let start be the left end of the current distinct window and let j move right. If s[j] was last seen at prev[s[j]] ≥ start, the window must begin after that occurrence: start = prev[s[j]] + 1. Taking start = max(start, prev[s[j]] + 1) handles both cases in one line; j − start + 1 is the length of the longest distinct substring ending at j. Each character is visited once.

The window start only ever moves right
s     :  a  b  c  d  a  b  c
j = 4 : 'a' last seen at 0 → start = 1, window "bcda" (length 4)
j = 5 : 'b' last seen at 1 → start = 2, window "cdab" (length 4)
j = 6 : 'c' last seen at 2 → start = 3, window "dabc" (length 4)
Python
def longest_distinct(s):
    prev = [-1] * 256                 # last index where each character was seen
    start = 0                         # left end of the current distinct window
    best = 0
    for j, ch in enumerate(s):
        start = max(start, prev[ord(ch)] + 1)   # jump past the previous occurrence
        best = max(best, j - start + 1)
        prev[ord(ch)] = j
    return best

for s in ["abcdabc", "aaa", "geeksforgeeks", "abcdefg"]:
    print(s, "→", longest_distinct(s))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int longestDistinct(const string& s) {
    int prev[256];
    fill(prev, prev + 256, -1);                  // last index where each character was seen
    int start = 0, best = 0;                     // start = left end of the current distinct window
    int n = s.size();
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        unsigned char ch = s[j];
        start = max(start, prev[ch] + 1);        // jump past the previous occurrence
        best = max(best, j - start + 1);
        prev[ch] = j;
    }
    return best;
}

int main() {
    for (string s : {"abcdabc", "aaa", "geeksforgeeks", "abcdefg"})
        cout << s << " → " << longestDistinct(s) << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static int longestDistinct(String s) {
        int[] prev = new int[256];
        Arrays.fill(prev, -1);                       // last index where each character was seen
        int start = 0, best = 0;                     // start = left end of the current distinct window
        for (int j = 0; j < s.length(); j++) {
            char ch = s.charAt(j);
            start = Math.max(start, prev[ch] + 1);   // jump past the previous occurrence
            best = Math.max(best, j - start + 1);
            prev[ch] = j;
        }
        return best;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[]{"abcdabc", "aaa", "geeksforgeeks", "abcdefg"})
            System.out.println(s + " → " + longestDistinct(s));
    }
}
JavaScript
function longestDistinct(s) {
    const prev = new Array(256).fill(-1);            // last index where each character was seen
    let start = 0, best = 0;                         // start = left end of the current distinct window
    for (let j = 0; j < s.length; j++) {
        const ch = s.charCodeAt(j);
        start = Math.max(start, prev[ch] + 1);       // jump past the previous occurrence
        best = Math.max(best, j - start + 1);
        prev[ch] = j;
    }
    return best;
}

for (const s of ["abcdabc", "aaa", "geeksforgeeks", "abcdefg"])
    console.log(s, "→", longestDistinct(s));
Output
abcdabc → 4
aaa → 1
geeksforgeeks → 7
abcdefg → 7
Time O(n)Space O(CHAR)
Pitfall

Writing start = prev[ch] + 1 without the max is wrong: a repeat that lies before the current window (prev[ch] < start) must not pull start backwards. In "abba" at j = 3 the earlier a is at 0, but the window already starts at 2.

Interview Q&A
KMP or Rabin–Karp — when do you pick which?

KMP gives a guaranteed O(n + m) for one pattern and is the safe default. Rabin–Karp shines when you search for many patterns of the same length at once (hash each pattern into a set, then one rolling pass over the text), or for 2-D / plagiarism-style matching where hashes of many windows must be compared. Its worst case is O(n · m), so it is a poor fit for adversarial inputs.

What exactly does lps[i] mean, and why is it the right amount to fall back?

lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pat[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch after matching j characters, the text we just consumed ends with pat[0..j−1]; its longest proper prefix-suffix (lps[j−1] characters) is the longest stretch of that text that could still be the beginning of a match. Anything longer is ruled out by maximality, and anything shorter would skip a possible match — so lps[j−1] is exactly the safe shift.

Why is KMP O(n + m) when it has a loop that does not advance i?

Charge each iteration to either i or j. Iterations that match advance i (at most n of them). Iterations that fall back strictly decrease j, and j only grows together with i, so there can be at most n fall-backs in total. The LPS construction is the same argument over m.

The Rabin–Karp hash matched but the strings differ — is the algorithm wrong?

No, that is a spurious hit, expected behaviour of any hash modulo q. Correctness comes from the character-by-character verification that runs only when hashes agree; the hash merely filters candidates. Pick a large prime (and 64-bit arithmetic) so spurious hits are rare, which keeps the expected time linear.

How would you return the anagram positions instead of Yes/No, and the substring instead of the length?

Anagram search: whenever ct == cp for the window starting at i − m, record i − m and continue instead of returning. Longest distinct substring: whenever j − start + 1 improves best, also remember start; the answer is s[start..start+best−1]. Both keep the same complexity.

Lexicographic rank with repeated characters?

Permutations with repeats are counted by the multinomial n! / (c1! · c2! · …). At position i, for each unused character smaller than s[i], add (n − i − 1)! / Π(count of each remaining character)! where that character's count is reduced by one. Same scan, one extra division per step; precompute factorials once.

Linked Lists, Stacks & Queues

LinkedList

Linked-list problems are pointer puzzles: almost every classic one is solved by two pointers moving at different speeds or distances, by reversing links in place, or by re-wiring nodes without allocating. This topic collects the problems interviewers actually ask and the handful of techniques that solve them.

Singly linked list — a chain of nodes where each node stores a value (data) and a reference to the next node (next); the last node's next is null. Only the head is kept — every other node is reached by following links, so random access is O(n) but splicing nodes in and out is O(1) once you stand next to them.

The list 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 — every solution below works on this shape
head
 ↓
┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐   ┌────┬───┐
│ 10 │ ●─┼──▶│ 20 │ ●─┼──▶│ 30 │ ●─┼──▶│ 40 │ ∅ │
└────┴───┘   └────┴───┘   └────┴───┘   └────┴───┘
 data next
Recap: what costs what
OperationSingly linked listDynamic array
Access i-th elementO(n) — walk from headO(1)
Insert / delete at headO(1)O(n) — shift everything
Insert / delete after a known nodeO(1) — re-wire two linksO(n)
Insert / delete at tailO(n) (O(1) with a tail pointer)amortised O(1)
SearchO(n)O(n) (O(log n) if sorted)
Memory per elementvalue + one pointer, scatteredvalue only, contiguous and cache-friendly

The problems in this topic exploit the one thing a list does better than an array: moving a node costs O(1) and no allocation. Reversing, merging, swapping pairs and segregating are all done by changing next pointers, never by copying values into a new container.

The techniques behind every problem

Slow and fast pointers

slow moves one node per step, fast two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; if fast ever catches slow, there is a loop. Used for: middle, palindrome, loop detection.

Two pointers a fixed gap apart

Send first ahead by n nodes, then move both together; when first falls off, second is n from the end. Used for: nth node from end, intersection (after aligning lengths).

Reverse links in place

Three pointers prev, curr, next flip each link in one pass. Used for: reverse, reverse in groups of k, palindrome (reverse the second half).

Dummy head node

A throwaway node in front of the list removes every “is this the first node?” special case. Used for: merge, pairwise swap, deleting nodes.

Hash the node references

A set or map keyed by node identity (not value) gives a straightforward O(n)-space solution — the baseline you beat with pointer tricks. Used for: loop, intersection, clone.

Re-wire instead of allocate

Thread existing nodes into new sublists (even/odd, merged) or interleave copies inside the original list (clone). Used for: segregate, clone with random pointers.

Node and helpers used in every solution

Every program below carries the same three pieces: a Node, build(values) that turns an array into a list, and toStr(head) that prints a list as space-separated values. They are the only boilerplate — the solutions themselves are the functions in between.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):                 # [1, 2, 3] → 1 → 2 → 3
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):     # prepend from the back, so order is kept
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):                  # "1 2 3"
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def length(head):
    n = 0
    while head:
        n += 1
        head = head.next
    return n

head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(to_str(head))
print("length:", length(head))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {            // {1, 2, 3} → 1 → 2 → 3
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {   // prepend from the back
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {                     // "1 2 3"
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

int length(Node* head) {
    int n = 0;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) n++;
    return n;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = build({10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
    cout << toStr(head) << "\n";
    cout << "length: " << length(head) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node build(int[] v) {                 // {1, 2, 3} → 1 → 2 → 3
        Node head = null;
        for (int i = v.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {   // prepend from the back
            Node node = new Node(v[i]);
            node.next = head;
            head = node;
        }
        return head;
    }

    static String toStr(Node head) {             // "1 2 3"
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) sb.append(c.data).append(c.next != null ? " " : "");
        return sb.toString();
    }

    static int length(Node head) {
        int n = 0;
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) n++;
        return n;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = build(new int[]{10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
        System.out.println(toStr(head));
        System.out.println("length: " + length(head));
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(data) { this.data = data; this.next = null; }
}

function build(values) {                       // [1, 2, 3] → 1 → 2 → 3
    let head = null;
    for (let i = values.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {   // prepend from the back
        const node = new Node(values[i]);
        node.next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

function toStr(head) {                         // "1 2 3"
    const parts = [];
    for (let c = head; c; c = c.next) parts.push(c.data);
    return parts.join(" ");
}

function length(head) {

    for (let c = head; c; c = c.next) n++;

const head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]);
console.log(toStr(head));
console.log("length:", length(head));
Output
10 20 30 40 50
length: 5
Key point

build prepends from the back of the array so the list comes out in array order without a tail pointer. In C++ the nodes are allocated with new and never freed in these short programs — fine for a demo, a leak in real code; a destructor or unique_ptr chain fixes that.

Middle of a linked list
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: 30
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40
Output: 30 (the second of the two middle nodes)

Idea

Two pointers start at the head. slow advances one node, fast two. When fast runs off the end, fast has covered the whole list and slow exactly half of it — slow is standing on the middle. One pass, no counting.

fast moves two for every one of slow, so slow ends at the middle
step 0:   slow            fast
           ↓               ↓
          10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
step 1:        slow       fast
step 2:             slow            fast = ∅ → stop, slow = 30
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:      # fast moves 2, slow moves 1
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow

for values in ([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], [10, 20, 30, 40]):
    head = build(values)
    print(to_str(head), "→ middle", middle(head).data)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* middle(Node* head) {
    Node* slow = head;
    Node* fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {       // fast moves 2, slow moves 1
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
    }
    return slow;
}

int main() {
    for (vector<int> values : {vector<int>{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, vector<int>{10, 20, 30, 40}}) {
        Node* head = build(values);
        cout << toStr(head) << " → middle " << middle(head)->data << "\n";
    }
}

Key point

For an even length this returns the second middle (30 of 10 20 30 40). To get the first middle instead, loop while fast.next and fast.next.next — that variant is exactly what the palindrome check below uses, because it wants slow at the end of the first half.

Nth node from the end
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, n = 2
Output: 40
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, n = 6
Output: none (list is shorter than n)

Idea

Move first ahead by n nodes. Now move first and second together; the gap between them stays n, so when first falls off the end, second is exactly n nodes from the end. The naive alternative — count the length, then walk len − n nodes — also works in O(n) but needs two passes.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def nth_from_end(head, n):
    first = head
    for _ in range(n):               # move first n nodes ahead
        if first is None:
            return None              # n is larger than the length
        first = first.next
    second = head
    while first:                     # now move both; the gap stays n
        first = first.next
        second = second.next
    return second

head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
for n in (1, 2, 5, 6):
    node = nth_from_end(head, n)
    print("n =", n, "→", node.data if node else "none")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

Node* nthFromEnd(Node* head, int n) {
    Node* first = head;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {        // move first n nodes ahead
        if (!first) return nullptr;      // n is larger than the length
        first = first->next;
    }
    Node* second = head;
    while (first) {                      // now move both; the gap stays n
        first = first->next;
        second = second->next;
    }
    return second;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = build({10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
    for (int n : {1, 2, 5, 6}) {
        Node* node = nthFromEnd(head, n);
        cout << "n = " << n << " → " << (node ? to_string(node->data) : "none") << "\n";
    }
}

public class Main {

        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

            Node node = new Node(v[i]);
            node.next = head;
            head = node;

    static Node nthFromEnd(Node head, int n) {

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {        // move first n nodes ahead
            if (first == null) return null;  // n is larger than the length
            first = first.next;
        }
        Node second = head;
        while (first != null) {              // now move both; the gap stays n
            first = first.next;
            second = second.next;
        }
        return second;

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Check first for null inside the first loop. Without that check, n larger than the length dereferences null — a crash in C++/Java/JavaScript and an AttributeError in Python. “Delete the nth node from the end” is the same walk with a dummy head so that deleting the first node is not a special case.

Reverse a linked list
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: 50 → 40 → 30 → 20 → 10

Idea

Iterative: walk the list once with three pointers. prev is the already-reversed part, curr is the node being flipped, next saves the rest so it is not lost when curr.next is overwritten. Recursive: reverse everything after head, then make the old second node (head.next) point back to head and set head.next = null — head becomes the tail.

One step of the iterative reversal — repeat until curr is ∅, then prev is the new head
before:   prev   curr   next
           ∅  ←  10  →  20 → 30 → 40 → 50

flip:      ∅  ←  10     20 → 30 → 40 → 50      curr.next = prev

advance:         prev   curr   next
           ∅  ←  10     20  →  30 → 40 → 50    prev = curr, curr = next
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def reverse_iter(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next              # save the rest of the list
        curr.next = prev             # flip the link
        prev, curr = curr, nxt       # advance both pointers
    return prev                      # prev is the new head

def reverse_rec(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head                  # empty or single node: already reversed
    rest = reverse_rec(head.next)    # reverse everything after head
    head.next.next = head            # old second node now points back at head
    head.next = None                 # head becomes the tail
    return rest

head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
head = reverse_iter(head)
print("iterative:", to_str(head))
head = reverse_rec(head)             # reverse it back
print("recursive:", to_str(head))

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* reverseIter(Node* head) {
    Node* prev = nullptr;
    Node* curr = head;
    while (curr) {
        Node* next = curr->next;         // save the rest of the list
        curr->next = prev;               // flip the link
        prev = curr;                     // advance both pointers
        curr = next;
    }
    return prev;                         // prev is the new head
}

Node* reverseRec(Node* head) {
    if (!head || !head->next) return head;   // empty or single node
    Node* rest = reverseRec(head->next);     // reverse everything after head
    head->next->next = head;                 // old second node points back at head
    head->next = nullptr;                    // head becomes the tail
    return rest;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = build({10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
    head = reverseIter(head);
    cout << "iterative: " << toStr(head) << "\n";
    head = reverseRec(head);                 // reverse it back
    cout << "recursive: " << toStr(head) << "\n";
}

recursive: 10 20 30 40 50
Time O(n)Space O(1) iterative · O(n) recursive (call stack)
Pitfall

Forgetting to save next before curr.next = prev loses the rest of the list. In the recursive version, forgetting head.next = null leaves a cycle between the last two nodes — the first node still points at the second, which now points back. Prefer the iterative version in production: the recursive one uses one stack frame per node and overflows on long lists (Python at ~1000).

Reverse a linked list in groups of k
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → 60, k = 3
Output: 30 → 20 → 10 → 60 → 50 → 40
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, k = 3
Output: 30 → 20 → 10 → 50 → 40

Idea

Reverse the first k nodes with the ordinary three-pointer loop. The group's old first node (head) is now its last node, so its next must point at the result of reversing the rest — either a recursive call, or the next group in an iterative loop. The last group is reversed even when it holds fewer than k nodes (the LeetCode variant leaves a short tail untouched — add a length check if that is required).

Each group is reversed on its own; the old head of a group links to the new head of the next
10 → 20 → 30 │ 40 → 50 → 60          groups of k = 3

reverse group 1:   30 → 20 → 10 → ?          10 was the head, now the tail
reverse group 2:                60 → 50 → 40
link:              30 → 20 → 10 → 60 → 50 → 40

Recursive — the natural way to express “reverse this group, then link to the reversed rest”:

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def reverse_k_rec(head, k):
    curr, prev = head, None
    count = 0
    while curr and count < k:        # reverse the first k nodes
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
        count += 1
    if curr:                         # more nodes left: reverse them and link
        head.next = reverse_k_rec(curr, k)   # head is now the tail of this group
    return prev                      # prev is the new head of this group

for values in ([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]):
    print(to_str(reverse_k_rec(build(values), 3)))

        count++;

    return prev;                         // prev is the new head of this group
}

Iterative — same work, constant extra space. Remember the first node of each group: after the group is reversed it is the group's tail, and the previous group's tail must be pointed at the new head of this group.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def reverse_k_iter(head, k):
    curr = head
    new_head = None
    prev_tail = None                 # tail of the previous reversed group
    while curr:
        group_first = curr           # will become this group's tail
        prev = None
        count = 0
        while curr and count < k:    # reverse one group
            nxt = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = nxt
            count += 1
        if new_head is None:
            new_head = prev          # first group's new head is the list's head
        else:
            prev_tail.next = prev    # link previous group to this one
        prev_tail = group_first
    return new_head

for values in ([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]):
    print(to_str(reverse_k_iter(build(values), 3)))

Pitfall

The two bugs here are both linking bugs: forgetting head.next = … after the recursive call (groups come back disconnected), or linking prev_tail to the group's first node instead of its new head prev.

Detect a loop — hash set of visited nodes
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, and 50 → 30
Output: Yes
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: No

A loop: the last node points back into the list
10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
          ↑          │
          └──────────┘          50.next = 30 — a traversal never ends
Idea

Walk the list, putting each node's reference (not its value — values may repeat) into a set. The first node already in the set is the loop entry; reaching null means no loop. Simple and O(n) time, but O(n) extra memory — the baseline Floyd's algorithm improves on.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def has_loop_set(head):
    seen = set()
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr in seen:             # visited before → we went round a loop
            return True
        seen.add(curr)               # nodes hash by identity, not by value
        curr = curr.next
    return False

head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print("10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50:", "Yes" if has_loop_set(head) else "No")
tail = head
while tail.next:
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = head.next.next           # 50 → 30 creates the loop
print("with 50 → 30:", "Yes" if has_loop_set(head) else "No")
Output
10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50: No
with 50 → 30: Yes
Key point

The set must hold references: in C++ an unordered_set<Node*> keyed by address, in Java a HashSet<Node> (identity semantics because Node does not override equals/hashCode), in JavaScript a Set of objects. A set of values would report a false loop on 1 → 2 → 1.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

Two other O(1)-space tricks you may see: a visited flag inside each node (needs a field you usually cannot add), or pointing every visited node's next at a sentinel dummy node (destroys the list). Floyd's algorithm needs neither.

Detect a loop — Floyd's cycle detection
Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, and 50 → 30
Output: Yes
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: No

Idea

Run slow (one step) and fast (two steps) from the head. If there is no loop, fast reaches null. If there is a loop, both pointers eventually circle inside it, and fast gains exactly one node on slow every step — so it must land on slow within one lap. Two pointers, no memory.

1
Initialise
slow = head, fast = head.
2
Advance
Each step: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next. Stop with “no loop” when fast or fast.next is null.
3
Compare
If slow is the same node as fast, there is a loop.

Why they must meet. fast enters the loop no later than slow. Suppose that when slow enters the loop, fast is k nodes ahead of it (0 ≤ k < n for a loop of length n) — equivalently, fast is n − k nodes behind slow going round the circle. Every step slow moves one and fast moves two, so the gap behind closes by exactly one node per step. After n − k steps the gap is zero: they stand on the same node. Because the gap shrinks by one (not two), fast can never jump over slow.

Trace on the example: slow enters the loop at step 2 with fast one ahead; one more step and they meet
10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → (back to 30)        loop length n = 3

step   slow   fast
  0     10     10
  1     20     30
  2     30     50
  3     40     40   ← meet
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def has_loop(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next             # one step
        fast = fast.next.next        # two steps
        if slow is fast:             # same node (not same value) → loop
            return True
    return False                     # fast ran off the end

head = build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print("10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50:", "Yes" if has_loop(head) else "No")
tail = head
while tail.next:
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = head.next.next           # 50 → 30 creates the loop
print("with 50 → 30:", "Yes" if has_loop(head) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

bool hasLoop(Node* head) {
    Node* slow = head;
    Node* fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;               // one step
        fast = fast->next->next;         // two steps
        if (slow == fast) return true;   // same address → loop
    }
    return false;                        // fast ran off the end
}

int main() {
    Node* head = build({10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
    cout << "10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50: " << (hasLoop(head) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    Node* tail = head;
    while (tail->next) tail = tail->next;
    tail->next = head->next->next;       // 50 → 30 creates the loop
    cout << "with 50 → 30: " << (hasLoop(head) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node build(int[] v) {
        Node head = null;
        for (int i = v.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            Node node = new Node(v[i]);
            node.next = head;
            head = node;
        }
        return head;
    }

    static boolean hasLoop(Node head) {
        Node slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;                // one step
            fast = fast.next.next;           // two steps
            if (slow == fast) return true;   // same reference → loop
        }
        return false;                        // fast ran off the end
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node head = build(new int[]{10, 20, 30, 40, 50});
        System.out.println("10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50: " + (hasLoop(head) ? "Yes" : "No"));
        Node tail = head;
        while (tail.next != null) tail = tail.next;
        tail.next = head.next.next;          // 50 → 30 creates the loop
        System.out.println("with 50 → 30: " + (hasLoop(head) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}

10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50: No
with 50 → 30: Yes
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Compare the nodes, not their values (slow is fast / == on references) — a list with repeated values has no loop. And test fast.next as well as fast before stepping twice; fast.next.next on the last node is a null dereference.

Detect and remove a loop
Example

Input: 10 → 15 → 5 → 20, and 20 → 15
Output: 10 → 15 → 5 → 20 (loop of length 3 starting at 15 removed)

Idea

Floyd's meeting point is not the loop's first node — but it is a fixed distance from it. Move slow back to head, keep fast at the meeting point, and advance both one step at a time: they meet exactly at the first node of the loop. Then walk round the loop once more to find the node whose next is that first node, and set its next to null.

1
Detect
Run Floyd's algorithm. If slow and fast never meet, there is no loop — stop.
2
Loop length (variation 1)
From the meeting point, walk round until you are back: the number of steps is the loop length n.
3
First node of the loop (variation 2)
Put slow at head, leave fast at the meeting point. Move both one step until they are equal — that node is the loop start.
4
Cut
From the loop start, walk until node.next is the loop start again; that node is the last node of the loop. Set its next = null.

Why moving one pointer back to the head works. Let m be the distance from head to the loop start, n the loop length, and k the distance from the loop start to the meeting point. When they meet, slow has walked m + k + x·n and fast twice that, m + k + y·n, for some lap counts x, y:

2(m + k + x·n) = m + k + y·n ⟹ m + k = (y − 2x)·n

So m + k is a multiple of the loop length. A pointer that starts at the meeting point (already k into the loop) and walks m more steps is m + k ≡ 0 (mod n) into the loop — i.e. back at the loop start. A pointer that starts at head and walks m steps is also at the loop start. Walking both at the same speed, they coincide for the first time exactly there.

Trace on the example
10 → 15 → 5 → 20 → (back to 15)        m = 1, n = 3

Floyd:   slow 10,15,5,20     fast 10,5,15,20  → meet at 20  (k = 2, m + k = 3 = n ✓)
phase 2: slow = head = 10, fast = 20
         one step each:  slow → 15, fast → 15   → loop starts at 15
cut:     from 15 walk to the node whose next is 15: that is 20 → 20.next = ∅
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def detect_and_remove(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:            # 1. Floyd: find a meeting point
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            break
    else:
        print("no loop")
        return
    length = 1                           # 2. loop length: walk round once
    p = fast.next
    while p is not fast:
        p = p.next
        length += 1
    print("loop length:", length)
    slow = head                          # 3. loop start: same speed from head and meeting point
    while slow is not fast:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    print("loop starts at:", slow.data)
    last = slow                          # 4. find the last node of the loop and cut
    while last.next is not slow:
        last = last.next
    last.next = None

head = build([10, 15, 5, 20])
head.next.next.next.next = head.next     # 20 → 15 creates the loop
detect_and_remove(head)
print("after removal:", to_str(head))
detect_and_remove(head)                  # run again: the list is clean now

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

void detectAndRemove(Node* head) {
    Node* slow = head;
    Node* fast = head;
    bool met = false;
    while (fast && fast->next) {             // 1. Floyd: find a meeting point
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) { met = true; break; }
    }
    if (!met) { cout << "no loop\n"; return; }
    int length = 1;                          // 2. loop length: walk round once
    for (Node* p = fast->next; p != fast; p = p->next) length++;
    cout << "loop length: " << length << "\n";
    slow = head;                             // 3. loop start: same speed from head and meeting point
    while (slow != fast) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next;
    }
    cout << "loop starts at: " << slow->data << "\n";
    Node* last = slow;                       // 4. find the last node of the loop and cut
    while (last->next != slow) last = last->next;
    last->next = nullptr;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = build({10, 15, 5, 20});
    head->next->next->next->next = head->next;   // 20 → 15 creates the loop
    detectAndRemove(head);
    cout << "after removal: " << toStr(head) << "\n";
    detectAndRemove(head);                   // run again: the list is clean now
}

Key point

When the loop starts at the head itself (m = 0), the meeting point is the loop start, so the phase-2 loop runs zero times — no special case needed. The original notes handled that separately; the version above does not have to because it compares slow and fast directly rather than slow.next and fast.next.

Intersection point of two linked lists
Example

Input: A: 5 → 8 → 7 → 10 → 12 → 15, B: 9 → 10 → 12 → 15 (B's second node is A's node 10)
Output: 10

Two lists sharing a tail — the intersection is the first shared node, by identity, not by value
A:  5 → 8 → 7 ─┐
               ├─▶ 10 → 12 → 15 → ∅
B:        9 ───┘

Baseline — hash set of nodes. Put every node of A in a set, then walk B and return the first node already present. O(m + n) time, O(m) space.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def intersection_set(a, b):
    seen = set()
    while a:
        seen.add(a)                  # node identity, not value
        a = a.next
    while b:
        if b in seen:
            return b
        b = b.next
    return None

a = build([5, 8, 7, 10, 12, 15])
b = Node(9)
b.next = a.next.next.next            # 9 → 10 → 12 → 15, sharing from 10
node = intersection_set(a, b)
print("intersection:", node.data if node else "none")
Output
intersection: 10

Efficient — align the lengths. Both lists share their whole tail from the intersection on, so they differ only in the number of nodes before it. Count both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk both together; the first time the two pointers are the same node is the intersection (or both reach null).

Idea

After skipping |len(A) − len(B)| nodes of the longer list, both pointers are the same distance from the end. From then on they move in lock-step, so they reach the shared tail at the same moment.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def length(head):
    n = 0
    while head:
        n += 1
        head = head.next
    return n

def intersection(a, b):
    la, lb = length(a), length(b)
    while la > lb:                   # advance the longer list by the difference
        a = a.next
        la -= 1
    while lb > la:
        b = b.next
        lb -= 1
    while a is not b:                # same distance from the end: walk together
        a = a.next
        b = b.next
    return a                         # None when both ran off the end

a = build([5, 8, 7, 10, 12, 15])
b = Node(9)
b.next = a.next.next.next            # 9 → 10 → 12 → 15, sharing from 10
print("A:", to_str(a))
print("B:", to_str(b))
node = intersection(a, b)
print("intersection:", node.data if node else "none")
node = intersection(a, build([1, 2]))
print("intersection with 1 → 2:", node.data if node else "none")

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

int length(Node* head) {
    int n = 0;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) n++;
    return n;
}

Node* intersection(Node* a, Node* b) {
    int la = length(a), lb = length(b);
    while (la > lb) { a = a->next; la--; }   // advance the longer list by the difference
    while (lb > la) { b = b->next; lb--; }
    while (a != b) {                         // same distance from the end: walk together
        a = a->next;
        b = b->next;
    }
    return a;                                // nullptr when both ran off the end
}

    Node* node = intersection(a, b);
    cout << "intersection: " << (node ? to_string(node->data) : "none") << "\n";
    node = intersection(a, build({1, 2}));
    cout << "intersection with 1 → 2: " << (node ? to_string(node->data) : "none") << "\n";

Key point

No-counting variant: walk pa over A then B, and pb over B then A. Both travel exactly len(A) + len(B) nodes, so they reach the intersection together — or both hit null after the second list. Same complexity, slightly less code, harder to explain in an interview.

Pitfall

Intersection means the same node object, not equal values — 1 → 2 → 3 and 9 → 3 with two different 3 nodes do not intersect. Compare references.

Segregate even and odd nodes
Example

Input: 17 → 15 → 8 → 12 → 5
Output: 8 → 12 → 17 → 15 → 5 (all even values first, relative order preserved)

Naive — move odd nodes to the end. Find the last node, then traverse once more: every odd node is detached and appended after the current last node. Stop after processing the original last node, otherwise the nodes you just appended are visited again and the loop never ends.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def segregate_naive(head):
    if head is None:
        return None
    last = head
    while last.next:
        last = last.next
    stop = last                      # original last node: do not go past it
    dummy = Node(0)
    dummy.next = head
    prev, curr = dummy, head
    while True:
        nxt = curr.next
        if curr.data % 2 == 1:       # odd: detach and append after last
            prev.next = nxt
            last.next = curr
            curr.next = None
            last = curr
        else:
            prev = curr
        if curr is stop:
            break
        curr = nxt
    return dummy.next

print(to_str(segregate_naive(build([17, 15, 8, 12, 5]))))
print(to_str(segregate_naive(build([1, 3, 5]))))
Output
8 12 17 15 5
1 3 5

One traversal — build two sublists and join them. Keep the start and end of an even sublist and of an odd sublist. Every node is appended to the end of its own sublist as it is visited, so each sublist keeps the original relative order. At the end, link the even tail to the odd head and terminate the odd tail.

Idea

Nothing is allocated and no node is moved twice: the four pointers even_start, even_end, odd_start, odd_end just thread the existing nodes into two chains, which are joined once.

Two chains threaded through the same nodes, then joined
input:   17 → 15 → 8 → 12 → 5

evens:   8 → 12                  even_start = 8,  even_end = 12
odds:    17 → 15 → 5             odd_start = 17,  odd_end = 5

join:    8 → 12 → 17 → 15 → 5 → ∅    even_end.next = odd_start, odd_end.next = ∅
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def segregate(head):
    even_start = even_end = None
    odd_start = odd_end = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.data % 2 == 0:
            if even_start is None:
                even_start = even_end = curr
            else:
                even_end.next = curr     # append to the even chain
                even_end = curr
        else:
            if odd_start is None:
                odd_start = odd_end = curr
            else:
                odd_end.next = curr      # append to the odd chain
                odd_end = curr
        curr = curr.next
    if even_start is None or odd_start is None:
        return head                  # all even or all odd: nothing to do
    even_end.next = odd_start        # join the chains
    odd_end.next = None              # terminate — or the list gets a cycle
    return even_start

for values in ([17, 15, 8, 12, 5], [1, 3, 5], [1, 2, 4]):
    print(to_str(segregate(build(values))))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* segregate(Node* head) {
    Node *evenStart = nullptr, *evenEnd = nullptr;
    Node *oddStart = nullptr, *oddEnd = nullptr;
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next) {
        if (curr->data % 2 == 0) {
            if (!evenStart) evenStart = evenEnd = curr;
            else { evenEnd->next = curr; evenEnd = curr; }   // append to the even chain
        } else {
            if (!oddStart) oddStart = oddEnd = curr;
            else { oddEnd->next = curr; oddEnd = curr; }     // append to the odd chain
        }
    }
    if (!evenStart || !oddStart) return head;   // all even or all odd: nothing to do
    evenEnd->next = oddStart;                    // join the chains
    oddEnd->next = nullptr;                      // terminate — or the list gets a cycle
    return evenStart;
}

int main() {
    for (vector<int> values : {vector<int>{17, 15, 8, 12, 5}, vector<int>{1, 3, 5}, vector<int>{1, 2, 4}})
        cout << toStr(segregate(build(values))) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node next;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static Node build(int[] v) {
        Node head = null;
        for (int i = v.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            Node node = new Node(v[i]);
            node.next = head;
            head = node;
        }
        return head;
    }

    static String toStr(Node head) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) sb.append(c.data).append(c.next != null ? " " : "");
        return sb.toString();
    }

    static Node segregate(Node head) {
        Node evenStart = null, evenEnd = null, oddStart = null, oddEnd = null;
        for (Node curr = head; curr != null; curr = curr.next) {
            if (curr.data % 2 == 0) {
                if (evenStart == null) evenStart = evenEnd = curr;
                else { evenEnd.next = curr; evenEnd = curr; }   // append to the even chain
            } else {
                if (oddStart == null) oddStart = oddEnd = curr;
                else { oddEnd.next = curr; oddEnd = curr; }     // append to the odd chain
            }
        }
        if (evenStart == null || oddStart == null) return head;  // all even or all odd
        evenEnd.next = oddStart;                 // join the chains
        oddEnd.next = null;                      // terminate — or the list gets a cycle
        return evenStart;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int[] values : new int[][]{{17, 15, 8, 12, 5}, {1, 3, 5}, {1, 2, 4}})
            System.out.println(toStr(segregate(build(values))));
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(data) { this.data = data; this.next = null; }
}

function build(values) {
    let head = null;
    for (let i = values.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        const node = new Node(values[i]);
        node.next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

function toStr(head) {
    const parts = [];
    for (let c = head; c; c = c.next) parts.push(c.data);
    return parts.join(" ");
}

function segregate(head) {
    let evenStart = null, evenEnd = null, oddStart = null, oddEnd = null;
    for (let curr = head; curr; curr = curr.next) {
        if (curr.data % 2 === 0) {
            if (!evenStart) evenStart = evenEnd = curr;
            else { evenEnd.next = curr; evenEnd = curr; }       // append to the even chain
        } else {
            if (!oddStart) oddStart = oddEnd = curr;
            else { oddEnd.next = curr; oddEnd = curr; }         // append to the odd chain
        }
    }
    if (!evenStart || !oddStart) return head;    // all even or all odd: nothing to do
    evenEnd.next = oddStart;                     // join the chains
    oddEnd.next = null;                          // terminate — or the list gets a cycle
    return evenStart;
}

for (const values of [[17, 15, 8, 12, 5], [1, 3, 5], [1, 2, 4]])
    console.log(toStr(segregate(build(values))));
Output
8 12 17 15 5
1 3 5
2 4 1
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

odd_end.next = None is the line everyone forgets. If the last node of the input is even, the odd tail still points at some even node that is now earlier in the list — and the result has a cycle that to_str would loop on forever. The same two-chain pattern solves “partition a list around a value x” and “odd/even positions” (LeetCode 328).

Pairwise swap nodes
Example

Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
Output: 2 → 1 → 4 → 3
Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
Output: 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5 (odd one out stays)

Swap the data. Walk two nodes at a time and exchange the values of each pair. Trivial — but it only works when swapping values is allowed and cheap. If nodes carry large payloads, or other code holds references to specific nodes (an LRU cache, an iterator), the values must stay with their nodes and the links have to be swapped instead.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def pairwise_swap_data(head):
    curr = head
    while curr and curr.next:        # at least one node ahead
        curr.data, curr.next.data = curr.next.data, curr.data
        curr = curr.next.next        # jump over the pair
    return head

for values in ([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]):
    print(to_str(pairwise_swap_data(build(values))))
Output
2 1 4 3
2 1 4 3 5
Time O(n)Space O(1)

Swap the links. For each pair a → b, make the node before the pair point at b, b point at a, and a point at whatever followed b. A dummy node in front of the head removes the special case for the first pair (whose “node before” would otherwise not exist), and the new head is simply dummy.next.

Three link changes per pair; prev moves to a, the pair's new tail
prev → a → b → rest            before

a.next = b.next   :  prev → a ─────▶ rest
                              b ──▶ rest
b.next = a        :  b → a → rest
prev.next = b     :  prev → b → a → rest
prev = a          :  ready for the next pair
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        node = Node(v)
        node.next = head
        head = node
    return head

def to_str(head):
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(str(head.data))
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def pairwise_swap(head):
    dummy = Node(0)                  # sits before the head: no special first pair
    dummy.next = head
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next and prev.next.next:
        a = prev.next                # first node of the pair
        b = a.next                   # second node of the pair
        a.next = b.next              # a now points past the pair
        b.next = a                   # b points back at a
        prev.next = b                # the node before the pair points at b
        prev = a                     # a is the pair's new tail
    return dummy.next

for values in ([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]):
    print(to_str(pairwise_swap(build(values))))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr) {}
};

Node* build(const vector<int>& v) {
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int i = (int)v.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        Node* node = new Node(v[i]);
        node->next = head;
        head = node;
    }
    return head;
}

string toStr(Node* head) {
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) s += to_string(c->data) + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* pairwiseSwap(Node* head) {
    Node dummy(0);                       // sits before the head: no special first pair
    dummy.next = head;
    Node* prev = &dummy;
    while (prev->next && prev->next->next) {
        Node* a = prev->next;            // first node of the pair
        Node* b = a->next;               // second node of the pair
        a->next = b->next;               // a now points past the pair
        b->next = a;                     // b points back at a
        prev->next = b;                  // the node before the pair points at b
        prev = a;                        // a is the pair's new tail
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

int main() {
    for (vector<int> values : {vector<int>{1, 2, 3, 4}, vector<int>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}})
        cout << toStr(pairwiseSwap(build(values))) << "\n";
}

            Node b = a.next;                 // second node of the pair

        const a = prev.next;                 // first node of the pair
        const b = a.next;                    // second node of the pair
        a.next = b.next;                     // a now points past the pair
        b.next = a;                          // b points back at a

2 1 4 3 5
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Pairwise swap is “reverse in groups of k” with k = 2 and a short tail left alone. The dummy-head trick is worth memorising: it turns every “what if it is the first node?” branch into ordinary code.

Clone a linked list with random pointers
Example

Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 with random links 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
Output: an independent copy with the same next and random structure

Each node has a second pointer, random, to any node in the list (or null). A plain copy that walks next cannot set random on the copies because the target copy may not exist yet — and even when it does, you have to find it. Two solutions: a map from original to copy, or a trick that stores the mapping inside the list itself.

A list whose random pointers can jump anywhere — forwards, backwards or to itself
        ┌─────────────────┐
        │        ┌────────┼───────┐
        ▼        │        │       ▼
1 ───▶ 2 ───▶ 3 ───▶ 4      next (solid)
│      ▲        │        ▲     random: 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
└──────┼────────┘        │
       └─────────────────┘

Method 1 — dictionary from original to copy. Pass 1 creates a copy of every node and records copy_of[original] = copy. Pass 2 sets copy_of[node].next = copy_of[node.next] and copy_of[node].random = copy_of[node.random]; mapping null → null makes the end of the list and missing randoms fall out for free.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None
        self.random = None

def pairs(head):                     # "data:random data:random …"
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(f"{head.data}:{head.random.data if head.random else '-'}")
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def clone(head):
    copy_of = {None: None}           # original → copy; None maps to None
    curr = head
    while curr:                      # pass 1: create the copies
        copy_of[curr] = Node(curr.data)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = head
    while curr:                      # pass 2: wire next and random via the map
        copy_of[curr].next = copy_of[curr.next]
        copy_of[curr].random = copy_of[curr.random]
        curr = curr.next
    return copy_of[head]

nodes = [Node(v) for v in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
for i in range(3):
    nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1]
for i, r in enumerate((2, 0, 3, 1)):     # 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
    nodes[i].random = nodes[r]
head = nodes[0]
copy = clone(head)
print("original:", pairs(head))
print("clone:   ", pairs(copy))
print("after adding 100 to every original node")
for n in nodes:
    n.data += 100
print("original:", pairs(head))
print("clone:   ", pairs(copy))      # unchanged: it shares no node with the original
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next; Node* random;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr), random(nullptr) {}
};

string pairs(Node* head) {                 // "data:random data:random …"
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next)
        s += to_string(c->data) + ":" + (c->random ? to_string(c->random->data) : "-") + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* clone(Node* head) {
    unordered_map<Node*, Node*> copyOf;    // original → copy
    copyOf[nullptr] = nullptr;             // nullptr maps to nullptr
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next)   // pass 1: create the copies
        copyOf[c] = new Node(c->data);
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next) { // pass 2: wire next and random via the map
        copyOf[c]->next = copyOf[c->next];
        copyOf[c]->random = copyOf[c->random];
    }
    return copyOf[head];
}

int main() {
    vector<Node*> nodes;
    for (int v : {1, 2, 3, 4}) nodes.push_back(new Node(v));
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) nodes[i]->next = nodes[i + 1];
    int r[] = {2, 0, 3, 1};                // 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) nodes[i]->random = nodes[r[i]];
    Node* head = nodes[0];
    Node* copy = clone(head);
    cout << "original: " << pairs(head) << "\n";
    cout << "clone:    " << pairs(copy) << "\n";
    cout << "after adding 100 to every original node\n";
    for (Node* n : nodes) n->data += 100;
    cout << "original: " << pairs(head) << "\n";
    cout << "clone:    " << pairs(copy) << "\n";   // unchanged: shares no node with the original
}
Java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int data; Node next, random;
        Node(int d) { data = d; }
    }

    static String pairs(Node head) {         // "data:random data:random …"
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next)
            sb.append(c.data).append(':').append(c.random != null ? String.valueOf(c.random.data) : "-").append(c.next != null ? " " : "");
        return sb.toString();
    }

    static Node clone(Node head) {
        Map<Node, Node> copyOf = new HashMap<>();   // original → copy
        copyOf.put(null, null);                     // null maps to null
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next)  // pass 1: create the copies
            copyOf.put(c, new Node(c.data));
        for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next) {   // pass 2: wire next and random via the map
            copyOf.get(c).next = copyOf.get(c.next);
            copyOf.get(c).random = copyOf.get(c.random);
        }
        return copyOf.get(head);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node[] nodes = new Node[4];
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) nodes[i] = new Node(i + 1);
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1];
        int[] r = {2, 0, 3, 1};                  // 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) nodes[i].random = nodes[r[i]];
        Node head = nodes[0];
        Node copy = clone(head);
        System.out.println("original: " + pairs(head));
        System.out.println("clone:    " + pairs(copy));
        System.out.println("after adding 100 to every original node");
        for (Node n : nodes) n.data += 100;
        System.out.println("original: " + pairs(head));
        System.out.println("clone:    " + pairs(copy));   // unchanged: shares no node with the original
    }
}

Time O(n)Space O(n) for the map

Method 2 — interleave the copies, O(1) extra space. Store the mapping in the list: insert each copy right after its original, so original.next is always its copy. Then copy.random = original.random.next finds the right copy in O(1) without a map. Finally unweave the two lists.

1
Interleave
For every original node o, create o' and insert it after o: 1 → 1' → 2 → 2' → 3 → 3' → 4 → 4'.
2
Set randoms
For every original o (step two at a time): o.next.random = o.random.next — the copy of o.random is the node right after it. Skip when o.random is null.
3
Unweave
Restore o.next = o.next.next and set o'.next = o'.next.next, splitting the chain back into the original list and the clone.
The copy of any node is always the node right after it — that is the whole trick
after step 1:   1 → 1' → 2 → 2' → 3 → 3' → 4 → 4'

step 2 for node 2 (random → 1):  2.next.random = 2.random.next
                                 2'.random     = 1.next = 1'  ✓

after step 3:   1 → 2 → 3 → 4          original restored
                1' → 2' → 3' → 4'      clone, with randoms among the primed nodes
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None
        self.random = None

def pairs(head):                     # "data:random data:random …"
    parts = []
    while head:
        parts.append(f"{head.data}:{head.random.data if head.random else '-'}")
        head = head.next
    return " ".join(parts)

def clone(head):
    if head is None:
        return None
    curr = head
    while curr:                      # 1. insert a copy after every original
        copy = Node(curr.data)
        copy.next = curr.next
        curr.next = copy
        curr = copy.next
    curr = head
    while curr:                      # 2. copy.random = the copy of original.random
        if curr.random:
            curr.next.random = curr.random.next
        curr = curr.next.next
    clone_head = head.next
    curr = head
    while curr:                      # 3. unweave originals and copies
        copy = curr.next
        curr.next = copy.next
        copy.next = copy.next.next if copy.next else None
        curr = curr.next
    return clone_head

nodes = [Node(v) for v in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
for i in range(3):

    nodes[i].random = nodes[r]

print("after adding 100 to every original node")
for n in nodes:

print("original:", pairs(head))
print("clone:   ", pairs(copy))

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int data; Node* next; Node* random;
    Node(int d) : data(d), next(nullptr), random(nullptr) {}
};

string pairs(Node* head) {                 // "data:random data:random …"
    string s;
    for (Node* c = head; c; c = c->next)
        s += to_string(c->data) + ":" + (c->random ? to_string(c->random->data) : "-") + (c->next ? " " : "");
    return s;
}

Node* clone(Node* head) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next->next) {   // 1. insert a copy after every original
        Node* copy = new Node(curr->data);
        copy->next = curr->next;
        curr->next = copy;
    }
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next->next)     // 2. copy->random = copy of original->random
        if (curr->random) curr->next->random = curr->random->next;
    Node* cloneHead = head->next;
    for (Node* curr = head; curr; curr = curr->next) {         // 3. unweave originals and copies
        Node* copy = curr->next;
        curr->next = copy->next;
        copy->next = copy->next ? copy->next->next : nullptr;
    }
    return cloneHead;
}
