2 3 1 * + 9 - = -4
100 20 5 / - = 96
2 3 ^ 1 - = 7
Time O(n)Space O(n) for the operand stack
Pitfall

op1 = pop(); op2 = pop(); push(op2 op op1) — the original notes wrote it correctly, but swapping the two is the single most common bug: 10 2 - must give 8, not -8. Also tokenise on spaces when operands can have several digits; a character-by-character scan silently reads 10 as 1 and 0.

Infix to prefix
Example

Input: x+y*z
Output: +x*yz
Input: (a+b)*c
Output: *+abc
Input: a+b*(c-d)/e
Output: +a/*b-cde

By hand: fully parenthesise and convert from the innermost bracket outwards, writing each operator before its operands — x + (y * z) → x + (* y z) → + x * y z. With a stack there are two routes; the reversal trick reuses the postfix code almost unchanged.

Idea

Prefix is almost postfix read backwards: reverse the infix string (swapping ( with )), run the postfix algorithm, and reverse the result. The one subtlety is associativity, which flips with the reversal: in the reversed string a left-associative operator must not pop an equal-precedence top (otherwise a-b-c would come out as -a-bc = a-(b-c)), while the right-associative ^ must.

1
Reverse
Reverse the infix string and swap every ( with ): (a+b)*c → c*(b+a).
2
Convert
Run infix-to-postfix on it, popping on strictly higher precedence (or equal precedence when the operator is right-associative): c*(b+a) → cba+*.
3
Reverse again
Reverse the output: cba+* → *+abc.
Python
PREC = {'+': 1, '-': 1, '*': 2, '/': 2, '^': 3}
RIGHT_ASSOC = {'^'}

def infix_to_prefix(expr):
    rev = ''.join(')' if c == '(' else '(' if c == ')' else c for c in reversed(expr))
    out, st = [], []
    for ch in rev:
        if ch == ' ':
            continue
        if ch.isalnum():
            out.append(ch)
        elif ch == '(':
            st.append(ch)
        elif ch == ')':
            while st[-1] != '(':
                out.append(st.pop())
            st.pop()
        else:
            while (st and st[-1] != '(' and
                   (PREC[st[-1]] > PREC[ch] or
                    (PREC[st[-1]] == PREC[ch] and ch in RIGHT_ASSOC))):   # associativity flipped
                out.append(st.pop())
            st.append(ch)
    while st:
        out.append(st.pop())
    return ''.join(reversed(out))                                       # undo the reversal

for e in ["x+y*z", "(a+b)*c", "a+b*(c-d)/e", "a^b^c", "a-b-c"]:
    print(e, "→", infix_to_prefix(e))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <cctype>
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int prec(char op) {
    if (op == '^') return 3;
    if (op == '*' || op == '/') return 2;
    if (op == '+' || op == '-') return 1;
    return 0;
}
bool rightAssoc(char op) { return op == '^'; }

string infixToPrefix(string expr) {
    reverse(expr.begin(), expr.end());
    for (char& c : expr) c = c == '(' ? ')' : c == ')' ? '(' : c;   // swap the brackets
    string out;
    stack<char> st;
    for (char ch : expr) {
        if (ch == ' ') continue;
        if (isalnum(static_cast<unsigned char>(ch))) {
            out += ch;
        } else if (ch == '(') {
            st.push(ch);
        } else if (ch == ')') {
            while (st.top() != '(') { out += st.top(); st.pop(); }
            st.pop();
        } else {
            while (!st.empty() && st.top() != '(' &&
                   (prec(st.top()) > prec(ch) || (prec(st.top()) == prec(ch) && rightAssoc(ch)))) {
                out += st.top(); st.pop();                        // associativity flipped
            }
            st.push(ch);
        }
    }
    while (!st.empty()) { out += st.top(); st.pop(); }
    reverse(out.begin(), out.end());                              // undo the reversal
    return out;
}

int main() {
    for (string e : {"x+y*z", "(a+b)*c", "a+b*(c-d)/e", "a^b^c", "a-b-c"})
        cout << e << " → " << infixToPrefix(e) << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static int prec(char op) {
        if (op == '^') return 3;
        if (op == '*' || op == '/') return 2;
        if (op == '+' || op == '-') return 1;
        return 0;
    }
    static boolean rightAssoc(char op) { return op == '^'; }

    static String infixToPrefix(String expr) {
        StringBuilder rev = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = expr.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {              // reverse and swap the brackets
            char c = expr.charAt(i);
            rev.append(c == '(' ? ')' : c == ')' ? '(' : c);
        }
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char ch : rev.toString().toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == ' ') continue;
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(ch)) {
                out.append(ch);
            } else if (ch == '(') {
                st.push(ch);
            } else if (ch == ')') {
                while (st.peek() != '(') out.append(st.pop());
                st.pop();
            } else {
                while (!st.isEmpty() && st.peek() != '(' &&
                       (prec(st.peek()) > prec(ch) || (prec(st.peek()) == prec(ch) && rightAssoc(ch))))
                    out.append(st.pop());                        // associativity flipped
                st.push(ch);
            }
        }
        while (!st.isEmpty()) out.append(st.pop());
        return out.reverse().toString();                         // undo the reversal
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String e : new String[]{"x+y*z", "(a+b)*c", "a+b*(c-d)/e", "a^b^c", "a-b-c"})
            System.out.println(e + " → " + infixToPrefix(e));
    }
}
JavaScript
const PREC = { '+': 1, '-': 1, '*': 2, '/': 2, '^': 3 };
const RIGHT_ASSOC = new Set(['^']);
const isOperand = ch => /[A-Za-z0-9]/.test(ch);

function infixToPrefix(expr) {
    const rev = [...expr].reverse().map(c => c === '(' ? ')' : c === ')' ? '(' : c);   // swap the brackets
    const out = [], st = [];
    const top = () => st[st.length - 1];
    for (const ch of rev) {
        if (ch === ' ') continue;
        if (isOperand(ch)) {
            out.push(ch);
        } else if (ch === '(') {
            st.push(ch);
        } else if (ch === ')') {
            while (top() !== '(') out.push(st.pop());
            st.pop();
        } else {
            while (st.length && top() !== '(' &&
                   (PREC[top()] > PREC[ch] || (PREC[top()] === PREC[ch] && RIGHT_ASSOC.has(ch))))
                out.push(st.pop());                              // associativity flipped
            st.push(ch);
        }
    }
    while (st.length) out.push(st.pop());
    return out.reverse().join('');                               // undo the reversal
}

for (const e of ["x+y*z", "(a+b)*c", "a+b*(c-d)/e", "a^b^c", "a-b-c"])
    console.log(e, "→", infixToPrefix(e));
Output
x+y*z → +x*yz
(a+b)*c → *+abc
a+b*(c-d)/e → +a/*b-cde
a^b^c → ^a^bc
a-b-c → --abc
Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

Direct route without reversal: scan the infix right to left, treating ) as the opener and ( as the closer, collect operands and popped operators into a list, and reverse that list at the end — this is exactly the step list in the original notes (push operands to prefix, push ) to the stack, pop on (, compare precedence, finally reverse). The code above is the same algorithm with the reversal done up front, which lets it share its structure with the postfix converter.

Evaluating a prefix expression
Example

Input: + 10 * 2 3
Output: 16
Input: - + 7 * 4 5 2
Output: 25
Input: / 100 - 20 15
Output: 20

Idea

Mirror the postfix evaluator: scan right to left. Operands are pushed; an operator pops two values, but now the first pop is the left operand (it was closer to the operator in the original text). Push the result; the last remaining value is the answer.

Python
def apply(op, a, b):
    if op == '+': return a + b
    if op == '-': return a - b
    if op == '*': return a * b
    if op == '/': return a // b
    raise ValueError(op)

def eval_prefix(expr):
    st = []
    for tok in reversed(expr.split()):      # right to left
        if tok.isdigit():
            st.append(int(tok))
        else:
            left = st.pop()                 # first pop is the LEFT operand this time
            right = st.pop()
            st.append(apply(tok, left, right))
    return st[-1]

for e in ["+ 10 * 2 3", "- + 7 * 4 5 2", "/ 100 - 20 15"]:
    print(e, "=", eval_prefix(e))
C++
#include <cctype>
#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <stack>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

long long apply(const string& op, long long a, long long b) {
    if (op == "+") return a + b;
    if (op == "-") return a - b;
    if (op == "*") return a * b;
    return a / b;
}

long long evalPrefix(const string& expr) {
    vector<string> toks;
    istringstream in(expr);
    for (string t; in >> t;) toks.push_back(t);
    stack<long long> st;
    for (int i = (int)toks.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {         // right to left
        if (isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char>(toks[i].back()))) {
            st.push(stoll(toks[i]));
        } else {
            long long left = st.top(); st.pop();              // first pop is the LEFT operand this time
            long long right = st.top(); st.pop();
            st.push(apply(toks[i], left, right));
        }
    }
    return st.top();
}

int main() {
    for (string e : {"+ 10 * 2 3", "- + 7 * 4 5 2", "/ 100 - 20 15"})
        cout << e << " = " << evalPrefix(e) << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static long apply(String op, long a, long b) {
        switch (op) {
            case "+": return a + b;
            case "-": return a - b;
            case "*": return a * b;
            default:  return a / b;
        }
    }

    static long evalPrefix(String expr) {
        String[] toks = expr.split(" ");
        Deque<Long> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = toks.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {              // right to left
            if (Character.isDigit(toks[i].charAt(toks[i].length() - 1))) {
                st.push(Long.parseLong(toks[i]));
            } else {
                long left = st.pop();                             // first pop is the LEFT operand this time
                long right = st.pop();
                st.push(apply(toks[i], left, right));
            }
        }
        return st.peek();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String e : new String[]{"+ 10 * 2 3", "- + 7 * 4 5 2", "/ 100 - 20 15"})
            System.out.println(e + " = " + evalPrefix(e));
    }
}
JavaScript
function apply(op, a, b) {
    switch (op) {
        case '+': return a + b;
        case '-': return a - b;
        case '*': return a * b;
        case '/': return Math.trunc(a / b);
    }
    throw new Error(op);
}

function evalPrefix(expr) {
    const toks = expr.split(' ');
    const st = [];
    for (let i = toks.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {                  // right to left
        if (/\d$/.test(toks[i])) {
            st.push(Number(toks[i]));
        } else {
            const left = st.pop();                                // first pop is the LEFT operand this time
            const right = st.pop();
            st.push(apply(toks[i], left, right));
        }
    }
    return st[st.length - 1];
}

for (const e of ["+ 10 * 2 3", "- + 7 * 4 5 2", "/ 100 - 20 15"])
    console.log(e, "=", evalPrefix(e));

+ 10 * 2 3 = 16
- + 7 * 4 5 2 = 25
/ 100 - 20 15 = 20

The three notations side by side
InfixPostfixPrefix
Operator positionbetween operandsafter operandsbefore operands
Needs brackets / precedenceyesnono
Evaluation scanneeds two stacks or a parserleft → right, one stackright → left, one stack
First pop on an operator is—the right operandthe left operand
Tree traversalinorderpostorderpreorder
Used bypeople, source codeJVM / CPython bytecode, PostScript, RPN calculatorsLisp, some compilers' IRs
Interview Q&A
Why do compilers and virtual machines prefer postfix?

Because it maps directly onto a stack machine: each operand becomes a push, each operator a pop-pop-compute-push. No lookahead, no precedence table, one pass. The parser deals with precedence once, when it converts the source expression; the runtime never sees it again.

How does the shunting-yard algorithm handle associativity?

Only in the equal-precedence case. For a left-associative incoming operator, an equal-precedence top is popped first (so a - b - c → a b - c -); for a right-associative one (^) it stays, so the later operator is output first (a ^ b ^ c → a b c ^ ^).

Can you evaluate an infix expression directly, without converting first?

Yes — Dijkstra's two-stack algorithm: one stack for values and one for operators. It is the shunting-yard algorithm where, instead of outputting a popped operator, you immediately apply it to the top two values. The conversion and the evaluation are the same control flow with a different action.

What is wrong with evaluating postfix character by character?

Multi-digit numbers break: 10 2 * would be read as 1, 0, 2. Tokenise on spaces (or scan runs of digits) first. The same goes for identifiers longer than one character and for a unary minus, which needs its own token type.

How are the three notations related to the expression tree?

They are its three depth-first traversals: preorder prints the operator first (prefix), inorder prints it between the subtrees (infix, which is why it needs brackets to recover the structure), postorder prints it last (postfix). Both prefix and postfix determine the tree uniquely; infix without brackets does not.

Linked Lists, Stacks & Queues

Queue & Deque

A queue is First In, First Out; a deque (double-ended queue) lets you insert and remove at both ends in O(1). The advanced problems here use the queue for breadth-first generation and the deque as a sliding window that keeps only the candidates that can still matter.

Deque — a linear container with O(1) pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack, front and back. Restricting it to pushBack + popFront gives a queue; pushBack + popBack gives a stack — one structure covers both.

A deque: both ends are open
pushFront(x) ──▶ ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ ◀── pushBack(x)
popFront()   ◀── │ 20 │ 10 │ 15 │ 30 │ 7  │ ──▶ popBack()
                 └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
                  front                back
Operations and the built-in containers
OperationPython collections.dequeC++ std::dequeJava ArrayDequeJavaScript
push backappend(x)push_back(x)addLast(x) / offer(x)arr.push(x)
push frontappendleft(x)push_front(x)addFirst(x) / push(x)arr.unshift(x) — O(n)
pop frontpopleft()pop_front() (+ front())pollFirst() / poll()arr.shift() — O(n)
pop backpop()pop_back() (+ back())pollLast()arr.pop()
peek front / backdq[0] / dq[-1]front() / back()peekFirst() / peekLast()arr[0] / arr[arr.length-1]
Watch out

JavaScript has no built-in deque. shift() and unshift() move every element, so a queue built on them is O(n) per operation. For small inputs it does not matter (the first two problems below use it for brevity); for real workloads keep a head index into the array (arr[head++] to dequeue — see the sliding-window solution) or write a small ring-buffer / two-index Deque class (see the min/max structure).

Python's deque, C++'s std::deque and Java's ArrayDeque are all O(1) at both ends. std::queue and std::stack are thin adapters over std::deque; Java's Queue and Deque interfaces are both implemented by ArrayDeque (prefer it over LinkedList, which allocates a node per element).

Reverse a queue
Example

Input: q = [20, 10, 15, 30] (20 at the front)
Output: 30 15 10 20

Idea

A stack reverses order. Dequeue everything into a stack, then pop everything back into the queue: the last element out of the queue is the first one pushed back. Only queue operations (enqueue, dequeue) and a stack are used — the queue is treated as a black box.

Python
from collections import deque

def reverse_queue(q):
    st = []
    while q:
        st.append(q.popleft())     # drain the queue into a stack
    while st:
        q.append(st.pop())         # refill: last out of the queue goes in first

q = deque([20, 10, 15, 30])
reverse_queue(q)
print(*q)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

void reverseQueue(queue<int>& q) {
    stack<int> st;
    while (!q.empty()) { st.push(q.front()); q.pop(); }   // drain the queue into a stack
    while (!st.empty()) { q.push(st.top()); st.pop(); }   // refill: last out goes in first
}

int main() {
    queue<int> q;
    for (int x : {20, 10, 15, 30}) q.push(x);
    reverseQueue(q);
    while (!q.empty()) { cout << q.front() << " "; q.pop(); }
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static void reverseQueue(Queue<Integer> q) {
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        while (!q.isEmpty()) st.push(q.poll());   // drain the queue into a stack
        while (!st.isEmpty()) q.add(st.pop());    // refill: last out goes in first
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int x : new int[]{20, 10, 15, 30}) q.add(x);
        reverseQueue(q);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (!q.isEmpty()) sb.append(q.poll()).append(' ');
        System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
    }
}
JavaScript
function reverseQueue(q) {
    const st = [];
    while (q.length) st.push(q.shift());     // drain the queue into a stack (shift is O(n) in JS)
    while (st.length) q.push(st.pop());      // refill: last out goes in first
}

const q = [20, 10, 15, 30];
reverseQueue(q);
console.log(q.join(" "));
Output
30 15 10 20
Time O(n)Space O(n) for the stack

Recursive version. The call stack is the stack: dequeue the front, reverse the rest recursively, then enqueue the front at the back. The deepest call enqueues the last element first.

Python
from collections import deque

def reverse_queue(q):
    if not q:
        return
    front = q.popleft()      # take the front out …
    reverse_queue(q)         # … reverse the remaining n-1 …
    q.append(front)          # … and put the old front at the back

q = deque([20, 10, 15, 30])
reverse_queue(q)
print(*q)

Pitfall

The recursive version uses n stack frames — Python's default limit is about 1000, so it is a teaching tool, not a production routine. The iterative version has the same complexity without the depth limit.

Generate the first n numbers with given digits
Example

Input: n = 10, digits = [5, 6]
Output: 5 6 55 56 65 66 555 556 565 566
Input: n = 7, digits = [1, 2, 3]
Output: 1 2 3 11 12 13 21

Print, in increasing order, the first n positive integers whose decimal digits all come from the given set.

Naive — test every natural number; with digits {5, 6} only 2^k of the k-digit numbers qualify, so this gets slow fast
def only_digits(num, digits):
    while num > 0:
        if num % 10 not in digits:
            return False
        num //= 10
    return True

def first_n_naive(n, digits):
    res, num = [], 1
    while len(res) < n:                 # try 1, 2, 3, … and keep the ones that qualify
        if only_digits(num, digits):
            res.append(num)
        num += 1
    return res

print(*first_n_naive(10, [5, 6]))
Output
5 6 55 56 65 66 555 556 565 566
Idea

The valid numbers form a tree: the children of x are x with each allowed digit appended. A breadth-first traversal of that tree visits the numbers in increasing order — all 1-digit numbers, then all 2-digit numbers (smaller prefixes first), and so on. BFS is a queue: start with the single digits, repeatedly dequeue a number, print it, and enqueue its children. Each dequeue produces exactly one answer, so the loop runs n times.

BFS order of the digit tree is numeric order, because every level is one digit longer and siblings are enqueued smallest-first
           (root)
        /          \
       5            6                 ← dequeued 1st, 2nd
     /   \        /   \
   55     56    65     66             ← 3rd … 6th
  /  \   /  \
555 556 565 566 …                     ← 7th … 10th
Python
from collections import deque

def first_n(n, digits):
    q = deque(str(d) for d in sorted(digits))   # level 1: the single digits, smallest first
    res = []
    while len(res) < n:
        cur = q.popleft()
        res.append(cur)
        for d in sorted(digits):
            q.append(cur + str(d))              # children: one digit longer
    return res

print(*first_n(10, [5, 6]))
print(*first_n(7, [1, 2, 3]))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<string> firstN(int n, vector<int> digits) {
    sort(digits.begin(), digits.end());
    queue<string> q;
    for (int d : digits) q.push(to_string(d));     // level 1: the single digits, smallest first
    vector<string> res;
    while ((int)res.size() < n) {
        string cur = q.front(); q.pop();
        res.push_back(cur);
        for (int d : digits) q.push(cur + to_string(d));   // children: one digit longer
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    for (const string& s : firstN(10, {5, 6})) cout << s << " ";
    cout << "\n";
    for (const string& s : firstN(7, {1, 2, 3})) cout << s << " ";
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static List<String> firstN(int n, int[] digits) {
        Arrays.sort(digits);
        Queue<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int d : digits) q.add(String.valueOf(d));   // level 1: the single digits, smallest first
        List<String> res = new ArrayList<>();
        while (res.size() < n) {
            String cur = q.poll();
            res.add(cur);
            for (int d : digits) q.add(cur + d);          // children: one digit longer
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(String.join(" ", firstN(10, new int[]{5, 6})));
        System.out.println(String.join(" ", firstN(7, new int[]{1, 2, 3})));
    }
}

function firstN(n, digits) {
    digits = [...digits].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const q = digits.map(String);                  // level 1: the single digits, smallest first
    const res = [];
    while (res.length < n) {
        const cur = q.shift();
        res.push(cur);
        for (const d of digits) q.push(cur + d);   // children: one digit longer
    }
    return res;
}

console.log(firstN(7, [1, 2, 3]).join(" "));

5 6 55 56 65 66 555 556 565 566
1 2 3 11 12 13 21
Time O(n × k) for k allowed digitsSpace O(n × k) queue
Key point

Work with strings, not integers: appending a digit is string concatenation, and the numbers quickly exceed 64 bits (the 20th number with digits {5, 6} already has 5 digits; the 10 000th has 13). The original notes hard-coded '5' and '6'; the version above takes any digit set and sorts it so BFS order is numeric order.

Data structure with min/max operations

Design a structure supporting all of the following in O(1): insertMin(x), insertMax(x), getMin(), getMax(), extractMin(), extractMax().

Example

Input: insertMin(5), insertMax(10), insertMin(3), insertMax(12); getMin, getMax, extractMin, getMin, extractMax, getMax
Output: 3 12 3 5 12 10

Idea

insertMin(x) is only ever called with a value that is the new minimum, and insertMax(x) only with the new maximum — that contract is what makes O(1) possible (a general priority queue needs O(log n)). So keep the elements sorted in a deque: the minimum lives at the front, the maximum at the back. insertMin = pushFront, insertMax = pushBack, getMin/getMax = front/back, extractMin/extractMax = popFront/popBack. Every operation is one deque operation.

The deque stays sorted because insertMin/insertMax only ever add at the correct end
insertMin(5)      [5]
insertMax(10)     [5, 10]
insertMin(3)      [3, 5, 10]          ← front is always the min
insertMax(12)     [3, 5, 10, 12]      ← back is always the max
extractMin() → 3  [5, 10, 12]
extractMax() → 12 [5, 10]
Python
from collections import deque

class MinMaxStructure:
    def __init__(self):
        self.dq = deque()            # kept sorted: front = min, back = max

    def insert_min(self, x):         # contract: x <= current min
        self.dq.appendleft(x)

    def insert_max(self, x):         # contract: x >= current max
        self.dq.append(x)

    def get_min(self):
        return self.dq[0]

    def get_max(self):
        return self.dq[-1]

    def extract_min(self):
        return self.dq.popleft()

    def extract_max(self):
        return self.dq.pop()

s = MinMaxStructure()
s.insert_min(5)
s.insert_max(10)
s.insert_min(3)
s.insert_max(12)
print("getMin:", s.get_min())
print("getMax:", s.get_max())
print("extractMin:", s.extract_min())
print("getMin:", s.get_min())
print("extractMax:", s.extract_max())
print("getMax:", s.get_max())

class MinMaxStructure {
    deque<int> dq;                   // kept sorted: front = min, back = max
public:
    void insertMin(int x) { dq.push_front(x); }   // contract: x <= current min
    void insertMax(int x) { dq.push_back(x); }    // contract: x >= current max
    int getMin() const { return dq.front(); }
    int getMax() const { return dq.back(); }
    int extractMin() { int x = dq.front(); dq.pop_front(); return x; }
    int extractMax() { int x = dq.back(); dq.pop_back(); return x; }
};

        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();     // kept sorted: front = min, back = max
        void insertMin(int x) { dq.addFirst(x); }   // contract: x <= current min
        void insertMax(int x) { dq.addLast(x); }    // contract: x >= current max
        int getMin() { return dq.peekFirst(); }
        int getMax() { return dq.peekLast(); }
        int extractMin() { return dq.pollFirst(); }

JavaScript
class Deque {                        // O(1) at both ends: indices grow outwards from 0
    constructor() { this.items = {}; this.head = 0; this.tail = 0; }   // tail = one past the last
    pushFront(x) { this.items[--this.head] = x; }
    pushBack(x) { this.items[this.tail++] = x; }
    popFront() { const x = this.items[this.head]; delete this.items[this.head++]; return x; }
    popBack() { const x = this.items[--this.tail]; delete this.items[this.tail]; return x; }
    front() { return this.items[this.head]; }
    back() { return this.items[this.tail - 1]; }
    get size() { return this.tail - this.head; }
}

class MinMaxStructure {
    constructor() { this.dq = new Deque(); }       // kept sorted: front = min, back = max
    insertMin(x) { this.dq.pushFront(x); }         // contract: x <= current min
    insertMax(x) { this.dq.pushBack(x); }          // contract: x >= current max
    getMin() { return this.dq.front(); }
    getMax() { return this.dq.back(); }
    extractMin() { return this.dq.popFront(); }
    extractMax() { return this.dq.popBack(); }
}

Pitfall

State the contract out loud in an interview: this structure is correct only if insertMin is always given a value no larger than the current minimum and insertMax a value no smaller than the current maximum (the original notes called it a 'MinMaxStack' and did not say so). Insert 7 into [3, 5, 10, 12] through either method and the sorted order — and every later answer — is wrong. For arbitrary inserts you need a min-max heap or two heaps (O(log n)).

Maximums of all subarrays of size k (sliding window maximum)
Example

Input: arr = [10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6], k = 3
Output: 10 12 15 15 15

For every window of k consecutive elements, print its maximum. The windows here are [10,8,5], [8,5,12], [5,12,15], [12,15,7], [15,7,6].

Naive — O(n·k): recompute the maximum of every window
def window_max_naive(arr, k):
    res = []
    for i in range(len(arr) - k + 1):
        res.append(max(arr[i:i + k]))    # rescan each window
    return res

print(*window_max_naive([10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6], 3))
Output
10 12 15 15 15
Idea

Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing from front to back — the monotonic-stack idea from the Stack topic, with one extra operation. When arr[i] arrives, pop from the back every index whose value is <= arr[i] (they can never be a window maximum again: arr[i] is bigger and will outlive them). Push i at the back. Pop from the front the index that has slid out of the window (front <= i − k). The front is now the maximum of the current window. The deque is the set of elements that are still useful — each is the maximum of the suffix of the window that starts at it.

Front of the deque = maximum of the current window; every index enters and leaves at most once
arr = [10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6], k = 3        deque holds indices; shown as values

i  arr[i]  pop back while <= arr[i]   push   drop front if out of window   deque (values)   window max
0   10     –                          0      –                             [10]             (window not full)
1    8     –                          1      –                             [10, 8]          (window not full)
2    5     –                          2      –                             [10, 8, 5]       10
3   12     5, 8, 10                   3      –                             [12]             12
4   15     12                         4      –                             [15]             15
5    7     –                          5      –                             [15, 7]          15
6    6     –                          6      index 4 still inside          [15, 7, 6]       15
Python
from collections import deque

def window_max(arr, k):
    dq = deque()                 # indices; arr values decreasing front → back
    res = []
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        while dq and arr[dq[-1]] <= arr[i]:   # smaller-or-equal older elements are useless now
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
        if dq[0] <= i - k:                    # front has slid out of the window
            dq.popleft()
        if i >= k - 1:                        # window is full: front is its maximum
            res.append(arr[dq[0]])
    return res

print(*window_max([10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6], 3))
C++
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> windowMax(const vector<int>& arr, int k) {
    deque<int> dq;               // indices; arr values decreasing front → back
    vector<int> res;
    int n = arr.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (!dq.empty() && arr[dq.back()] <= arr[i]) dq.pop_back();   // useless now
        dq.push_back(i);
        if (dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();   // front has slid out of the window
        if (i >= k - 1) res.push_back(arr[dq.front()]);   // window is full: front is its max
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    for (int x : windowMax({10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6}, 3)) cout << x << " ";
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static int[] windowMax(int[] arr, int k) {
        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();   // indices; arr values decreasing front → back
        int n = arr.length;
        int[] res = new int[n - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && arr[dq.peekLast()] <= arr[i]) dq.pollLast();   // useless now
            dq.addLast(i);
            if (dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // front has slid out of the window
            if (i >= k - 1) res[i - k + 1] = arr[dq.peekFirst()];   // window full: front is its max
        }
        return res;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int x : windowMax(new int[]{10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6}, 3)) sb.append(x).append(' ');
        System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
    }
}
JavaScript
function windowMax(arr, k) {
    const dq = [];               // indices; arr values decreasing front → back
    let head = 0;                // dq[head] is the front — no O(n) shift()
    const res = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
        while (dq.length > head && arr[dq[dq.length - 1]] <= arr[i]) dq.pop();   // useless now
        dq.push(i);
        if (dq[head] <= i - k) head++;                 // front has slid out of the window
        if (i >= k - 1) res.push(arr[dq[head]]);       // window is full: front is its maximum
    }
    return res;
}

console.log(windowMax([10, 8, 5, 12, 15, 7, 6], 3).join(" "));
Output
10 12 15 15 15
Time O(n) — each index is pushed and popped at most onceSpace O(k) for the deque
Pitfall

Store indices, not values — you need the index to know when the front has left the window. And pop from the back on <=, not <: an older equal element leaves the window earlier than the new one, so keeping it would only make the deque longer. The first k − 1 iterations do not emit anything; the original notes handled that with a separate warm-up loop, the version above folds it into one loop with the i >= k − 1 test.

Variants

The same deque gives the sliding window minimum by flipping the comparison to >=. It is also the engine behind O(n) solutions for shortest subarray with sum at least k and the monotonic-queue optimisation of some DP recurrences.

First circular tour (petrol pumps)
Example

Input: petrol = [4, 8, 7, 4], dist = [6, 5, 3, 5] (pumps numbered from 1)
Output: 2
Input: petrol = [1, 2, 3], dist = [3, 3, 3]
Output: -1

n petrol pumps sit on a circle. Pump i offers petrol[i] litres, and dist[i] litres are burned driving from pump i to pump i + 1. Starting with an empty tank, find the first pump from which a truck can complete the full circle, or report that none exists. Here the net gain at each pump is -2, 3, 4, -1; starting at pump 2 the tank reads 3 → 7 → 6 → 4, never negative.

Naive — O(n²): simulate the circle from every start
def first_tour_naive(petrol, dist):
    n = len(petrol)
    for start in range(n):             # try every start …
        fuel, i = 0, start
        while True:                    # … and simulate the whole circle
            fuel += petrol[i] - dist[i]
            if fuel < 0:
                break
            i = (i + 1) % n
            if i == start:
                return start + 1
    return -1

print(first_tour_naive([4, 8, 7, 4], [6, 5, 3, 5]))
print(first_tour_naive([1, 2, 3], [3, 3, 3]))
Output
2
-1
Idea

Think of the visited pumps as a queue. If the tank goes negative on reaching pump i after starting at s, then every start between s and i fails too: the tank was non-negative on arrival at each of them, so starting there with an empty tank only makes things worse. Dequeue them all at once — the next candidate start is i + 1. Each pump is enqueued (visited as part of a tour) and dequeued (ruled out) at most once, so one pass suffices. Finally, the candidate that survives to the end is valid only if the total surplus (what it gains after its start plus the deficit of the skipped prefix it still has to cross) is >= 0.

1
Scan once
Keep start = 0, fuel = 0 (fuel since start) and deficit = 0 (total shortfall of all ruled-out prefixes).
2
On a negative tank at pump i
Everything from start to i is ruled out: deficit += fuel, start = i + 1, fuel = 0.
3
At the end
start completes the circle only if fuel + deficit >= 0 — the surplus it collects from start to n − 1 must cover the deficit of the wrapped-around prefix. Otherwise no pump works (equivalently, sum(petrol) < sum(dist)).
Python
def first_tour(petrol, dist):
    start, fuel, deficit = 0, 0, 0
    for i in range(len(petrol)):
        fuel += petrol[i] - dist[i]
        if fuel < 0:                 # pumps start..i are all ruled out at once
            deficit += fuel          # remember how short that stretch was
            start = i + 1
            fuel = 0
    return start + 1 if fuel + deficit >= 0 else -1   # 1-based pump number

print(first_tour([4, 8, 7, 4], [6, 5, 3, 5]))
print(first_tour([1, 2, 3], [3, 3, 3]))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int firstTour(const vector<int>& petrol, const vector<int>& dist) {
    int start = 0, fuel = 0, deficit = 0;
    int n = petrol.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        fuel += petrol[i] - dist[i];
        if (fuel < 0) {              // pumps start..i are all ruled out at once
            deficit += fuel;         // remember how short that stretch was
            start = i + 1;
            fuel = 0;
        }
    }
    return fuel + deficit >= 0 ? start + 1 : -1;   // 1-based pump number
}

int main() {
    cout << firstTour({4, 8, 7, 4}, {6, 5, 3, 5}) << "\n";
    cout << firstTour({1, 2, 3}, {3, 3, 3}) << "\n";
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Why the final check is enough. If sum(petrol) >= sum(dist) a tour always exists, and the scan above finds the first one: every start before start was explicitly ruled out, and start itself never ran dry on the stretch to the end; wrapping around, it meets the ruled-out prefixes with fuel in the tank, and fuel + deficit >= 0 says that is enough. The explicit queue version (two indices start, end walking around the circle, dequeuing from the front while the tank is negative) is the same argument spelled out with (end + 1) % n arithmetic.

Pitfall

The answer is the pump number, and the original notes count from 1 (start + 1); many online judges count from 0. Say which convention you use. Also do not forget the -1 case — with start ending at n (every pump ruled out) the start + 1 formula would otherwise return a nonsense n + 1.

Interview Q&A
Queue vs deque vs priority queue — when do I use which?

A queue when the order of processing is the order of arrival (BFS, task scheduling). A deque when you also need the other end: sliding windows, work-stealing, palindromes, undo/redo with a bounded history. A priority queue when the next element is determined by a key, not by position — it costs O(log n) per operation instead of O(1).

Why is the sliding window maximum O(n) if there is a while loop inside the for loop?

Every index is appended once and removed at most once (from the back by a bigger element, or from the front by sliding out). Total deque operations are at most 2n, so the amortised cost per element is constant — the same argument as for the monotonic stack.

How would you implement a deque yourself?

A circular array with head and tail indices (and either a size counter or one wasted slot to tell full from empty) gives O(1) at both ends with cache-friendly storage; grow by doubling when full. A doubly linked list also works but spends a node per element. collections.deque uses blocks of 64 pointers in a doubly linked list of blocks; ArrayDeque is a circular array.

How would you generate the numbers in the digit problem without a queue?

Treat the index as a counter in base k (the number of digits) with a bijective numeration: the m-th number's digits are the base-k representation of m with digits mapped through the sorted digit set. That is O(log m) per number and needs no memory — but the BFS version is the one interviewers expect first, because it generalises to any 'generate in order by extending' problem.

Why does the petrol-pump argument rule out all pumps between the start and the failure point?

Suppose the tour from s first goes negative on arriving at i. For any s < t <= i, the tank on arrival at t (from s) was non-negative, so starting at t with an empty tank gives at every later pump at most the fuel the s-tour had there — and that went negative at i. So t fails too, and the next possible start is i + 1.

Trees & Heaps

Tree Data Structure

You already know the traversals and height(). This topic is the problem toolkit for binary trees: level-by-level BFS, horizontal distances, the return height, record the answer on the side pattern, two-stack tricks and (de)serialisation — the handful of techniques behind almost every tree interview question.

Binary tree — a hierarchical structure in which every node has at most two children, left and right. Unlike a BST there is no ordering rule, so every problem here must be solved by visiting nodes, not by comparing keys.

The sample tree used by every program in this topic (9 nodes, height 4)
      10
    /    \
  20      30
 /  \    /  \
40  50  60   70
            /  \
           80   90
Conventions used in these notes
TermMeaning hereSample tree
Heightnumber of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path; an empty tree has height 04 (10 → 30 → 70 → 80)
Levelroot is level 0, its children level 1, …4 levels (0–3)
Diameternumber of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes6 (40 20 10 30 70 80)
Horizontal distance (hd)root 0; a left child is hd − 1, a right child hd + 140 is at −2, 90 at +3
Balancedfor every node, |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1yes
Completeall levels full except possibly the last, which is filled left to rightno (gap under 40/50/60)
Key point

Height is counted in nodes here, as in the original notes (a single node has height 1). Some books count edges — then every formula shifts by one. State your convention in an interview before writing code.

Node class and the sample tree

Every program in this topic starts with the same Node class and a sample() builder that constructs the tree above by nesting constructor calls. Here it is with three warm-ups you already know: inorder, height and node count.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():                      # the tree used throughout these notes
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def inorder(n):
    if n is None:
        return
    inorder(n.left)
    print(n.key, end=" ")
    inorder(n.right)

def height(n):                     # in nodes: a single node has height 1
    if n is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(height(n.left), height(n.right))

def count_nodes(n):
    return 0 if n is None else 1 + count_nodes(n.left) + count_nodes(n.right)

root = sample()
print("inorder:", end=" "); inorder(root); print()
print("height:", height(root))
print("nodes:", count_nodes(root))

Key point

JavaScript's console.log always ends the line, so the programs use process.stdout.write when a value must be followed by a space instead of a newline — exactly what print(x, end=" ") does in Python.

The technique toolbox

Almost every problem below is one of five patterns. Recognise the pattern and the code writes itself.

Level-by-level BFS

Queue; take len(queue) nodes per round. Gives level order, width, zigzag, bottom view.

Return height, record on the side

A post-order recursion returns one value (height) while a shared variable collects the answer: balanced, diameter, burn time.

Horizontal distance map

Carry hd with each node; group by it in an ordered map: vertical traversal, top/bottom view.

Preorder + inorder

Preorder gives the root, inorder splits left from right: tree construction, serialisation.

Explicit stack

Simulate the recursion yourself: iterative inorder/preorder, two-stack spiral.

Structural shortcuts

Exploit shape: a perfect subtree has 2^h − 1 nodes, so a complete tree is counted in O(log² n).

Level order traversal line by line
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 | 20 30 | 40 50 60 70 | 80 90 (| = new line)

Plain BFS prints all keys on one line. To start a new line after every level you need to know where a level ends. There are two classic ways.

Idea

Method 1 — a marker. Push a None sentinel after the root. Whenever the sentinel comes out of the queue the current level is finished: print a newline and push the sentinel again so it sits behind the next level. Stop when the sentinel is the only thing left.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def print_levels(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    q = deque([root, None])          # None marks the end of a level
    while len(q) > 1:                # only the marker left → done
        curr = q.popleft()
        if curr is None:
            print()                  # level finished: newline, re-arm the marker
            q.append(None)
            continue
        print(curr.key, end=" ")
        if curr.left:
            q.append(curr.left)
        if curr.right:
            q.append(curr.right)
    print()

40 50 60 70

Time O(n)Space O(w) — w = maximum width
Pitfall

Looping while q instead of while len(q) > 1 never terminates: the marker keeps re-adding itself to an otherwise empty queue. In Java, ArrayDeque throws on add(null) — use LinkedList for this method, or the count method below which needs no marker.

Idea

Method 2 — count the level. At the start of each round len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes on the current level. Pop that many, printing them and enqueuing their children, then print a newline. No sentinel, no special cases — this is the version to remember, and the backbone of width, zigzag and bottom-view problems.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def print_levels(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        for _ in range(len(q)):      # exactly the nodes of this level
            curr = q.popleft()
            print(curr.key, end=" ")
            if curr.left:
                q.append(curr.left)
            if curr.right:
                q.append(curr.right)
        print()                      # level done

Time O(n)Space O(w)
Pitfall

Read len(q) once, before the inner loop. Writing for _ in range(len(q)) is safe in Python because the range is evaluated once, but while i < q.size() in C++/Java re-reads a size that grows as children are added and merges levels.

Check for balanced binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: Yes
Input: the sample tree with 100 added under 80
Output: No

A tree is balanced when every node's two subtrees differ in height by at most 1
balanced (Yes)                         not balanced (No)
          10                                   10
        /    \                               /    \
      20      30                           20      30   ← left height 1,
     /  \    /  \                         /  \    /  \    right height 3
    40  50  60   70                      40  50  60   70
                /  \                                 /  \
               80   90                              80   90
                                                   /
                                                 100
Idea

Naive: for every node compute the heights of both subtrees and compare, then recurse into the children. Correct, but height() is itself O(n), and it is called again for every node — O(n · h), which is O(n²) on a skewed tree.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def height(n):
    return 0 if n is None else 1 + max(height(n.left), height(n.right))

def is_balanced(n):
    if n is None:
        return True
    lh, rh = height(n.left), height(n.right)          # O(n) each, for every node
    return abs(lh - rh) <= 1 and is_balanced(n.left) and is_balanced(n.right)

root = sample()
print("sample tree:", "Yes" if is_balanced(root) else "No")
root.right.right.left.left = Node(100)                # hang 100 under 80
print("with 100 under 80:", "Yes" if is_balanced(root) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdlib>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

int height(Node* n) { return n ? 1 + max(height(n->left), height(n->right)) : 0; }

bool isBalanced(Node* n) {
    if (!n) return true;
    int lh = height(n->left), rh = height(n->right);   // O(n) each, for every node
    return abs(lh - rh) <= 1 && isBalanced(n->left) && isBalanced(n->right);
}

int main() {
    Node* root = sample();
    cout << "sample tree: " << (isBalanced(root) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    root->right->right->left->left = new Node(100);    // hang 100 under 80
    cout << "with 100 under 80: " << (isBalanced(root) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}

with 100 under 80: No
Time O(n · h) — O(n²) when skewedSpace O(h) recursion
Idea

Efficient — the −1 trick. Let one post-order function return the height of a subtree, but return −1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced. A parent that receives −1 from a child passes it straight up without recursing further. Each node is visited once, so the whole check is O(n).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def check(n):                      # height of n, or -1 if the subtree is unbalanced
    if n is None:
        return 0
    lh = check(n.left)
    if lh == -1:
        return -1                  # short-circuit: no need to look at the right side
    rh = check(n.right)
    if rh == -1 or abs(lh - rh) > 1:
        return -1
    return 1 + max(lh, rh)

def is_balanced(root):
    return check(root) != -1

root = sample()
print("sample tree:", "Yes" if is_balanced(root) else "No")
root.right.right.left.left = Node(100)
print("with 100 under 80:", "Yes" if is_balanced(root) else "No")

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pattern

The same shape — a post-order function that returns one quantity and smuggles a second one out — solves diameter, burn time and many more. Learn it once.

Vertical traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 | 20 | 10 50 60 | 30 80 | 70 | 90 (| = new line, one line per column)

Every node gets a horizontal distance: left child hd − 1, right child hd + 1
hd:   -2   -1    0    1    2    3
                10
           20        30
      40       50 60      70
                     80       90

column -2: 40      column 1: 30 80
column -1: 20      column 2: 70
column  0: 10 50 60   column 3: 90
Idea

Carry the horizontal distance with every node in a level-order traversal and group keys by it in an ordered map. BFS order guarantees that inside one column the upper node comes before the lower one, and that at the same level the left one comes first — exactly the order a vertical traversal wants. Sorting the keys of the map (or using an ordered map) prints the columns from left to right.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def vertical(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    groups = {}                                   # hd → keys in level order
    q = deque([(root, 0)])                        # node travels with its hd
    while q:
        node, hd = q.popleft()
        groups.setdefault(hd, []).append(node.key)
        if node.left:
            q.append((node.left, hd - 1))
        if node.right:
            q.append((node.right, hd + 1))
    for hd in sorted(groups):                     # leftmost column first
        print(*groups[hd])

vertical(sample())
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

void vertical(Node* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    map<int, vector<int>> groups;                 // std::map is ordered: leftmost column first
    queue<pair<Node*, int>> q;                    // node travels with its hd
    q.push({root, 0});
    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto [node, hd] = q.front(); q.pop();
        groups[hd].push_back(node->key);
        if (node->left) q.push({node->left, hd - 1});
        if (node->right) q.push({node->right, hd + 1});
    }
    for (auto& column : groups) {
        const vector<int>& keys = column.second;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < keys.size(); i++) cout << (i ? " " : "") << keys[i];
        cout << "\n";
    }
}

int main() { vertical(sample()); }
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
        Node(int k, Node l, Node r) { key = k; left = l; right = r; }
    }
    static Node sample() {
        return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                            new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
    }

    static void vertical(Node root) {
        if (root == null) return;
        TreeMap<Integer, List<Integer>> groups = new TreeMap<>();   // sorted by hd
        Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Queue<Integer> hds = new ArrayDeque<>();                     // hd travels next to its node
        q.add(root); hds.add(0);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            Node node = q.poll();
            int hd = hds.poll();
            groups.computeIfAbsent(hd, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(node.key);
            if (node.left != null) { q.add(node.left); hds.add(hd - 1); }
            if (node.right != null) { q.add(node.right); hds.add(hd + 1); }
        }
        for (List<Integer> keys : groups.values()) {           // leftmost column first
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int k : keys) sb.append(k).append(' ');
            System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { vertical(sample()); }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(key, left = null, right = null) { this.key = key; this.left = left; this.right = right; }
}
const sample = () =>
    new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                 new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));

function vertical(root) {
    if (!root) return;
    const groups = new Map();                       // hd → keys in level order
    const q = [[root, 0]];                          // node travels with its hd
    while (q.length) {
        const [node, hd] = q.shift();
        if (!groups.has(hd)) groups.set(hd, []);
        groups.get(hd).push(node.key);
        if (node.left) q.push([node.left, hd - 1]);
        if (node.right) q.push([node.right, hd + 1]);
    }
    const hds = [...groups.keys()].sort((a, b) => a - b);   // leftmost column first
    for (const hd of hds) console.log(groups.get(hd).join(" "));
}

vertical(sample());

40
20
10 50 60
30 80
70
90
Time O(n log n) — sorting / ordered map over the columnsSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Use BFS, not a preorder DFS, to fill the map. With DFS the node 50 (hd 0, level 2) would be recorded before 60 (hd 0, level 2) — fine — but 80 (hd 1, level 3) would come before 30 (hd 1, level 1), which is wrong: within a column the order must be top to bottom.

Bottom view of a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 60 80 70 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(30, 40), 50(60, 70))
Output: 30 20 60 50 70

Idea

The bottom view shows, for every column (hd), the lowest node — and when two nodes share both the column and the level, the one further to the right (the one BFS visits later). So run the same hd-tagged BFS and simply let every node overwrite its column's entry: the last write per column is the bottom view. Keeping the first write per column instead gives the top view for free.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def views(root):
    bottom, top = {}, {}
    q = deque([(root, 0)])
    while q:
        node, hd = q.popleft()
        bottom[hd] = node.key                 # a later node in BFS order overwrites
        if hd not in top:
            top[hd] = node.key                # the first node seen in a column stays
        if node.left:
            q.append((node.left, hd - 1))
        if node.right:
            q.append((node.right, hd + 1))
    print("bottom:", *(bottom[hd] for hd in sorted(bottom)))
    print("top:", *(top[hd] for hd in sorted(top)))

Key point

In the original notes' tree, 40 (right child of 20) and 60 (left child of 50) both sit at hd 0 on the same level. BFS visits 40 first and 60 second, so 60 overwrites and wins — that is the convention: ties go to the node further right. Had you used a DFS the winner would depend on traversal order, which is why the queue matters here.

Maximum width of a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 4 (level 2 holds 40 50 60 70)
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40(80)), 30(50, 60))
Output: 3

Idea

Width is the number of nodes on a level, and the level-by-level BFS already knows that number: it is len(queue) at the start of each round. Keep the maximum over all rounds — no printing needed.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def max_width(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    q = deque([root])
    best = 0
    while q:
        count = len(q)                   # size of the current level
        best = max(best, count)
        for _ in range(count):
            node = q.popleft()
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
    return best

print("max width:", max_width(sample()))

    if (!root) return 0;
    queue<Node*> q;

        best = max(best, count);

            if (node->left) q.push(node->left);

    }
    return best;
}

Variant

This counts present nodes per level. LeetCode's Maximum Width of Binary Tree counts the span between the leftmost and rightmost node including gaps — for that, carry an index i with each node (2i and 2i + 1 for its children) and take last − first + 1 per level.

Convert a binary tree to a doubly linked list
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 <-> 20 <-> 50 <-> 10 <-> 60 <-> 30 <-> 80 <-> 70 <-> 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(5, 20(30, 35))
Output: 5 <-> 10 <-> 30 <-> 20 <-> 35

Idea

The list must be in inorder, and the node's own left / right pointers become prev / next — no new nodes. Do an inorder traversal and keep a shared prev, the node visited just before the current one: link prev.right = node, node.left = prev, then advance prev. The first node ever visited (when prev is still None) is the head.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

prev = None                                   # node visited just before the current one

def to_dll(node):                             # returns the head of the list
    global prev
    if node is None:
        return None
    head = to_dll(node.left)                  # inorder: left subtree first
    if prev is None:
        head = node                           # first node visited → head
    else:
        prev.right = node                     # link prev <-> node
        node.left = prev
    prev = node
    to_dll(node.right)
    return head

head = to_dll(sample())
keys, tail = [], None
n = head
while n:
    keys.append(str(n.key)); tail = n; n = n.right
print("forward:", " <-> ".join(keys))
print("backward:", end=" ")
while tail:
    print(tail.key, end=" "); tail = tail.left
print()
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

Node* last = nullptr;                          // node visited just before the current one (`prev` would clash with std::prev)

Node* toDLL(Node* node) {                      // returns the head of the list
    if (!node) return nullptr;
    Node* head = toDLL(node->left);            // inorder: left subtree first
    if (!last) {
        head = node;                           // first node visited → head
    } else {
        last->right = node;                    // link last <-> node
        node->left = last;
    }
    last = node;
    toDLL(node->right);
    return head;
}

int main() {
    Node* head = toDLL(sample());
    Node* tail = nullptr;
    cout << "forward: ";
    for (Node* n = head; n; n = n->right) {
        cout << (n == head ? "" : " <-> ") << n->key;
        tail = n;
    }
    cout << "\nbackward: ";
    for (Node* n = tail; n; n = n->left) cout << n->key << " ";
    cout << "\n";
}

public class Main {

        Node(int k) { key = k; }

        if (prev == null) {

        } else {

            node.left = prev;

backward: 90 70 80 30 60 10 50 20 40
Time O(n)Space O(h) recursion — no extra nodes
Pitfall

Recurse into node.left before touching node.left — the recursion needs the original pointer. Setting node.left = prev first and then calling to_dll(node.left) walks back into the list and loops forever. The same applies to prev: it must be a variable shared across all calls (global / static / closure), not a parameter, or a deeper call's update is lost.

Construct a binary tree from inorder and preorder
Example

Input: pre = [10 20 40 50 30 60 70 80 90], in = [40 20 50 10 60 30 80 70 90]
Output: the sample tree (printed level by level)
Input: pre = [10 20 30], in = [20 10 30]
Output: 10 | 20 30

Idea

Preorder tells you the root, inorder tells you the split. The first preorder key is the root. Find it in the inorder sequence: everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Recurse on the two halves, consuming preorder keys from a shared index — the left subtree is built first, so it takes the next keys, exactly as preorder lays them out.

One step of the construction: the next 3 preorder keys build the left subtree, the remaining 5 the right one
pre = 10 | 20 40 50 | 30 60 70 80 90           root = pre[0] = 10
in  = 40 20 50 | 10 | 60 30 80 70 90           left of 10 in inorder → left subtree
      ^^^^^^^^        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^           right of 10 → right subtree
      left (3 keys)   right (5 keys)

The straightforward version searches the inorder slice linearly for the root — O(n) per node, O(n²) in total on a skewed tree:

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

pre_index = 0                                   # next preorder key to use

def build(pre, ino, lo, hi):                    # builds the subtree whose inorder is ino[lo..hi]
    global pre_index
    if lo > hi:
        return None
    root = Node(pre[pre_index])
    pre_index += 1
    mid = ino.index(root.key, lo, hi + 1)       # linear search → O(n) per node
    root.left = build(pre, ino, lo, mid - 1)    # left first: it consumes the next preorder keys
    root.right = build(pre, ino, mid + 1, hi)
    return root

def print_levels(root):
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        print(*(n.key for n in q))
        q = deque(c for n in q for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)

pre = [10, 20, 40, 50, 30, 60, 70, 80, 90]
ino = [40, 20, 50, 10, 60, 30, 80, 70, 90]
print_levels(build(pre, ino, 0, len(ino) - 1))
Output
10
20 30
40 50 60 70
80 90
Idea

Efficient: store the inorder position of every key in a hash map once (O(n)); then each root is located in O(1) and the whole tree is built in O(n). This is the version to remember.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def build_tree(pre, ino):
    pos = {key: i for i, key in enumerate(ino)}     # key → index in inorder
    state = {"next": 0}                             # next preorder key to use

    def build(lo, hi):                              # subtree whose inorder is ino[lo..hi]
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root = Node(pre[state["next"]])
        state["next"] += 1
        mid = pos[root.key]                         # O(1) split point
        root.left = build(lo, mid - 1)              # left first (preorder order)
        root.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return root

    return build(0, len(ino) - 1)

def print_levels(root):
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        print(*(n.key for n in q))
        q = deque(c for n in q for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)

pre = [10, 20, 40, 50, 30, 60, 70, 80, 90]
ino = [40, 20, 50, 10, 60, 30, 80, 70, 90]
print_levels(build_tree(pre, ino))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};

unordered_map<int, int> pos;                      // key → index in inorder
int nextPre = 0;                                  // next preorder key to use

Node* build(const vector<int>& pre, int lo, int hi) {   // subtree whose inorder is in[lo..hi]
    if (lo > hi) return nullptr;
    Node* root = new Node(pre[nextPre++]);
    int mid = pos[root->key];                     // O(1) split point
    root->left = build(pre, lo, mid - 1);         // left first (preorder order)
    root->right = build(pre, mid + 1, hi);
    return root;
}

void printLevels(Node* root) {
    queue<Node*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int count = q.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            Node* n = q.front(); q.pop();
            cout << (i ? " " : "") << n->key;
            if (n->left) q.push(n->left);
            if (n->right) q.push(n->right);
        }
        cout << "\n";
    }
}

int main() {
    vector<int> pre = {10, 20, 40, 50, 30, 60, 70, 80, 90};
    vector<int> in = {40, 20, 50, 10, 60, 30, 80, 70, 90};
    int n = in.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pos[in[i]] = i;
    printLevels(build(pre, 0, n - 1));
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Map<Integer, Integer> pos = new HashMap<>();   // key → index in inorder
    static int nextPre = 0;                               // next preorder key to use

    static Node build(int[] pre, int lo, int hi) {        // subtree whose inorder is in[lo..hi]
        if (lo > hi) return null;
        Node root = new Node(pre[nextPre++]);
        int mid = pos.get(root.key);                      // O(1) split point
        root.left = build(pre, lo, mid - 1);              // left first (preorder order)
        root.right = build(pre, mid + 1, hi);
        return root;
    }

    static void printLevels(Node root) {
        Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.add(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int count = q.size();
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                Node n = q.poll();
                sb.append(i > 0 ? " " : "").append(n.key);
                if (n.left != null) q.add(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.add(n.right);
            }
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] pre = {10, 20, 40, 50, 30, 60, 70, 80, 90};
        int[] in = {40, 20, 50, 10, 60, 30, 80, 70, 90};
        for (int i = 0; i < in.length; i++) pos.put(in[i], i);
        printLevels(build(pre, 0, in.length - 1));
    }
}

class Node {

}

    let nextPre = 0;                                        // next preorder key to use

        if (lo > hi) return null;
        const root = new Node(pre[nextPre++]);
        const mid = pos.get(root.key);                      // O(1) split point
        root.left = build(lo, mid - 1);                     // left first (preorder order)

40 50 60 70
80 90
Time O(n)Space O(n) for the map + O(h) recursion
Pitfall

Build the left subtree before the right one — the shared preorder index only works in that order. And the method assumes distinct keys: with duplicates the inorder position is ambiguous and no inorder + preorder pair identifies a unique tree. (Inorder + postorder works the same way, reading postorder from the back; preorder + postorder alone is not enough.)

Corrected

The original notes' 'efficient' version used a stack and stack[-1].key in io[:mp[value]], which re-scans a slice of the inorder list for every node — O(n²) again. The hash-map recursion above is the genuinely linear version.

Spiral (zigzag) level order traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 30 20 40 50 60 70 90 80
Input: the original notes' tree 10(5, 20(30, 35))
Output: 10 20 5 30 35

Even levels (0, 2, …) are printed left to right, odd levels right to left — so level 1 of the sample prints 30 20 and level 3 prints 90 80.

Idea

Method 1 — level order + a stack. Run the count-based level-by-level BFS. On a normal level print each node as it is dequeued; on a reversed level push the keys onto a stack instead and pop them all once the level is done — popping reverses the order. Toggle the flag after every level.

Python
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def spiral(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    q = deque([root])
    stack = []
    reverse = False                           # level 0 is left to right
    while q:
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            if reverse:
                stack.append(node.key)        # hold back, print reversed later
            else:
                print(node.key, end=" ")
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        while stack:                          # empty only on reversed levels
            print(stack.pop(), end=" ")
        reverse = not reverse
    print()

            else cout << node->key << " ";

            cout << st.top() << " ";
            st.pop();
        }
        reverse = !reverse;
    }

        Queue<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        boolean reverse = false;                  // level 0 is left to right

                else sb.append(node.key).append(' ');

                if (node.right != null) q.add(node.right);

            while (!stack.isEmpty()) sb.append(stack.pop()).append(' ');   // reversed levels only
            reverse = !reverse;
        }

Idea

Method 2 — two stacks. Let s1 hold the current left-to-right level and s2 the next one. Pop everything from s1, printing and pushing each node's children left then right into s2; because a stack reverses, s2 now pops right to left. Then pop everything from s2, pushing children right then left into s1, which reverses them back. Each stack hands the other exactly one level, already in the required order.

1
Start
Push the root onto s1.
2
While either stack is non-empty
Drain s1 (prints left → right): for each popped node push left, then right onto s2.
3
Then drain s2
(prints right → left): for each popped node push right, then left onto s1.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def spiral(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    s1, s2 = [root], []                       # s1: left→right level, s2: right→left level
    while s1 or s2:
        while s1:
            node = s1.pop()
            print(node.key, end=" ")
            if node.left:                     # left then right → s2 pops right first
                s2.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                s2.append(node.right)
        while s2:
            node = s2.pop()
            print(node.key, end=" ")
            if node.right:                    # right then left → s1 pops left first
                s1.append(node.right)
            if node.left:
                s1.append(node.left)
    print()

Pitfall

The two inner loops push children in opposite orders (left, right into s2 but right, left into s1). Swap one of them and every other level comes out in the wrong direction — trace the sample by hand once and the asymmetry becomes obvious.

Diameter of a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 6 (40 → 20 → 10 → 30 → 70 → 80, counted in nodes)

The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes — it need not pass through the root
              10
            /    \
          20      30
         /  \    /  \
        40  50  60   70
                    /  \
                   80   90

longest path: 40 – 20 – 10 – 30 – 70 – 80  (6 nodes, through the root)
another:      80 – 70 – 90                 (3 nodes, not through the root)
Idea

For every node, the longest path through it has 1 + height(left) + height(right) nodes. The diameter is the maximum of this value over all nodes. Naive: compute it at every node with a fresh height() call — O(n · h):

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def height(n):
    return 0 if n is None else 1 + max(height(n.left), height(n.right))

def diameter(n):
    if n is None:
        return 0
    through = 1 + height(n.left) + height(n.right)   # longest path through n — O(n) each time
    return max(through, diameter(n.left), diameter(n.right))

print("diameter:", diameter(sample()))
Output
diameter: 6
Idea

Efficient — return height, record the diameter on the side. The post-order function returns the height of its subtree (what the parent needs) and, before returning, updates a shared best with 1 + lh + rh (what the problem wants). Every node is visited once. The notes' intermediate version — a first pass that stores every height in a hash map, then a second pass — is also O(n), but the single-pass version below needs no map.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

best = 0                                   # the diameter, recorded on the side

def height(n):                             # returns height, updates best
    global best
    if n is None:
        return 0
    lh = height(n.left)
    rh = height(n.right)
    best = max(best, 1 + lh + rh)          # longest path through n
    return 1 + max(lh, rh)

height(sample())
print("diameter:", best)
