Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Do not return the diameter from the recursion — the parent needs the height. Returning max(lh, rh) + 1 while storing 1 + lh + rh elsewhere is the whole trick. (If the question counts edges, the answer is lh + rh with heights in edges — one less than here: 5 for the sample.)

Lowest common ancestor (LCA)
Example

Input: the sample tree, (40, 50)
Output: 20
Input: (80, 30)
Output: 30
Input: (50, 90)
Output: 10
Input: (80, 90)
Output: 70

Lowest common ancestor of `a` and `b` — the deepest node that has both a and b in its subtree. A node counts as its own ancestor, so LCA(80, 30) = 30.

Idea

Method 1 — two root-to-node paths. Record the path from the root to a and to b (a DFS that appends on the way down and pops on backtracking). Both paths start at the root; walk them in parallel while they agree — the last common node is the LCA. Two traversals and two O(h) paths; it also reports when a key is missing.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def find_path(n, key, path):               # fills path with root → key; False if absent
    if n is None:
        return False
    path.append(n.key)
    if n.key == key or find_path(n.left, key, path) or find_path(n.right, key, path):
        return True
    path.pop()                             # key not below n: backtrack
    return False

def lca(root, a, b):
    pa, pb = [], []
    if not find_path(root, a, pa) or not find_path(root, b, pb):
        return None                        # one of the keys is missing
    i = 0
    while i < len(pa) and i < len(pb) and pa[i] == pb[i]:
        i += 1                             # walk while the paths agree
    return pa[i - 1]                       # last node they shared

root = sample()
for a, b in [(40, 50), (80, 30), (50, 90), (80, 90)]:
    print(f"LCA({a}, {b}) = {lca(root, a, b)}")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

bool findPath(Node* n, int key, vector<int>& path) {   // fills path with root → key
    if (!n) return false;
    path.push_back(n->key);
    if (n->key == key || findPath(n->left, key, path) || findPath(n->right, key, path))
        return true;
    path.pop_back();                                   // key not below n: backtrack
    return false;
}

int lca(Node* root, int a, int b) {
    vector<int> pa, pb;
    if (!findPath(root, a, pa) || !findPath(root, b, pb)) return -1;   // a key is missing
    size_t i = 0;
    while (i < pa.size() && i < pb.size() && pa[i] == pb[i]) i++;    // walk while they agree
    return pa[i - 1];                                                 // last shared node
}

int main() {
    Node* root = sample();
    int pairs[4][2] = {{40, 50}, {80, 30}, {50, 90}, {80, 90}};
    for (auto& p : pairs)
        cout << "LCA(" << p[0] << ", " << p[1] << ") = " << lca(root, p[0], p[1]) << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
        Node(int k, Node l, Node r) { key = k; left = l; right = r; }
    }
    static Node sample() {
        return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                            new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
    }

    static boolean findPath(Node n, int key, List<Integer> path) {   // fills path with root → key
        if (n == null) return false;
        path.add(n.key);
        if (n.key == key || findPath(n.left, key, path) || findPath(n.right, key, path))
            return true;
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);                                // key not below n: backtrack
        return false;
    }

    static Integer lca(Node root, int a, int b) {
        List<Integer> pa = new ArrayList<>(), pb = new ArrayList<>();
        if (!findPath(root, a, pa) || !findPath(root, b, pb)) return null;   // a key is missing
        int i = 0;
        while (i < pa.size() && i < pb.size() && pa.get(i).equals(pb.get(i))) i++;   // walk while they agree
        return pa.get(i - 1);                                                        // last shared node
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node root = sample();
        int[][] pairs = {{40, 50}, {80, 30}, {50, 90}, {80, 90}};
        for (int[] p : pairs)
            System.out.println("LCA(" + p[0] + ", " + p[1] + ") = " + lca(root, p[0], p[1]));
    }
}

LCA(80, 30) = 30
LCA(50, 90) = 10
LCA(80, 90) = 70
Time O(n)Space O(h) for the two paths
Idea

Method 2 — one traversal. Ask each node what does your subtree contain? A node returns itself if its key is a or b; otherwise it asks both children. If both sides return something, the two keys are on different sides and this node is the LCA. If only one side does, pass that result up — it is either the LCA found deeper or the single key seen so far. Four cases, one post-order pass.

Case at node nReturn
n is a or bn (no need to look below: if the other key is beneath, n is still the LCA)
left returns a node and right returns a noden — the keys are on different sides
only one side returns a nodethat node (both keys are below it, or only one was found)
neither side returns a nodeNone
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def lca(n, a, b):
    if n is None:
        return None
    if n.key == a or n.key == b:
        return n                               # case 1: found one of the keys
    left = lca(n.left, a, b)
    right = lca(n.right, a, b)
    if left and right:
        return n                               # case 2: one key on each side → n is the LCA
    return left if left else right             # case 3/4: pass up whatever was found

root = sample()
for a, b in [(40, 50), (80, 30), (50, 90), (80, 90)]:
    print(f"LCA({a}, {b}) = {lca(root, a, b).key}")
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

Node* lca(Node* n, int a, int b) {
    if (!n) return nullptr;
    if (n->key == a || n->key == b) return n;         // case 1: found one of the keys
    Node* left = lca(n->left, a, b);
    Node* right = lca(n->right, a, b);
    if (left && right) return n;                      // case 2: one key on each side → n is the LCA
    return left ? left : right;                       // case 3/4: pass up whatever was found
}

int main() {
    Node* root = sample();
    int pairs[4][2] = {{40, 50}, {80, 30}, {50, 90}, {80, 90}};
    for (auto& p : pairs)
        cout << "LCA(" << p[0] << ", " << p[1] << ") = " << lca(root, p[0], p[1])->key << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
        Node(int k, Node l, Node r) { key = k; left = l; right = r; }
    }
    static Node sample() {
        return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                            new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
    }

    static Node lca(Node n, int a, int b) {
        if (n == null) return null;
        if (n.key == a || n.key == b) return n;           // case 1: found one of the keys
        Node left = lca(n.left, a, b);
        Node right = lca(n.right, a, b);
        if (left != null && right != null) return n;      // case 2: one key on each side → n is the LCA
        return left != null ? left : right;               // case 3/4: pass up whatever was found
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node root = sample();
        int[][] pairs = {{40, 50}, {80, 30}, {50, 90}, {80, 90}};
        for (int[] p : pairs)
            System.out.println("LCA(" + p[0] + ", " + p[1] + ") = " + lca(root, p[0], p[1]).key);
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(key, left = null, right = null) { this.key = key; this.left = left; this.right = right; }
}
const sample = () =>
    new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                 new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));

function lca(n, a, b) {
    if (!n) return null;
    if (n.key === a || n.key === b) return n;         // case 1: found one of the keys
    const left = lca(n.left, a, b);
    const right = lca(n.right, a, b);
    if (left && right) return n;                      // case 2: one key on each side → n is the LCA
    return left ? left : right;                       // case 3/4: pass up whatever was found
}

const root = sample();
for (const [a, b] of [[40, 50], [80, 30], [50, 90], [80, 90]])
    console.log(`LCA(${a}, ${b}) = ${lca(root, a, b).key}`);
Output
LCA(40, 50) = 20
LCA(80, 30) = 30
LCA(50, 90) = 10
LCA(80, 90) = 70
Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Method 2 assumes both keys exist. Ask for LCA(40, 999) and it happily returns 40 — the single key it found — because case 1 stops looking. Method 1 reports the missing key correctly. If keys may be absent, either verify existence first or have the recursion also return how many of the two keys it saw.

Burn a binary tree from a leaf
Example

Input: the sample tree, fire starts at leaf 50
Output: 5
Input: fire starts at leaf 60
Output: 4
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60)), leaf 50
Output: 4

Burn time = the distance from the leaf to the farthest node
fire starts at 50; each second it spreads to every neighbour (parent and children)

t=0: 50                       10 ←t=2
t=1: 20                     /    \
t=2: 10, 40           t=1→ 20      30 ←t=3
t=3: 30                   /  \    /  \
t=4: 60, 70       t=2→ 40  50  60   70 ←t=4
t=5: 80, 90                t=0  t=4   /  \
                                    80   90 ←t=5  → answer 5
Idea

The farthest node from the leaf is reached by going up to some ancestor and then down into that ancestor's other subtree. So for every ancestor n of the leaf, the candidate answer is dist(leaf, n) + height(other child of n). One post-order pass computes both: the function returns the height of a subtree (like before) and reports the leaf's distance through an out-parameter dist (−1 when the leaf is not below). At a node where dist came back from one side, update the answer with the other side's height.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

best = 0

def burn(n, leaf, dist):          # returns height; dist[0] = distance of leaf below n, or -1
    global best
    dist[0] = -1
    if n is None:
        return 0
    if n.key == leaf:
        dist[0] = 0               # the fire starts here
        return 1
    ldist, rdist = [-1], [-1]
    lh = burn(n.left, leaf, ldist)
    rh = burn(n.right, leaf, rdist)
    if ldist[0] != -1:            # leaf is in the left subtree
        dist[0] = ldist[0] + 1
        best = max(best, dist[0] + rh)    # up to n, then down the right side
    elif rdist[0] != -1:          # leaf is in the right subtree
        dist[0] = rdist[0] + 1
        best = max(best, dist[0] + lh)
    return 1 + max(lh, rh)

def burn_time(root, leaf):
    global best
    best = 0
    burn(root, leaf, [-1])
    return best

root = sample()
print("burn from 50:", burn_time(root, 50))
print("burn from 60:", burn_time(root, 60))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

int best = 0;

int burn(Node* n, int leaf, int& dist) {   // returns height; dist = distance of leaf below n, or -1
    dist = -1;
    if (!n) return 0;
    if (n->key == leaf) { dist = 0; return 1; }      // the fire starts here
    int ldist, rdist;
    int lh = burn(n->left, leaf, ldist);
    int rh = burn(n->right, leaf, rdist);
    if (ldist != -1) {                               // leaf is in the left subtree
        dist = ldist + 1;
        best = max(best, dist + rh);                 // up to n, then down the right side
    } else if (rdist != -1) {                        // leaf is in the right subtree
        dist = rdist + 1;
        best = max(best, dist + lh);
    }
    return 1 + max(lh, rh);
}

int burnTime(Node* root, int leaf) {
    best = 0;
    int d;
    burn(root, leaf, d);
    return best;
}

int main() {
    Node* root = sample();
    cout << "burn from 50: " << burnTime(root, 50) << "\n";
    cout << "burn from 60: " << burnTime(root, 60) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }

    }
    static Node sample() {
        return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                            new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
    }

    static int best = 0;

    static int burn(Node n, int leaf, int[] dist) {   // returns height; dist[0] = distance of leaf below n, or -1
        dist[0] = -1;
        if (n == null) return 0;
        if (n.key == leaf) { dist[0] = 0; return 1; }   // the fire starts here
        int[] ldist = {-1}, rdist = {-1};
        int lh = burn(n.left, leaf, ldist);
        int rh = burn(n.right, leaf, rdist);
        if (ldist[0] != -1) {                           // leaf is in the left subtree
            dist[0] = ldist[0] + 1;
            best = Math.max(best, dist[0] + rh);        // up to n, then down the right side
        } else if (rdist[0] != -1) {                    // leaf is in the right subtree

            best = Math.max(best, dist[0] + lh);
        }
        return 1 + Math.max(lh, rh);
    }

        best = 0;
        burn(root, leaf, new int[]{-1});
        return best;

let best = 0;

function burn(n, leaf, dist) {        // returns height; dist.v = distance of leaf below n, or -1
    dist.v = -1;
    if (!n) return 0;
    if (n.key === leaf) { dist.v = 0; return 1; }   // the fire starts here
    const ldist = { v: -1 }, rdist = { v: -1 };
    const lh = burn(n.left, leaf, ldist);
    const rh = burn(n.right, leaf, rdist);
    if (ldist.v !== -1) {                           // leaf is in the left subtree
        dist.v = ldist.v + 1;
        best = Math.max(best, dist.v + rh);         // up to n, then down the right side
    } else if (rdist.v !== -1) {                    // leaf is in the right subtree
        dist.v = rdist.v + 1;
        best = Math.max(best, dist.v + lh);
    }
    return 1 + Math.max(lh, rh);

    burn(root, leaf, { v: -1 });
    return best;

burn from 50: 5
burn from 60: 4
Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

The function returns 1 at the leaf and uses dist + height — this only adds up when the fire really starts at a leaf. Starting at an internal node also needs max(lh, rh) of that node's own subtree as a candidate, and the height returned there must be the real height, not 1. Interviewers love asking for that generalisation (minimum time to burn from any node); the BFS-on-parent-pointers approach handles it directly.

Count nodes in a complete binary tree
Example

Input: complete tree 10(20(40(80, 90), 50(100)), 30(60, 70))
Output: 10
Input: perfect tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60, 70))
Output: 7

A complete tree: every level full except the last, which fills from the left
        10                 left height  (10 20 40 80) = 4
      /    \               right height (10 30 70)    = 3   → not perfect, recurse
    20      30
   /  \    /  \            subtree 30: left 2, right 2 → perfect → 2² − 1 = 3 nodes
  40  50  60   70          subtree 20: left 3, right 2 → recurse
 /  \  /                     subtree 40: left 2, right 2 → perfect → 3 nodes
80 90 100                    subtree 50: left 2, right 1 → recurse → 2 nodes
                           total = 1 + (1 + 3 + 2) + 3 = 10
Idea

1 + count(left) + count(right) is O(n) and works for any tree. A complete tree has structure to exploit: walk down the leftmost and the rightmost path of a subtree. If the two heights are equal the subtree is perfect and has exactly 2^h − 1 nodes — no need to visit them. Otherwise recurse into both children, but at least one of them is perfect and answers immediately, so only one branch keeps recursing. O(log n) levels × O(log n) to measure the two heights = O(log² n).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def count_complete(n):
    lh = rh = 0
    cur = n
    while cur:                                # height along the leftmost path
        lh += 1
        cur = cur.left
    cur = n
    while cur:                                # height along the rightmost path
        rh += 1
        cur = cur.right
    if lh == rh:
        return (1 << lh) - 1                  # perfect subtree: 2^h - 1 nodes, no visit needed
    return 1 + count_complete(n.left) + count_complete(n.right)

complete = Node(10, Node(20, Node(40, Node(80), Node(90)), Node(50, Node(100))),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70)))
perfect = Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)), Node(30, Node(60), Node(70)))
print("complete tree (10 nodes):", count_complete(complete))
print("perfect tree (7 nodes):", count_complete(perfect))
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};

int countComplete(Node* n) {
    int lh = 0, rh = 0;
    for (Node* cur = n; cur; cur = cur->left) lh++;     // height along the leftmost path
    for (Node* cur = n; cur; cur = cur->right) rh++;    // height along the rightmost path
    if (lh == rh) return (1 << lh) - 1;                 // perfect subtree: 2^h - 1 nodes
    return 1 + countComplete(n->left) + countComplete(n->right);
}

int main() {
    Node* complete = new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40, new Node(80), new Node(90)), new Node(50, new Node(100))),
                                  new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70)));
    Node* perfect = new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)), new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70)));
    cout << "complete tree (10 nodes): " << countComplete(complete) << "\n";
    cout << "perfect tree (7 nodes): " << countComplete(perfect) << "\n";
}

public class Main {

        int lh = 0, rh = 0;
        for (Node cur = n; cur != null; cur = cur.left) lh++;     // height along the leftmost path
        for (Node cur = n; cur != null; cur = cur.right) rh++;    // height along the rightmost path
        if (lh == rh) return (1 << lh) - 1;                       // perfect subtree: 2^h - 1 nodes
        return 1 + countComplete(n.left) + countComplete(n.right);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Node perfect = new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)), new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70)));

JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(key, left = null, right = null) { this.key = key; this.left = left; this.right = right; }
}

function countComplete(n) {
    let lh = 0, rh = 0;
    for (let cur = n; cur; cur = cur.left) lh++;      // height along the leftmost path
    for (let cur = n; cur; cur = cur.right) rh++;     // height along the rightmost path
    if (lh === rh) return (1 << lh) - 1;              // perfect subtree: 2^h - 1 nodes
    return 1 + countComplete(n.left) + countComplete(n.right);
}

const complete = new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40, new Node(80), new Node(90)), new Node(50, new Node(100))),
                              new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70)));
const perfect = new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)), new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70)));

console.log("perfect tree (7 nodes):", countComplete(perfect));
Output
complete tree (10 nodes): 10
perfect tree (7 nodes): 7
Time O(log² n)Space O(log n)
Pitfall

The shortcut is only valid for a complete tree. On an arbitrary tree lh == rh does not imply a perfect subtree (a node with a left-only chain of 2 and a right-only chain of 2 has equal heights but 5 nodes, not 7) — use the plain O(n) count there. This is also why heaps, which are complete trees, can live in arrays.

Serialize and deserialize a binary tree
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 -1 -1 50 -1 -1 30 60 -1 -1 70 80 -1 -1 90 -1 -1 (preorder, −1 = empty)
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20, 30)
Output: 10 20 -1 -1 30 -1 -1

Serialization — turning a tree into a flat sequence (string or array) that can be stored or sent, such that deserialization rebuilds exactly the same tree. A single traversal order is not enough on its own — 10 20 could be a left child or a right child.

Idea

Approach A — inorder + separator + preorder. Two traversals identify a tree with distinct keys (see Construct from inorder and preorder). Store the inorder, a separator such as −1, then the preorder, and rebuild with the hash-map construction. It works, but needs distinct keys and twice the space:

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def inorder(n, out):
    if n:
        inorder(n.left, out); out.append(n.key); inorder(n.right, out)

def preorder(n, out):
    if n:
        out.append(n.key); preorder(n.left, out); preorder(n.right, out)

def serialize(root):
    arr = []
    inorder(root, arr)
    arr.append(-1)                                # separator
    preorder(root, arr)
    return arr

def deserialize(arr):
    sep = arr.index(-1)
    ino, pre = arr[:sep], arr[sep + 1:]
    pos = {key: i for i, key in enumerate(ino)}
    state = {"next": 0}
    def build(lo, hi):
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root = Node(pre[state["next"]]); state["next"] += 1
        mid = pos[root.key]
        root.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
        root.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return root
    return build(0, len(ino) - 1)

data = serialize(sample())
print("serialized:", *data)
again = serialize(deserialize(data))
print("round trip identical:", "Yes" if again == data else "No")
Output
serialized: 40 20 50 10 60 30 80 70 90 -1 10 20 40 50 30 60 70 80 90
round trip identical: Yes
Idea

Approach B — preorder with explicit empties (the one to remember). A preorder traversal becomes unambiguous as soon as every missing child is written down too: emit the key, recurse left, recurse right, and emit −1 for None. Deserialization reads the sequence in the same order with a shared index: read a value; if it is −1 return None, otherwise create the node and build its left then right child from the following values. Duplicates are fine, and the output is 2n + 1 values.

The −1 markers make the sequence decodable (assumption: −1 never appears as a key)
   10            preorder with empties:
  /  \           10  20 -1 -1  30 -1 -1
20    30             ^^^^^^^^  ^^^^^^^^
                 20 has no children, 30 has no children
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

EMPTY = -1

def serialize(n, out):                    # preorder, writing EMPTY for every missing child
    if n is None:
        out.append(EMPTY)
        return
    out.append(n.key)
    serialize(n.left, out)
    serialize(n.right, out)

def deserialize(arr, pos):                # pos[0] = next value to read, shared by all calls
    val = arr[pos[0]]
    pos[0] += 1
    if val == EMPTY:
        return None
    n = Node(val)
    n.left = deserialize(arr, pos)        # the following values describe the left subtree…
    n.right = deserialize(arr, pos)       # …then the right one
    return n

def inorder(n):
    if n:
        inorder(n.left); print(n.key, end=" "); inorder(n.right)

data = []
serialize(sample(), data)
print("serialized:", *data)
rebuilt = deserialize(data, [0])
print("rebuilt inorder:", end=" "); inorder(rebuilt); print()
again = []
serialize(rebuilt, again)
print("round trip identical:", "Yes" if again == data else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key; Node *left, *right;
    Node(int k, Node* l = nullptr, Node* r = nullptr) : key(k), left(l), right(r) {}
};
Node* sample() {
    return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                        new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
}

const int EMPTY = -1;

void serialize(Node* n, vector<int>& out) {     // preorder, writing EMPTY for every missing child
    if (!n) { out.push_back(EMPTY); return; }
    out.push_back(n->key);
    serialize(n->left, out);
    serialize(n->right, out);
}

Node* deserialize(const vector<int>& arr, int& pos) {   // pos = next value to read, shared
    int val = arr[pos++];
    if (val == EMPTY) return nullptr;
    Node* n = new Node(val);
    n->left = deserialize(arr, pos);            // the following values describe the left subtree…
    n->right = deserialize(arr, pos);           // …then the right one
    return n;
}

void inorder(Node* n) {
    if (!n) return;
    inorder(n->left); cout << n->key << " "; inorder(n->right);
}

int main() {
    vector<int> data;
    serialize(sample(), data);
    cout << "serialized:";
    for (int v : data) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
    int pos = 0;
    Node* rebuilt = deserialize(data, pos);
    cout << "rebuilt inorder: "; inorder(rebuilt); cout << "\n";
    vector<int> again;
    serialize(rebuilt, again);
    cout << "round trip identical: " << (again == data ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
        Node(int k, Node l, Node r) { key = k; left = l; right = r; }
    }
    static Node sample() {
        return new Node(10, new Node(20, new Node(40), new Node(50)),
                            new Node(30, new Node(60), new Node(70, new Node(80), new Node(90))));
    }

    static final int EMPTY = -1;
    static int pos = 0;                                 // next value to read, shared by all calls

    static void serialize(Node n, List<Integer> out) {  // preorder, writing EMPTY for every missing child
        if (n == null) { out.add(EMPTY); return; }
        out.add(n.key);
        serialize(n.left, out);
        serialize(n.right, out);
    }

    static Node deserialize(List<Integer> arr) {
        int val = arr.get(pos++);
        if (val == EMPTY) return null;
        Node n = new Node(val);
        n.left = deserialize(arr);                      // the following values describe the left subtree…
        n.right = deserialize(arr);                     // …then the right one
        return n;
    }

    static void inorder(Node n, StringBuilder sb) {
        if (n == null) return;
        inorder(n.left, sb); sb.append(n.key).append(' '); inorder(n.right, sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> data = new ArrayList<>();
        serialize(sample(), data);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("serialized:");
        for (int v : data) sb.append(' ').append(v);
        System.out.println(sb);
        pos = 0;
        Node rebuilt = deserialize(data);
        sb = new StringBuilder("rebuilt inorder: ");
        inorder(rebuilt, sb);
        System.out.println(sb.toString().trim());
        List<Integer> again = new ArrayList<>();
        serialize(rebuilt, again);
        System.out.println("round trip identical: " + (again.equals(data) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}

    n.right = deserialize(arr);               // …then the right one

Pitfall

The read index must be shared across the recursive calls (a global, a reference, or a one-element list) — passing an int by value makes every call re-read the same position. And reset it to 0 before deserializing a second sequence. If −1 can be a real key, pick a different marker (a string such as # or N in a text format).

Iterative inorder traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 50 10 60 30 80 70 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30)
Output: 40 20 10 30

Idea

Recursion keeps the pending nodes on the call stack; do it yourself with an explicit stack. From the current node, push every node on the way down the left spine. Then pop: the popped node is the next one in inorder (its left side is finished), print it, and move to its right child — and push that child's left spine in the same way. Stop when both the stack and the current pointer are empty.

1
Go left
While curr is not empty: push curr, curr = curr.left.
2
Visit
Pop the stack into curr and print it — everything to its left has been printed.
3
Go right
curr = curr.right, then repeat from step 1. Finished when the stack is empty and curr is empty.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def inorder(root):
    stack, curr = [], root
    while stack or curr:
        while curr:                        # push the whole left spine
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()                 # leftmost pending node
        print(curr.key, end=" ")
        curr = curr.right                  # now its right subtree, same procedure
    print()

Key point

The loop condition is stack or curr, not just stack: after popping the root (10) the stack may be empty while curr still points at the unvisited right subtree. The original notes avoided this by pre-pushing the left spine before the loop and re-pushing inside it — equivalent, but with the spine-push code written twice.

Iterative preorder traversal
Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 50 30 60 70 80 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60))
Output: 10 20 40 50 30 60

Idea

Version 1 — push right, then left. Preorder visits a node before its children, so a node can be printed the moment it is popped. Push the root; then repeatedly pop, print, and push the right child first and the left child second — the stack is LIFO, so the left child comes out next, exactly as preorder requires.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def preorder(root):
    if root is None:
        return
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        curr = stack.pop()
        print(curr.key, end=" ")           # visit on pop
        if curr.right:
            stack.append(curr.right)       # right first …
        if curr.left:
            stack.append(curr.left)        # … so that left is popped next
    print()

Idea

Version 2 — push only right children (space-optimised). Left children never need the stack: walk down the left spine printing each node as you go, and push only the right children you pass. When the spine ends, pop the most recent right child and continue from it. The stack now holds at most one node per level — O(h) instead of O(n).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right

def sample():
    return Node(10, Node(20, Node(40), Node(50)),
                    Node(30, Node(60), Node(70, Node(80), Node(90))))

def preorder(root):
    stack, curr = [], root
    while stack or curr:
        while curr:
            print(curr.key, end=" ")       # visit on the way down
            if curr.right:
                stack.append(curr.right)   # remember the right child for later
            curr = curr.left               # keep walking the left spine
        if stack:
            curr = stack.pop()             # resume at the most recent right child
    print()

Pitfall

Version 1 pushes the right child before the left. Push them the other way round and you get 10 30 70 90 80 60 20 50 40 — a mirrored preorder. The rule of thumb for every stack-based traversal: push in the reverse of the order you want to see.

Interview Q&A
Height, depth, level, diameter — what is the difference, and does it count nodes or edges?

Depth of a node is its distance from the root; level is depth (root = level 0). Height of a node is the longest downward path to a leaf; height of the tree is the root's height. Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes. Each may be counted in nodes or edges — the two conventions differ by one (a single node has height 1 in nodes, 0 in edges). These notes count nodes, like the original; say which you use before you code, and remember that the edge-diameter is lh + rh while the node-diameter is 1 + lh + rh.

Why does the 'return height, record the answer on the side' pattern keep showing up?

Because many tree quantities (balanced, diameter, burn time, maximum path sum) are defined per node as a combination of its two subtree heights, yet a parent only needs the height back. A single post-order pass returns the height to the parent and updates a shared answer variable as a side effect — O(n) instead of the O(n · h) you get from calling height() afresh at every node. Balanced-check uses −1 as a poison value so the recursion short-circuits.

Which traversals uniquely determine a binary tree?

Inorder together with preorder (or postorder) and distinct keys: the (pre/post)order supplies the root, the inorder splits left from right. Preorder + postorder alone do not (a root with a single child is ambiguous). Any single order determines a tree only if empties are recorded too — which is exactly the preorder-with-−1 serialization. For a BST preorder alone suffices, since inorder is implied by sorting.

How do the bottom view, top view and vertical traversal differ in code?

All three run the same BFS with a horizontal distance per node and a map keyed by hd. Vertical traversal appends every key to its column; top view keeps the first key per column (putIfAbsent); bottom view keeps the last (overwrite on every visit). BFS, not DFS, is what guarantees the top-to-bottom, left-to-right tie-breaking.

When would you choose the two-paths LCA over the single-traversal one?

The single traversal is O(n) time, O(h) space and the version interviewers expect, but it silently returns a wrong node when one of the keys is absent. The two-paths method also runs in O(n) and reports a missing key honestly, at the cost of two traversals and two O(h) path lists. For BSTs neither is needed: walk down comparing keys in O(h). For many LCA queries on a fixed tree, preprocess with binary lifting (O(n log n) build, O(log n) per query).

Why is counting a complete binary tree O(log² n) and not O(n)?

At any node of a complete tree the left or the right subtree is perfect, and a perfect subtree of height h has 2^h − 1 nodes without being visited. Measuring the left and right spine heights costs O(log n); only one child needs a recursive call, so there are O(log n) such calls — O(log n) × O(log n). The same completeness is why heaps fit in an array with children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

Trees & Heaps

Binary Search Tree

A binary search tree keeps its keys ordered: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger. That one invariant is what every problem here exploits — the inorder traversal is sorted, every search is a single root-to-leaf walk, and a count stored in each node turns order statistics into O(h) queries.

Binary Search Tree (BST) — a binary tree in which, for every node, all keys in the left subtree are < the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are > it. The rule applies to whole subtrees, not just to the two children — this is the detail most wrong solutions miss.

Tree A — the sample tree used throughout this topic
            20
          /    \
         8      22
       /   \
      4     12
           /  \
         10    14

inorder:  4  8  10  12  14  20  22      (always sorted)
What the problems rely on

The reader already knows search, insert and delete. The advanced problems are built from four consequences of the BST invariant:

Inorder is sorted

Left, node, right visits keys in ascending order. Anything you can do on a sorted array (two pointers, previous-element checks, kth element) you can do on a BST without materialising the array.

One path answers a query

Search, floor, ceiling, predecessor and successor each follow a single root-to-leaf path: O(h) time, where h is the height.

Ancestors bound a node

A node must lie strictly inside the range (lower, upper) set by all of its ancestors — not only by its parent.

Nodes can carry extra data

Storing the size of the left subtree (an augmented BST) makes “kth smallest” and “rank of x” O(h) queries.

OperationTimeNote
search / insert / deleteO(h)h = O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed
floor / ceiling / successorO(h)one path down, remember the best candidate
kth smallest (plain)O(h + k)inorder traversal stopped after k nodes
kth smallest (augmented)O(h)each node stores the size of its left subtree
check if a tree is a BSTO(n)range method or inorder-previous method
inorder traversalO(n)stack holds at most h nodes
Key point

The library ordered containers — C++ std::set / std::map, Java TreeSet / TreeMap — are self-balancing BSTs (red-black trees), so h = O(log n) is guaranteed. Python and JavaScript ship no ordered set; you either write a small BST, keep a sorted list with bisect (O(n) inserts) or use a third-party package.

Floor and ceiling of a key
Example

Input: tree A, x = 11
Output: floor 10, ceiling 12
Input: tree A, x = 23
Output: floor 22, ceiling -1 (none)
Input: tree A, x = 3
Output: floor -1 (none), ceiling 4

Idea

Walk down from the root. For the floor (largest key <= x): when the current key is too big go left; when it is <= x it is a candidate — record it and go right to look for a closer one. The ceiling is the mirror image. The answer is the last candidate recorded on the path — no backtracking, no recursion.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root

def floor_of(root, x):
    res = -1
    while root:
        if root.key == x:
            return x
        if root.key > x:
            root = root.left        # too big: only the left subtree can hold a floor
        else:
            res = root.key          # candidate; a closer one may sit to the right
            root = root.right
    return res

def ceil_of(root, x):
    res = -1
    while root:
        if root.key == x:
            return x
        if root.key < x:
            root = root.right       # too small: only the right subtree can hold a ceiling
        else:
            res = root.key          # candidate; a closer one may sit to the left
            root = root.left
    return res

root = None
for k in [20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14]:
    root = insert(root, k)
for x in [11, 23, 3, 12]:
    print(f"x={x}: floor {floor_of(root, x)} ceiling {ceil_of(root, x)}")
C++
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;
}

int floorOf(Node* root, int x) {
    int res = -1;
    while (root) {
        if (root->key == x) return x;
        if (root->key > x) root = root->left;          // too big: go left
        else { res = root->key; root = root->right; }  // candidate, look right for a closer one
    }
    return res;
}

int ceilOf(Node* root, int x) {
    int res = -1;
    while (root) {
        if (root->key == x) return x;
        if (root->key < x) root = root->right;         // too small: go right
        else { res = root->key; root = root->left; }   // candidate, look left for a closer one
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int k : {20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14}) root = insert(root, k);
    for (int x : {11, 23, 3, 12})
        cout << "x=" << x << ": floor " << floorOf(root, x) << " ceiling " << ceilOf(root, x) << "\n";
}

        else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);

        while (root != null) {
            if (root.key == x) return x;
            if (root.key > x) root = root.left;            // too big: go left
            else { res = root.key; root = root.right; }    // candidate, look right for a closer one
        }

            else { res = root.key; root = root.left; }     // candidate, look left for a closer one
        }

Pitfall

Returning as soon as you see a key <= x gives a valid floor but not the greatest one — floor(11) would stop at 8 instead of continuing right to 10. Always keep walking and overwrite the candidate.

Ceiling on the left side of every element
Example

Input: arr = [2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12]
Output: -1 -1 -1 30 30 15
Input: arr = [30, 20, 10]
Output: -1 30 20

For every arr[i], print the smallest element among arr[0..i-1] that is >= arr[i], or -1 if there is none. The first element never has one.

The obvious solution rescans the prefix for each element:

Python
def left_ceilings_naive(arr):
    res = [-1]
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):
        best = -1
        for j in range(i):                                # scan everything to the left
            if arr[j] >= arr[i] and (best == -1 or arr[j] < best):
                best = arr[j]
        res.append(best)
    return res

print(*left_ceilings_naive([2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12]))
Output
-1 -1 -1 30 30 15
Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Keep the elements seen so far in an ordered set (a self-balancing BST). The ceiling of arr[i] is then one O(log n) query — lower_bound in C++, TreeSet.ceiling in Java — and inserting arr[i] afterwards is another. Python uses bisect on a sorted list (the query is O(log n), the insert O(n) but with a very small constant); JavaScript reuses the hand-written BST from the previous section.

Python
from bisect import bisect_left, insort

def left_ceilings(arr):
    seen = []                              # kept sorted
    res = []
    for x in arr:
        i = bisect_left(seen, x)           # index of the first element >= x
        res.append(seen[i] if i < len(seen) else -1)
        insort(seen, x)                    # O(n) shift, but a tight memmove
    return res

for arr in ([2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12], [30, 20, 10]):
    print(*left_ceilings(arr))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <set>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> leftCeilings(const vector<int>& arr) {
    set<int> seen;                                   // red-black tree
    vector<int> res;
    for (int x : arr) {
        auto it = seen.lower_bound(x);               // first element >= x, O(log n)
        res.push_back(it == seen.end() ? -1 : *it);
        seen.insert(x);
    }
    return res;
}

int main() {
    for (const vector<int>& arr : {vector<int>{2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12}, vector<int>{30, 20, 10}}) {
        vector<int> res = leftCeilings(arr);
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)res.size(); i++) cout << (i ? " " : "") << res[i];
        cout << "\n";
    }
}

import java.util.TreeSet;

public class Main {
    static String leftCeilings(int[] arr) {
        TreeSet<Integer> seen = new TreeSet<>();      // red-black tree
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int x : arr) {
            Integer c = seen.ceiling(x);              // smallest element >= x, or null
            sb.append(c == null ? -1 : c).append(' ');
            seen.add(x);
        }
        return sb.toString().trim();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(leftCeilings(new int[]{2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12}));
        System.out.println(leftCeilings(new int[]{30, 20, 10}));

JavaScript
// JavaScript has no ordered set: reuse the BST insert + ceiling from above
class Node {
    constructor(key) { this.key = key; this.left = null; this.right = null; }
}

function insert(root, key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
    return root;
}

function ceilOf(root, x) {
    let res = -1;
    while (root) {
        if (root.key === x) return x;
        if (root.key < x) root = root.right;
        else { res = root.key; root = root.left; }
    }
    return res;
}

function leftCeilings(arr) {
    let seen = null;
    const res = [];
    for (const x of arr) {
        res.push(ceilOf(seen, x));              // query the elements to the left
        seen = insert(seen, x);                 // then add the current one
    }
    return res;
}

for (const arr of [[2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12], [30, 20, 10]])
    console.log(leftCeilings(arr).join(" "));
Output
-1 -1 -1 30 30 15
-1 30 20
Time O(n log n)Space O(n)
Key point

Query before insert: if you insert arr[i] first, its own ceiling is itself and every answer becomes arr[i]. The same pattern (ordered set of the prefix + one query per element) solves floor on the left, ceiling on the right (scan from the end) and count of smaller elements to the left.

Kth smallest element
Example

Input: tree A, k = 3
Output: 10
Input: tree A, k = 7
Output: 22
Input: tree A, k = 8
Output: -1 (fewer than 8 nodes)

Idea

Inorder visits keys in ascending order, so the kth node visited is the kth smallest. Run an iterative inorder traversal with an explicit stack, count the nodes as they are popped, and stop as soon as the count reaches k — no need to finish the traversal.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root

def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:                  # go as far left as possible
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()           # the next key in sorted order
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return node.key
        node = node.right
    return -1                        # fewer than k nodes

root = None
for x in [20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14]:
    root = insert(root, x)
for k in (3, 7, 8):
    print(f"k={k}: {kth_smallest(root, k)}")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;
}

int kthSmallest(Node* root, int k) {
    stack<Node*> st;
    Node* node = root;
    while (!st.empty() || node) {
        while (node) { st.push(node); node = node->left; }   // go as far left as possible
        node = st.top(); st.pop();                           // next key in sorted order
        if (--k == 0) return node->key;
        node = node->right;
    }
    return -1;                                               // fewer than k nodes
}

int main() {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int x : {20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14}) root = insert(root, x);
    for (int k : {3, 7, 8}) cout << "k=" << k << ": " << kthSmallest(root, k) << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node insert(Node root, int key) {
        if (root == null) return new Node(key);
        if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
        else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
        return root;
    }

    static int kthSmallest(Node root, int k) {
        Deque<Node> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Node node = root;
        while (!stack.isEmpty() || node != null) {
            while (node != null) { stack.push(node); node = node.left; }   // go as far left as possible
            node = stack.pop();                                             // next key in sorted order
            if (--k == 0) return node.key;
            node = node.right;
        }
        return -1;                                                          // fewer than k nodes
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node root = null;

Time O(h + k)Space O(h)
Pitfall

The original notes used a recursive traversal with a global counter and a return after printing — but the return only leaves the current frame, the parent frames continue into their right subtrees, and the counter is never reset for a second query. An explicit stack (or a counter object passed down and a boolean found flag) avoids both bugs.

When the tree is queried many times, or k is large, pay a little memory to make every query O(h): store in each node the number of nodes in its left subtree (lcount). Insert maintains it — every time the new key goes left, the node it passes gains one left descendant.

Augmented tree A: each node knows the size of its left subtree
            20 (lcount 5)
          /    \
 (lcount 1) 8    22 (0)
       /   \
  (0) 4     12 (lcount 1)
           /  \
     (0) 10    14 (0)

kth(k=3) at 20: lcount+1 = 6 > 3   → go left, k stays 3
          at 8: lcount+1 = 2 < 3   → go right, k = 3-2 = 1
         at 12: lcount+1 = 2 > 1   → go left
         at 10: lcount+1 = 1 == 1  → answer 10
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None
        self.lcount = 0              # number of nodes in the left subtree

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
        root.lcount += 1             # one more node went into my left subtree
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root

def kth_smallest(root, k):
    while root:
        rank = root.lcount + 1       # this node is the rank-th smallest of its subtree
        if rank == k:
            return root.key
        if k < rank:
            root = root.left         # answer is in the left subtree
        else:
            k -= rank                # skip the left subtree and this node
            root = root.right
    return -1

for x in [20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14]:
    root = insert(root, x)
for k in (3, 7, 8):
    print(f"k={k}: {kth_smallest(root, k)}")

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    int lcount = 0;                      // number of nodes in the left subtree
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) {
        root->left = insert(root->left, key);
        root->lcount++;                  // one more node went into my left subtree
    } else if (key > root->key) {
        root->right = insert(root->right, key);

    return root;
}

    while (root) {
        int rank = root->lcount + 1;     // this node is the rank-th smallest of its subtree
        if (rank == k) return root->key;
        if (k < rank) root = root->left;             // answer is in the left subtree
        else { k -= rank; root = root->right; }      // skip the left subtree and this node
    }
    return -1;
}

Key point

The same lcount field answers rank(x) (how many keys are < x) in O(h), and n - k + 1 turns kth smallest into kth largest. If the tree also supports delete, every node on the deletion path whose left subtree shrank must have its lcount decremented — forgetting that silently corrupts later queries.

Check whether a binary tree is a BST
Every node of tree B passes a parent-vs-children check, yet tree B is not a BST
tree A (valid)             tree B (NOT a BST)
      20                         20
    /    \                     /    \
   8      22                  8      22
 /   \                      /   \
4     12                   4     25   ← 25 > 20 but sits in 20's left subtree
     /  \
   10    14
Example

Input: tree A
Output: Yes
Input: tree B
Output: No

The tempting solution compares each node with its two children only. It accepts tree B:

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def looks_like_bst(root):                 # WRONG: only compares a node with its own children
    if root is None:
        return True
    if root.left and root.left.key > root.key:
        return False
    if root.right and root.right.key < root.key:
        return False
    return looks_like_bst(root.left) and looks_like_bst(root.right)

b = Node(20)
b.left, b.right = Node(8), Node(22)
b.left.left, b.left.right = Node(4), Node(25)      # 25 violates the rule at its grandparent 20
print("tree B:", "Yes" if looks_like_bst(b) else "No")
Output
tree B: Yes
Avoid

8 < 20, 4 < 8 < 25, 20 < 22 — every local check passes, yet 25 is in the left subtree of 20. The BST rule constrains a node by all of its ancestors, not just its parent.

A correct but slow fix checks, for every node, the maximum of the whole left subtree and the minimum of the whole right subtree. Each node is scanned by each of its ancestors, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree:

Python
import sys

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def max_key(root):
    if root is None:
        return -sys.maxsize
    return max(root.key, max_key(root.left), max_key(root.right))

def min_key(root):
    if root is None:
        return sys.maxsize
    return min(root.key, min_key(root.left), min_key(root.right))

def is_bst_slow(root):
    if root is None:
        return True
    if root.left and max_key(root.left) >= root.key:        # whole left subtree must be smaller
        return False
    if root.right and min_key(root.right) <= root.key:      # whole right subtree must be larger
        return False
    return is_bst_slow(root.left) and is_bst_slow(root.right)

a = Node(20)
a.left, a.right = Node(8), Node(22)
a.left.left, a.left.right = Node(4), Node(12)
a.left.right.left, a.left.right.right = Node(10), Node(14)

b = Node(20)
b.left, b.right = Node(8), Node(22)
b.left.left, b.left.right = Node(4), Node(25)

print("tree A:", "Yes" if is_bst_slow(a) else "No")
print("tree B:", "Yes" if is_bst_slow(b) else "No")
Output
tree A: Yes
tree B: No
Time O(n²) worst caseSpace O(h)
Idea

Range method. Pass down the open interval (lo, hi) that the ancestors allow. The root may be anything; going left tightens hi to the current key, going right tightens lo. Each node is visited once and checked against two numbers — O(n).

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def is_bst(root, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    if root is None:
        return True
    if not (lo < root.key < hi):             # must lie strictly inside the ancestors' range
        return False
    return (is_bst(root.left, lo, root.key)   # left subtree: everything < root.key
            and is_bst(root.right, root.key, hi))   # right subtree: everything > root.key

a = Node(20)
a.left, a.right = Node(8), Node(22)
a.left.left, a.left.right = Node(4), Node(12)
a.left.right.left, a.left.right.right = Node(10), Node(14)

b = Node(20)
b.left, b.right = Node(8), Node(22)
b.left.left, b.left.right = Node(4), Node(25)

print("tree A:", "Yes" if is_bst(a) else "No")
print("tree B:", "Yes" if is_bst(b) else "No")
C++
#include <climits>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

bool isBST(Node* root, long long lo, long long hi) {
    if (!root) return true;
    if (root->key <= lo || root->key >= hi) return false;     // outside the ancestors' range
    return isBST(root->left, lo, root->key)                  // left: everything < key
        && isBST(root->right, root->key, hi);                // right: everything > key
}

int main() {
    Node* a = new Node(20);
    a->left = new Node(8); a->right = new Node(22);
    a->left->left = new Node(4); a->left->right = new Node(12);
    a->left->right->left = new Node(10); a->left->right->right = new Node(14);

    Node* b = new Node(20);
    b->left = new Node(8); b->right = new Node(22);
    b->left->left = new Node(4); b->left->right = new Node(25);

    cout << "tree A: " << (isBST(a, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    cout << "tree B: " << (isBST(b, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Using INT_MIN / INT_MAX as the initial bounds with int keys rejects a tree that legitimately contains INT_MIN or INT_MAX (the check is strict). Use a wider type for the bounds (long long / long), ±Infinity in JavaScript, or None sentinels meaning unbounded.

Idea

Inorder-previous method. Inorder of a BST is strictly increasing. Traverse inorder and remember the previous key; the moment the current key is <= the previous one, the tree is not a BST. One pass, no bounds, and it stops at the first violation.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def is_bst(root):
    stack, node, prev = [], root, None
    while stack or node:
        while node:                        # iterative inorder traversal
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        if prev is not None and node.key <= prev:     # inorder must strictly increase
            return False
        prev = node.key
        node = node.right
    return True

a = Node(20)
a.left, a.right = Node(8), Node(22)
a.left.left, a.left.right = Node(4), Node(12)
a.left.right.left, a.left.right.right = Node(10), Node(14)

b = Node(20)
b.left, b.right = Node(8), Node(22)
b.left.left, b.left.right = Node(4), Node(25)

print("tree A:", "Yes" if is_bst(a) else "No")
print("tree B:", "Yes" if is_bst(b) else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

bool isBST(Node* root) {
    stack<Node*> st;
    Node* node = root;
    bool havePrev = false;
    int prev = 0;
    while (!st.empty() || node) {
        while (node) { st.push(node); node = node->left; }   // iterative inorder traversal
        node = st.top(); st.pop();
        if (havePrev && node->key <= prev) return false;     // inorder must strictly increase
        prev = node->key; havePrev = true;
        node = node->right;
    }
    return true;
}

int main() {
    Node* a = new Node(20);
    a->left = new Node(8); a->right = new Node(22);
    a->left->left = new Node(4); a->left->right = new Node(12);
    a->left->right->left = new Node(10); a->left->right->right = new Node(14);

    Node* b = new Node(20);
    b->left = new Node(8); b->right = new Node(22);
    b->left->left = new Node(4); b->left->right = new Node(25);

    cout << "tree A: " << (isBST(a) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    cout << "tree B: " << (isBST(b) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static boolean isBST(Node root) {
        Deque<Node> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Node node = root;
        Integer prev = null;
        while (!stack.isEmpty() || node != null) {
            while (node != null) { stack.push(node); node = node.left; }   // iterative inorder
            node = stack.pop();
            if (prev != null && node.key <= prev) return false;             // must strictly increase
            prev = node.key;
            node = node.right;
        }
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node a = new Node(20);
        a.left = new Node(8); a.right = new Node(22);
        a.left.left = new Node(4); a.left.right = new Node(12);
        a.left.right.left = new Node(10); a.left.right.right = new Node(14);

        Node b = new Node(20);
        b.left = new Node(8); b.right = new Node(22);
        b.left.left = new Node(4); b.left.right = new Node(25);

        System.out.println("tree A: " + (isBST(a) ? "Yes" : "No"));
        System.out.println("tree B: " + (isBST(b) ? "Yes" : "No"));
    }
}
JavaScript
class Node {
    constructor(key) { this.key = key; this.left = null; this.right = null; }
}

function isBST(root) {
    const stack = [];
    let node = root, prev = null;
    while (stack.length || node) {
        while (node) { stack.push(node); node = node.left; }   // iterative inorder traversal
        node = stack.pop();
        if (prev !== null && node.key <= prev) return false;    // inorder must strictly increase
        prev = node.key;
        node = node.right;
    }
    return true;
}

const a = new Node(20);
a.left = new Node(8); a.right = new Node(22);
a.left.left = new Node(4); a.left.right = new Node(12);
a.left.right.left = new Node(10); a.left.right.right = new Node(14);

const b = new Node(20);
b.left = new Node(8); b.right = new Node(22);
b.left.left = new Node(4); b.left.right = new Node(25);

console.log("tree A:", isBST(a) ? "Yes" : "No");
console.log("tree B:", isBST(b) ? "Yes" : "No");
Output
tree A: Yes
tree B: No
Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

Both methods use a strict comparison, so a tree with duplicate keys is rejected. If your definition allows duplicates on one side (say left <= node), relax exactly that one bound — and say so in the interview before you code.

Fix a BST with two nodes swapped
Swapping 60 and 8 back restores the sorted inorder sequence
    given (two keys swapped)             fixed
            20                             20
          /    \                         /    \
        60      80        ──▶           8      80
       /  \    /  \                   /  \    /  \
      4   10  8   100                4   10  60   100

inorder:  4  60  10  20  8  80  100   →   4  8  10  20  60  80  100
             ^^^^^^      ^^^^^
              dip 1       dip 2
Example

Input: tree above
Output: inorder before: 4 60 10 20 8 80 100, after: 4 8 10 20 60 80 100

Idea

The inorder sequence of a BST is sorted; swapping two keys creates one or two dips (a place where a key is smaller than its predecessor). With two dips, the swapped nodes are the larger element of the first dip and the smaller element of the second; with one dip (the two nodes are inorder-adjacent) they are the two elements of that dip. Record first at the first dip and overwrite second at every dip, then swap their keys.

1
Traverse inorder, remembering prev
At each node compare node.key with prev.key.
2
First dip (node.key < prev.key)
Set first = prev and second = node.
3
Second dip
Only second = node changes — first stays the larger element of the first dip.
4
Swap
Exchange first.key and second.key. The structure of the tree is untouched.
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

class Fixer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.prev = self.first = self.second = None

    def visit(self, node):                        # inorder, looking for dips
        if node is None:
            return
        self.visit(node.left)
        if self.prev and node.key < self.prev.key:  # a dip: smaller key after a larger one
            if self.first is None:
                self.first = self.prev            # first dip: remember the larger element
            self.second = node                    # the smaller element (overwritten by a 2nd dip)
        self.prev = node
        self.visit(node.right)

def fix_bst(root):
    f = Fixer()
    f.visit(root)
    if f.first and f.second:
        f.first.key, f.second.key = f.second.key, f.first.key

def inorder(node, out):
    if node:
        inorder(node.left, out)
        out.append(node.key)
        inorder(node.right, out)

root = Node(20)
root.left, root.right = Node(60), Node(80)
root.left.left, root.left.right = Node(4), Node(10)
root.right.left, root.right.right = Node(8), Node(100)

before = []
inorder(root, before)
print("before:", *before)
fix_bst(root)
after = []
inorder(root, after)
print("after:", *after)
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

struct Fixer {
    Node *prev = nullptr, *first = nullptr, *second = nullptr;
    void visit(Node* node) {                           // inorder, looking for dips
        if (!node) return;
        visit(node->left);
        if (prev && node->key < prev->key) {           // a dip: smaller key after a larger one
            if (!first) first = prev;                  // first dip: remember the larger element
            second = node;                             // the smaller element (overwritten by a 2nd dip)
        }
        prev = node;
        visit(node->right);
    }
};

void fixBST(Node* root) {
    Fixer f;
    f.visit(root);
    if (f.first && f.second) swap(f.first->key, f.second->key);
}

void inorder(Node* node, vector<int>& out) {
    if (!node) return;
    inorder(node->left, out);
    out.push_back(node->key);
    inorder(node->right, out);
}

void printKeys(const char* label, Node* root) {
    vector<int> keys;
    inorder(root, keys);
    cout << label;
    for (int k : keys) cout << " " << k;
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    Node* root = new Node(20);
    root->left = new Node(60); root->right = new Node(80);
    root->left->left = new Node(4); root->left->right = new Node(10);
    root->right->left = new Node(8); root->right->right = new Node(100);

    printKeys("before:", root);
    fixBST(root);
    printKeys("after:", root);
}

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static class Fixer {
        Node prev, first, second;
        void visit(Node node) {                        // inorder, looking for dips
            if (node == null) return;
            visit(node.left);
            if (prev != null && node.key < prev.key) { // a dip: smaller key after a larger one
                if (first == null) first = prev;       // first dip: remember the larger element
                second = node;                         // the smaller element (overwritten by a 2nd dip)
            }
            prev = node;
            visit(node.right);
        }
    }

    static void fixBST(Node root) {
        Fixer f = new Fixer();
        f.visit(root);
        if (f.first != null && f.second != null) {
            int t = f.first.key; f.first.key = f.second.key; f.second.key = t;
        }
    }

    static void inorder(Node node, List<Integer> out) {
        if (node == null) return;
        inorder(node.left, out);
        out.add(node.key);
        inorder(node.right, out);
    }

    static void printKeys(String label, Node root) {
        List<Integer> keys = new ArrayList<>();
        inorder(root, keys);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(label);
        for (int k : keys) sb.append(' ').append(k);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node root = new Node(20);
        root.left = new Node(60); root.right = new Node(80);
        root.left.left = new Node(4); root.left.right = new Node(10);
        root.right.left = new Node(8); root.right.right = new Node(100);

        printKeys("before:", root);
        fixBST(root);
        printKeys("after:", root);
    }
}

Pitfall

Setting second = prev at the second dip (instead of second = node) picks the wrong node. Trace the adjacent case too: in 8 / 20 22 (the root 20 swapped with its child 8) the inorder is 20 8 22 — a single dip, so first = 20, second = 8, and the single swap is correct. The original notes kept prev/first/second as globals, which breaks as soon as the function is called twice; the Fixer object above resets them per call.

Pair with a given sum in a BST
Example

Input: tree A, sum = 30
Output: Yes (8 + 22, or 10 + 20)
Input: tree A, sum = 29
Output: No

Idea

Method 1 — inorder + two pointers. Inorder gives the keys sorted. Then the classic sorted-array trick: a pointer at each end, move the left one right when the sum is too small and the right one left when it is too large. O(n) time, O(n) for the array.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root

def inorder(node, out):
    if node:
        inorder(node.left, out)
        out.append(node.key)
        inorder(node.right, out)

def pair_sum(root, target):
    keys = []
    inorder(root, keys)                     # sorted keys
    i, j = 0, len(keys) - 1
    while i < j:                            # two pointers on a sorted array
        s = keys[i] + keys[j]
        if s == target:
            return (keys[i], keys[j])
        if s < target:
            i += 1                          # need a bigger sum
        else:
            j -= 1                          # need a smaller sum
    return None

root = None
for x in [20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14]:
    root = insert(root, x)
for target in (30, 29):
    res = pair_sum(root, target)
    print(f"sum={target}:", f"Yes ({res[0]} + {res[1]})" if res else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;
}

void inorder(Node* node, vector<int>& out) {
    if (!node) return;
    inorder(node->left, out);
    out.push_back(node->key);
    inorder(node->right, out);
}

bool pairSum(Node* root, int target, int& a, int& b) {
    vector<int> keys;
    inorder(root, keys);                              // sorted keys
    int i = 0, j = (int)keys.size() - 1;
    while (i < j) {                                   // two pointers on a sorted array
        int s = keys[i] + keys[j];
        if (s == target) { a = keys[i]; b = keys[j]; return true; }
        if (s < target) i++;                          // need a bigger sum
        else j--;                                     // need a smaller sum
    }
    return false;
}

int main() {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int x : {20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14}) root = insert(root, x);
    for (int target : {30, 29}) {
        int a, b;
        if (pairSum(root, target, a, b)) cout << "sum=" << target << ": Yes (" << a << " + " << b << ")\n";
        else cout << "sum=" << target << ": No\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;
        Node(int k) { key = k; }
    }

    static Node insert(Node root, int key) {
        if (root == null) return new Node(key);
        if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
        else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
        return root;
    }

    static void inorder(Node node, List<Integer> out) {
        if (node == null) return;
        inorder(node.left, out);
        out.add(node.key);
        inorder(node.right, out);
    }

    static int[] pairSum(Node root, int target) {
        List<Integer> keys = new ArrayList<>();
        inorder(root, keys);                              // sorted keys
        int i = 0, j = keys.size() - 1;
        while (i < j) {                                   // two pointers on a sorted array
            int s = keys.get(i) + keys.get(j);
            if (s == target) return new int[]{keys.get(i), keys.get(j)};
            if (s < target) i++;                          // need a bigger sum
            else j--;                                     // need a smaller sum
        }
        return null;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node root = null;
        for (int x : new int[]{20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14}) root = insert(root, x);
        for (int target : new int[]{30, 29}) {
            int[] res = pairSum(root, target);
            System.out.println("sum=" + target + ": " + (res == null ? "No" : "Yes (" + res[0] + " + " + res[1] + ")"));
        }
    }
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Idea

Method 2 — hash set during the traversal. Visit the nodes (inorder here, but any order works) and keep the keys seen so far in a set. At each node ask whether target - key has already been seen; if not, add key. This is exactly the array “pair sum with hashing” solution, run on the tree in place. It reports a different (equally valid) pair than the two-pointer method — 10 + 20 is complete as soon as 20 is visited, before 22 is reached.

Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root

def pair_sum(node, target, seen):
    if node is None:
        return None
    found = pair_sum(node.left, target, seen)
    if found:
        return found
    if target - node.key in seen:            # the partner was visited earlier
        return (target - node.key, node.key)
    seen.add(node.key)
    return pair_sum(node.right, target, seen)

root = None
for x in [20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14]:
    root = insert(root, x)
for target in (30, 29):
    res = pair_sum(root, target, set())      # a fresh set per query
    print(f"sum={target}:", f"Yes ({res[0]} + {res[1]})" if res else "No")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_set>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    int key;
    Node *left = nullptr, *right = nullptr;
    Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

Node* insert(Node* root, int key) {
    if (!root) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root->key) root->left = insert(root->left, key);
    else if (key > root->key) root->right = insert(root->right, key);
    return root;
}

bool pairSum(Node* node, int target, unordered_set<int>& seen, int& a, int& b) {
    if (!node) return false;
    if (pairSum(node->left, target, seen, a, b)) return true;
    if (seen.count(target - node->key)) {               // the partner was visited earlier
        a = target - node->key; b = node->key;
        return true;
    }
    seen.insert(node->key);
    return pairSum(node->right, target, seen, a, b);
}

int main() {
    Node* root = nullptr;
    for (int x : {20, 8, 22, 4, 12, 10, 14}) root = insert(root, x);
    for (int target : {30, 29}) {
        unordered_set<int> seen;                         // a fresh set per query
        int a, b;
        if (pairSum(root, target, seen, a, b)) cout << "sum=" << target << ": Yes (" << a << " + " << b << ")\n";
        else cout << "sum=" << target << ": No\n";
    }
}

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class Main {
    static class Node {
        int key; Node left, right;

    static Node insert(Node root, int key) {

        if (key < root.key) root.left = insert(root.left, key);
        else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);

        if (node == null) return null;

            return new int[]{target - node.key, node.key};
