Pitfall

Recursive DFS on a long path uses one stack frame per vertex: Python stops at ~1000 frames and Java/C++ crash on graphs with tens of thousands of vertices in a chain. For large inputs convert to an explicit stack — but note that the naive iterative version (push all neighbours, pop one) visits in a different order than the recursive one.

DFS on a disconnected graph and counting components

Exactly as with BFS: an outer loop over all vertices, a shared visited array, and one recursive DFS per unvisited vertex. The number of calls made by the outer loop is the number of connected components.

Example

Input: edges = 0-2, 2-1, 3-4, 5-7, 5-6, 6-7, V = 8
Output: 3 components

Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def dfs_rec(adj, u, visited, comp):
    visited[u] = True
    comp.append(u)
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs_rec(adj, v, visited, comp)

def count_components(adj):
    visited = [False] * len(adj)      # shared by every DFS call
    count = 0
    for u in range(len(adj)):
        if not visited[u]:            # unvisited vertex = start of a new component
            count += 1
            comp = []
            dfs_rec(adj, u, visited, comp)
            print(f"component {count}:", *comp)
    return count

adj = build(8, [(0, 2), (2, 1), (3, 4), (5, 7), (5, 6), (6, 7)])
print("components:", count_components(adj))

    visited[u] = true;
    comp.push_back(u);

        if (!visited[v]) dfsRec(adj, v, visited, comp);

int countComponents(const vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    vector<bool> visited(adj.size(), false);   // shared by every DFS call
    int count = 0;
    for (int u = 0; u < (int)adj.size(); u++) {
        if (visited[u]) continue;                // unvisited vertex = start of a new component
        count++;
        vector<int> comp;
        dfsRec(adj, u, visited, comp);
        cout << "component " << count << ":";
        for (int x : comp) cout << " " << x;
        cout << "\n";
    }
    return count;
}

}

Applications of DFS
  • Cycle detection — a back edge to a vertex that is still on the recursion stack (directed) or to a visited non-parent (undirected).
  • Topological sorting — vertices in decreasing order of DFS finish time.
  • Strongly connected components — Kosaraju's and Tarjan's algorithms are two DFS passes, or one DFS with low-link values.
  • Mazes and puzzles — explore one path to the end before trying another; backtracking is DFS over the state space.
  • Path finding — any path (not necessarily shortest) between two vertices; articulation points and bridges via discovery times.
BFSDFS
Data structureQueueStack / recursion
VisitsBy distance (level order)Along one branch, then backtracks
Finds shortest paths (unweighted)YesNo
MemoryO(width) — the frontierO(depth) — the current path
Typical usesShortest path, nearest neighbour, level-wise processingCycles, topological order, SCCs, connectivity, backtracking
Detect a cycle in an undirected graph
Edges 0-1, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 versus 0-1, 1-2, 1-3
Graph 1 (cycle)              Graph 2 (no cycle — a tree)

0 ───── 1 ───── 2            0 ───── 1 ───── 2
        │     ╱                      │
        │   ╱                        │
        3 ╱                          3
Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3
Output: cycle
Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 1-3
Output: no cycle

Idea

Run DFS remembering each vertex's parent (the vertex we came from). Reaching a neighbour that is already visited and is not the parent means there are two different routes to it — a cycle. Without the parent check every undirected edge would look like a cycle, because u → v and v → u are the same edge.

Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def has_cycle_from(adj, u, parent, visited):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            if has_cycle_from(adj, v, u, visited):
                return True
        elif v != parent:             # visited, and not the edge we arrived by -> cycle
            return True
    return False

def has_cycle(adj):
    visited = [False] * len(adj)
    for u in range(len(adj)):         # every component
        if not visited[u] and has_cycle_from(adj, u, -1, visited):
            return True
    return False

g1 = build(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])
g2 = build(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3)])
print("graph 1:", "cycle" if has_cycle(g1) else "no cycle")
print("graph 2:", "cycle" if has_cycle(g2) else "no cycle")
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> build(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) { adj[u].push_back(v); adj[v].push_back(u); }
    return adj;
}

bool hasCycleFrom(const vector<vector<int>>& adj, int u, int parent, vector<bool>& visited) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u]) {
        if (!visited[v]) {
            if (hasCycleFrom(adj, v, u, visited)) return true;
        } else if (v != parent) {      // visited, and not the edge we arrived by -> cycle
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

bool hasCycle(const vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    vector<bool> visited(adj.size(), false);
    for (int u = 0; u < (int)adj.size(); u++)   // every component
        if (!visited[u] && hasCycleFrom(adj, u, -1, visited)) return true;
    return false;
}

int main() {
    auto g1 = build(4, {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}});
    auto g2 = build(4, {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}});
    cout << "graph 1: " << (hasCycle(g1) ? "cycle" : "no cycle") << "\n";
    cout << "graph 2: " << (hasCycle(g2) ? "cycle" : "no cycle") << "\n";
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static List<List<Integer>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) { adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]); }
        return adj;
    }

    static boolean hasCycleFrom(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, int parent, boolean[] visited) {
        visited[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (!visited[v]) {
                if (hasCycleFrom(adj, v, u, visited)) return true;
            } else if (v != parent) {      // visited, and not the edge we arrived by -> cycle
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    static boolean hasCycle(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
        boolean[] visited = new boolean[adj.size()];
        for (int u = 0; u < adj.size(); u++)   // every component
            if (!visited[u] && hasCycleFrom(adj, u, -1, visited)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<List<Integer>> g1 = build(4, new int[][]{{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}});
        List<List<Integer>> g2 = build(4, new int[][]{{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}});
        System.out.println("graph 1: " + (hasCycle(g1) ? "cycle" : "no cycle"));
        System.out.println("graph 2: " + (hasCycle(g2) ? "cycle" : "no cycle"));
    }

JavaScript
function build(n, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) { adj[u].push(v); adj[v].push(u); }
    return adj;
}

function hasCycleFrom(adj, u, parent, visited) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (const v of adj[u]) {
        if (!visited[v]) {
            if (hasCycleFrom(adj, v, u, visited)) return true;
        } else if (v !== parent) {         // visited, and not the edge we arrived by -> cycle
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

function hasCycle(adj) {
    const visited = new Array(adj.length).fill(false);
    for (let u = 0; u < adj.length; u++)   // every component
        if (!visited[u] && hasCycleFrom(adj, u, -1, visited)) return true;
    return false;
}

const g1 = build(4, [[0, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]]);
const g2 = build(4, [[0, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]]);
console.log("graph 1:", hasCycle(g1) ? "cycle" : "no cycle");
console.log("graph 2:", hasCycle(g2) ? "cycle" : "no cycle");
Output
graph 1: cycle
graph 2: no cycle
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

The parent check breaks down with parallel edges (two edges between the same pair) — they form a cycle, yet the second one looks like the edge we arrived by. Track the parent edge index instead of the parent vertex if the input may contain multi-edges. Shortcut: a connected undirected graph with E ≥ V edges always has a cycle.

Detect a cycle in a directed graph
Edges 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1 versus 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3
Graph 1 (cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 1)      Graph 2 (no cycle — a DAG)

0 ────▶ 1 ────▶ 2                  0 ────▶ 1
        ▲       │                  │       │
        │       ▼                  ▼       ▼
        └────── 3                  2 ────▶ 3
Example

Input: edges = 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1
Output: cycle
Input: edges = 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3
Output: no cycle

Idea

In a digraph “visited” is not enough: graph 2 reaches 3 twice (via 1 and via 2) without any cycle. A cycle exists only when DFS reaches a vertex that is still on the recursion stack — an ancestor of the current call. Keep a second array onStack that is set on entry and cleared on exit; a neighbour with onStack[v] true is a back edge.

Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)                  # directed: one direction only
    return adj

def has_cycle_from(adj, u, visited, on_stack):
    visited[u] = True
    on_stack[u] = True                    # u is an ancestor of everything below
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            if has_cycle_from(adj, v, visited, on_stack):
                return True
        elif on_stack[v]:                 # back edge to an ancestor -> cycle
            return True
    on_stack[u] = False                   # done with u's subtree
    return False

def has_cycle(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    visited, on_stack = [False] * n, [False] * n
    for u in range(n):
        if not visited[u] and has_cycle_from(adj, u, visited, on_stack):
            return True
    return False

g1 = build(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)])
g2 = build(4, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])
print("graph 1:", "cycle" if has_cycle(g1) else "no cycle")
print("graph 2:", "cycle" if has_cycle(g2) else "no cycle")

        } else if (onStack[v]) {          // back edge to an ancestor -> cycle
            return true;

}

Key point

The same idea is often written with three colours: white = unvisited, grey = on the recursion stack, black = finished. An edge to a grey vertex is a back edge (cycle); an edge to a black vertex is a cross/forward edge and harmless. Kahn's algorithm below detects directed cycles without recursion.

Topological sort — Kahn's algorithm (BFS)

Topological order — a linear ordering of the vertices of a DAG such that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. It is the order in which tasks with dependencies can be executed. A graph with a cycle has no topological order; a DAG may have several.

The DAG used for both topological sorts: edges 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1
5 ────▶ 2 ────▶ 3
│               │
▼               ▼
0 ◀──── 4 ────▶ 1
Example

Input: edges = 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1, V = 6
Output: 4 5 2 0 3 1 (one valid order; 5 4 2 3 1 0 is another)

Idea

A vertex with indegree 0 has no unfinished prerequisites, so it can go first. Output it, then “delete” it by decrementing the indegree of each neighbour; any neighbour that drops to 0 is now free and joins the queue. Repeat until the queue is empty.

1
Count indegrees
indeg[v] = number of edges into v, one pass over the adjacency lists.
2
Seed the queue
Enqueue every vertex with indeg[v] == 0.
3
Process
Dequeue u, append it to the order; for every neighbour v: indeg[v] -= 1, and enqueue v when it reaches 0.
4
Finish
When the queue is empty the order is complete — if it holds fewer than V vertices, the graph has a cycle (next section).
Python
from collections import deque

def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
    return adj

def kahn(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    indeg = [0] * n
    for u in range(n):
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] += 1                 # step 1: indegrees
    q = deque(u for u in range(n) if indeg[u] == 0)   # step 2: no prerequisites
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1                 # "remove" edge u -> v
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)               # all prerequisites of v are done
    return order

adj = build(6, [(5, 2), (5, 0), (4, 0), (4, 1), (2, 3), (3, 1)])
print("topological order:", *kahn(adj))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> build(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) adj[u].push_back(v);
    return adj;
}

vector<int> kahn(const vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    int n = adj.size();
    vector<int> indeg(n, 0);
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
        for (int v : adj[u]) indeg[v]++;              // step 1: indegrees
    queue<int> q;
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (indeg[u] == 0) q.push(u);                 // step 2: no prerequisites
    vector<int> order;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop();
        order.push_back(u);
        for (int v : adj[u])
            if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);           // all prerequisites of v are done
    }
    return order;
}

int main() {
    auto adj = build(6, {{5, 2}, {5, 0}, {4, 0}, {4, 1}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}});
    cout << "topological order:";
    for (int u : kahn(adj)) cout << " " << u;
    cout << "\n";
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static List<List<Integer>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        return adj;
    }

    static List<Integer> kahn(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
        int n = adj.size();
        int[] indeg = new int[n];
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) indeg[v]++;          // step 1: indegrees
        Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            if (indeg[u] == 0) q.add(u);                  // step 2: no prerequisites
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int u = q.poll();
            order.add(u);
            for (int v : adj.get(u))
                if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.add(v);            // all prerequisites of v are done
        }
        return order;
    }

JavaScript
function build(n, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) adj[u].push(v);
    return adj;
}

function kahn(adj) {
    const n = adj.length;
    const indeg = new Array(n).fill(0);
    for (const nbrs of adj)
        for (const v of nbrs) indeg[v]++;                 // step 1: indegrees
    const q = [];
    for (let u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (indeg[u] === 0) q.push(u);                    // step 2: no prerequisites
    const order = [];
    let head = 0;
    while (head < q.length) {
        const u = q[head++];
        order.push(u);
        for (const v of adj[u])
            if (--indeg[v] === 0) q.push(v);              // all prerequisites of v are done
    }
    return order;
}

const adj = build(6, [[5, 2], [5, 0], [4, 0], [4, 1], [2, 3], [3, 1]]);
console.log("topological order:", kahn(adj).join(" "));
Output
topological order: 4 5 2 0 3 1
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

Swap the queue for a min-priority queue and Kahn's algorithm yields the lexicographically smallest topological order — a common follow-up question.

Cycle detection with Kahn's algorithm

Kahn's algorithm only ever outputs vertices whose indegree reached 0. The vertices on a cycle depend on each other, so none of them ever reaches 0 and they are never output. Therefore: fewer than V vertices in the result ⇔ the graph has a cycle. This is the iterative alternative to the recursion-stack method.

Example

Input: edges = 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1, V = 6
Output: no cycle
Input: edges = 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, V = 4
Output: cycle

Python
from collections import deque

def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
    return adj

def kahn_count(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    indeg = [0] * n
    for u in range(n):
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] += 1
    q = deque(u for u in range(n) if indeg[u] == 0)
    count = 0                             # vertices that made it into the order
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        count += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return count                          # vertices on a cycle never reach indegree 0

def report(name, adj):
    c = kahn_count(adj)
    verdict = "no cycle" if c == len(adj) else "cycle"
    print(f"{name}: {verdict} ({c} of {len(adj)} vertices ordered)")

report("graph 1", build(6, [(5, 2), (5, 0), (4, 0), (4, 1), (2, 3), (3, 1)]))
report("graph 2", build(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)]))

Topological sort using DFS
Idea

When dfs(u) finishes, every vertex reachable from u has already finished (it was either visited inside the call or earlier). So a vertex finishes after all of its descendants — reversing the finish order puts every u before everything it points to. Push each vertex onto a stack as its DFS returns, then pop the stack.

1
Visit every vertex
For u in 0 … V−1: if u is unvisited, call dfs(u) — this covers disconnected DAGs.
2
dfs(u)
Mark u visited, recurse into every unvisited neighbour, and then push u onto the stack (post-order).
3
Read the stack
Pop until empty — the pop order is a topological order.
Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
    return adj

def dfs(adj, u, visited, stack):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(adj, v, visited, stack)
    stack.append(u)                       # post-order: u is pushed after all its descendants

def topo_sort(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    visited = [False] * n
    stack = []
    for u in range(n):
        if not visited[u]:
            dfs(adj, u, visited, stack)
    return stack[::-1]                    # pop everything = reverse finish order

adj = build(6, [(5, 2), (5, 0), (4, 0), (4, 1), (2, 3), (3, 1)])
print("topological order:", *topo_sort(adj))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> build(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) adj[u].push_back(v);
    return adj;
}

void dfs(const vector<vector<int>>& adj, int u, vector<bool>& visited, vector<int>& stack) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, stack);
    stack.push_back(u);                   // post-order: u is pushed after all its descendants
}

vector<int> topoSort(const vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
    int n = adj.size();
    vector<bool> visited(n, false);
    vector<int> stack;
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
    reverse(stack.begin(), stack.end());  // pop everything = reverse finish order
    return stack;
}

int main() {
    auto adj = build(6, {{5, 2}, {5, 0}, {4, 0}, {4, 1}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}});
    cout << "topological order:";
    for (int u : topoSort(adj)) cout << " " << u;
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static List<List<Integer>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        return adj;
    }

    static void dfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, boolean[] visited, Deque<Integer> stack) {
        visited[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj.get(u))
            if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, stack);
        stack.push(u);                        // post-order: u is pushed after all its descendants
    }

    static List<Integer> topoSort(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
        int n = adj.size();
        boolean[] visited = new boolean[n];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) order.add(stack.pop());   // pop everything = reverse finish order
        return order;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = build(6, new int[][]{{5, 2}, {5, 0}, {4, 0}, {4, 1}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}});
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("topological order:");
        for (int u : topoSort(adj)) sb.append(' ').append(u);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }
}
JavaScript
function build(n, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) adj[u].push(v);
    return adj;
}

function dfs(adj, u, visited, stack) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (const v of adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, stack);
    stack.push(u);                            // post-order: u is pushed after all its descendants
}

function topoSort(adj) {
    const n = adj.length;
    const visited = new Array(n).fill(false);
    const stack = [];
    for (let u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
    return stack.reverse();                   // pop everything = reverse finish order
}

const adj = build(6, [[5, 2], [5, 0], [4, 0], [4, 1], [2, 3], [3, 1]]);
console.log("topological order:", topoSort(adj).join(" "));
Output
topological order: 5 4 2 3 1 0
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

The DFS version silently produces a (wrong) order when the graph has a cycle — it never checks. Either run the directed-cycle check first (onStack) or use Kahn's algorithm, which detects the cycle for free.

Shortest path in a DAG

In a DAG a vertex's distance is final as soon as every vertex that can reach it is settled — and a topological order lists exactly those vertices first. One relaxation pass in topological order therefore gives all shortest paths, even with negative weights, in linear time. No priority queue, no repeated passes.

Weighted DAG: 0→1 (2), 0→4 (1), 1→2 (3), 4→2 (2), 4→5 (4), 2→3 (6), 5→3 (1)
     2        3        6
0 ──────▶ 1 ──────▶ 2 ──────▶ 3
│                   ▲         ▲
│ 1               2 │         │ 1
▼                   │         │
4 ──────────────────┘         │
│                             │
└────────────▶ 5 ─────────────┘
       4
Example

Input: edges above, s = 0
Output: 0 2 3 6 1 5
Input: s = 1
Output: INF 0 3 9 INF INF

1
Initialise
dist[v] = INF for all v, dist[s] = 0.
2
Topological order
DFS-based (or Kahn's) topological sort of the whole graph.
3
Relax in order
For each u in topological order with dist[u] != INF: for each edge u → v with weight w, if dist[u] + w < dist[v] set dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
Python
INF = 10 ** 9

def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))             # weighted, directed
    return adj

def dfs(adj, u, visited, stack):
    visited[u] = True
    for v, _ in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(adj, v, visited, stack)
    stack.append(u)

def dag_shortest(adj, s):
    n = len(adj)
    visited, stack = [False] * n, []
    for u in range(n):
        if not visited[u]:
            dfs(adj, u, visited, stack)
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    for u in reversed(stack):             # topological order
        if dist[u] == INF:
            continue                      # unreachable: nothing to relax from here
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w     # relax u -> v
    return dist

adj = build(6, [(0, 1, 2), (0, 4, 1), (1, 2, 3), (4, 2, 2), (4, 5, 4), (2, 3, 6), (5, 3, 1)])
for s in (0, 1):
    print(f"from {s}:", *("INF" if d == INF else d for d in dag_shortest(adj, s)))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

const int INF = 1e9;
struct Edge { int u, v, w; };

vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> build(int n, const vector<Edge>& edges) {
    vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> adj(n);
    for (auto& e : edges) adj[e.u].push_back({e.v, e.w});   // weighted, directed
    return adj;
}

void dfs(const vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj, int u, vector<bool>& visited, vector<int>& stack) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (auto [v, w] : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, stack);
    stack.push_back(u);
}

vector<int> dagShortest(const vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj, int s) {
    int n = adj.size();
    vector<bool> visited(n, false);
    vector<int> stack;
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
    vector<int> dist(n, INF);
    dist[s] = 0;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {          // topological order = reverse finish order
        int u = stack[i];
        if (dist[u] == INF) continue;           // unreachable: nothing to relax from here
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u])
            if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = dist[u] + w;   // relax u -> v
    }
    return dist;
}

int main() {
    auto adj = build(6, {{0, 1, 2}, {0, 4, 1}, {1, 2, 3}, {4, 2, 2}, {4, 5, 4}, {2, 3, 6}, {5, 3, 1}});
    for (int s : {0, 1}) {
        cout << "from " << s << ":";
        for (int d : dagShortest(adj, s)) {
            if (d == INF) cout << " INF"; else cout << " " << d;
        }
        cout << "\n";
    }
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static final int INF = 1_000_000_000;

    static List<List<int[]>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(new int[]{e[1], e[2]});   // weighted, directed
        return adj;
    }

    static void dfs(List<List<int[]>> adj, int u, boolean[] visited, Deque<Integer> stack) {
        visited[u] = true;
        for (int[] e : adj.get(u))
            if (!visited[e[0]]) dfs(adj, e[0], visited, stack);
        stack.push(u);
    }

    static int[] dagShortest(List<List<int[]>> adj, int s) {
        int n = adj.size();
        boolean[] visited = new boolean[n];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
        int[] dist = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        dist[s] = 0;
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {                  // popping gives topological order
            int u = stack.pop();
            if (dist[u] == INF) continue;           // unreachable: nothing to relax from here
            for (int[] e : adj.get(u))
                if (dist[u] + e[1] < dist[e[0]]) dist[e[0]] = dist[u] + e[1];   // relax u -> v
        }
        return dist;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = build(6, new int[][]{{0, 1, 2}, {0, 4, 1}, {1, 2, 3}, {4, 2, 2}, {4, 5, 4}, {2, 3, 6}, {5, 3, 1}});
        for (int s : new int[]{0, 1}) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("from " + s + ":");
            for (int d : dagShortest(adj, s)) sb.append(' ').append(d == INF ? "INF" : String.valueOf(d));
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
    }
}

const INF = 1e9;

function build(n, edges) {

function dfs(adj, u, visited, stack) {

    for (const [v] of adj[u])

    stack.push(u);

function dagShortest(adj, s) {
    const n = adj.length;
    const visited = new Array(n).fill(false), stack = [];
    for (let u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, stack);
    const dist = new Array(n).fill(INF);
    dist[s] = 0;
    for (const u of stack.reverse()) {            // topological order
        if (dist[u] === INF) continue;            // unreachable: nothing to relax from here
        for (const [v, w] of adj[u])

const adj = build(6, [[0, 1, 2], [0, 4, 1], [1, 2, 3], [4, 2, 2], [4, 5, 4], [2, 3, 6], [5, 3, 1]]);

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

Negate every weight (or use max instead of min) and the same pass gives the longest path in a DAG — the critical path in project scheduling. Longest path in a general graph is NP-hard; the DAG structure is what makes it easy.

Dijkstra's algorithm

Single-source shortest paths in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It is a greedy BFS: instead of a FIFO queue it always expands the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, so each vertex is settled exactly once, in increasing order of distance.

The weighted graph used for Dijkstra, Prim and Kruskal: 0-1 (4), 0-2 (1), 1-2 (2), 1-3 (5), 2-3 (8), 2-4 (10), 3-4 (2)
           4
  0 ─────────── 1
  │           ╱ │
1 │        2 ╱  │ 5
  │        ╱    │
  2 ─────────── 3
   ╲     8     ╱
 10 ╲         ╱ 2
     ╲       ╱
         4
Example

Input: edges above (undirected), s = 0
Output: dist = 0 3 1 8 10, path 0→4 = 0 2 1 3 4

Idea

Suppose u has the smallest tentative distance among the unsettled vertices. Any other route to u would have to leave the settled set through some unsettled vertex x with dist[x] ≥ dist[u], and with non-negative weights it can only get longer from there — so dist[u] is already optimal. Settle u, relax its edges, repeat. A negative edge breaks the “can only get longer” step, which is why Dijkstra fails with negative weights.

1
Initialise
dist[s] = 0, every other dist[v] = INF; push (0, s) into a min-heap keyed by distance.
2
Extract-min
Pop (d, u). If d > dist[u] it is a stale entry — skip it (lazy deletion).
3
Relax
For every edge u → v with weight w: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w, parent[v] = u, and push (dist[v], v).
4
Stop
When the heap is empty every reachable vertex is settled; INF marks the unreachable ones.
Python
import heapq

INF = 10 ** 9

def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
        adj[v].append((u, w))             # undirected, weighted
    return adj

def dijkstra(adj, s):
    n = len(adj)
    dist, parent = [INF] * n, [-1] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    pq = [(0, s)]                         # (distance, vertex) min-heap
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                      # stale entry: u was already settled with a smaller d
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if d + w < dist[v]:           # relax u -> v
                dist[v] = d + w
                parent[v] = u
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
    return dist, parent

def path_to(parent, t):
    path = []
    while t != -1:
        path.append(t)
        t = parent[t]
    return path[::-1]

adj = build(5, [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (1, 2, 2), (1, 3, 5), (2, 3, 8), (2, 4, 10), (3, 4, 2)])
dist, parent = dijkstra(adj, 0)
print("dist:", *dist)
print("path 0 -> 4:", *path_to(parent, 4))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

const int INF = 1e9;
struct Edge { int u, v, w; };

vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> build(int n, const vector<Edge>& edges) {
    vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> adj(n);
    for (auto& e : edges) {
        adj[e.u].push_back({e.v, e.w});
        adj[e.v].push_back({e.u, e.w});   // undirected, weighted
    }
    return adj;
}

vector<int> dijkstra(const vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj, int s, vector<int>& parent) {
    int n = adj.size();
    vector<int> dist(n, INF);
    parent.assign(n, -1);
    dist[s] = 0;
    priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<pair<int,int>>> pq;   // min-heap of (distance, vertex)
    pq.push({0, s});
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;        // stale entry: u was already settled with a smaller d
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
            if (d + w < dist[v]) {        // relax u -> v
                dist[v] = d + w;
                parent[v] = u;
                pq.push({dist[v], v});
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

int main() {
    auto adj = build(5, {{0, 1, 4}, {0, 2, 1}, {1, 2, 2}, {1, 3, 5}, {2, 3, 8}, {2, 4, 10}, {3, 4, 2}});
    vector<int> parent;
    vector<int> dist = dijkstra(adj, 0, parent);
    cout << "dist:";
    for (int d : dist) cout << " " << d;
    cout << "\npath 0 -> 4:";
    vector<int> path;
    for (int t = 4; t != -1; t = parent[t]) path.push_back(t);
    reverse(path.begin(), path.end());
    for (int v : path) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static final int INF = 1_000_000_000;

    static List<List<int[]>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            adj.get(e[0]).add(new int[]{e[1], e[2]});
            adj.get(e[1]).add(new int[]{e[0], e[2]});   // undirected, weighted
        }
        return adj;
    }

    static int[] parent;

    static int[] dijkstra(List<List<int[]>> adj, int s) {
        int n = adj.size();
        int[] dist = new int[n];
        parent = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        Arrays.fill(parent, -1);
        dist[s] = 0;
        // min-heap of {distance, vertex}
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        pq.add(new int[]{0, s});
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = pq.poll();
            int d = top[0], u = top[1];
            if (d > dist[u]) continue;        // stale entry: u was already settled with a smaller d
            for (int[] e : adj.get(u)) {
                int v = e[0], w = e[1];
                if (d + w < dist[v]) {        // relax u -> v
                    dist[v] = d + w;
                    parent[v] = u;
                    pq.add(new int[]{dist[v], v});
                }
            }
        }
        return dist;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = build(5, new int[][]{{0, 1, 4}, {0, 2, 1}, {1, 2, 2}, {1, 3, 5}, {2, 3, 8}, {2, 4, 10}, {3, 4, 2}});
        int[] dist = dijkstra(adj, 0);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("dist:");
        for (int d : dist) sb.append(' ').append(d);
        System.out.println(sb);
        List<Integer> path = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 4; t != -1; t = parent[t]) path.add(t);
        Collections.reverse(path);
        sb = new StringBuilder("path 0 -> 4:");
        for (int v : path) sb.append(' ').append(v);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }
}
JavaScript
const INF = 1e9;

// Minimal binary min-heap of [key, value] pairs (JavaScript has no built-in priority queue).
class MinHeap {
    constructor() { this.a = []; }
    get size() { return this.a.length; }
    less(i, j) { const x = this.a[i], y = this.a[j]; return x[0] !== y[0] ? x[0] < y[0] : x[1] < y[1]; }
    swap(i, j) { [this.a[i], this.a[j]] = [this.a[j], this.a[i]]; }
    push(item) {
        this.a.push(item);
        for (let i = this.a.length - 1; i > 0; i = (i - 1) >> 1)
            if (this.less(i, (i - 1) >> 1)) this.swap(i, (i - 1) >> 1); else break;
    }
    pop() {
        const top = this.a[0], last = this.a.pop();
        if (this.a.length) {
            this.a[0] = last;
            for (let i = 0; ;) {
                let m = i;
                const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
                if (l < this.a.length && this.less(l, m)) m = l;
                if (r < this.a.length && this.less(r, m)) m = r;
                if (m === i) break;
                this.swap(i, m); i = m;
            }
        }
        return top;
    }
}

function build(n, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [u, v, w] of edges) { adj[u].push([v, w]); adj[v].push([u, w]); }   // undirected, weighted
    return adj;
}

function dijkstra(adj, s) {
    const n = adj.length;
    const dist = new Array(n).fill(INF), parent = new Array(n).fill(-1);
    dist[s] = 0;
    const pq = new MinHeap();                 // [distance, vertex]
    pq.push([0, s]);
    while (pq.size) {
        const [d, u] = pq.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;            // stale entry: u was already settled with a smaller d
        for (const [v, w] of adj[u]) {
            if (d + w < dist[v]) {            // relax u -> v
                dist[v] = d + w;
                parent[v] = u;
                pq.push([dist[v], v]);
            }
        }
    }
    return { dist, parent };
}

const adj = build(5, [[0, 1, 4], [0, 2, 1], [1, 2, 2], [1, 3, 5], [2, 3, 8], [2, 4, 10], [3, 4, 2]]);
const { dist, parent } = dijkstra(adj, 0);
console.log("dist:", dist.join(" "));
const path = [];
for (let t = 4; t !== -1; t = parent[t]) path.push(t);
console.log("path 0 -> 4:", path.reverse().join(" "));
Output
dist: 0 3 1 8 10
path 0 -> 4: 0 2 1 3 4
Time O((V + E) log V) with a binary heapSpace O(V + E)

The textbook version without a heap scans the whole dist array to find the minimum each round. It is O(V²) — fine for dense graphs or an adjacency matrix, and worth knowing because it is what the heap version optimises:

Python — O(V²) array version
INF = 10 ** 9

def dijkstra_matrix(graph, src):          # graph[u][v] = weight, 0 = no edge
    n = len(graph)
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    settled = [False] * n
    for _ in range(n):
        u = -1                            # O(V) scan for the closest unsettled vertex
        for i in range(n):
            if not settled[i] and (u == -1 or dist[i] < dist[u]):
                u = i
        if dist[u] == INF:
            break                         # the rest is unreachable
        settled[u] = True
        for v in range(n):
            if graph[u][v] and not settled[v]:
                dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + graph[u][v])
    return dist

graph = [[0, 4, 1, 0, 0],
         [4, 0, 2, 5, 0],
         [1, 2, 0, 8, 10],
         [0, 5, 8, 0, 2],
         [0, 0, 10, 2, 0]]
print(*dijkstra_matrix(graph, 0))
Output
0 3 1 8 10
Pitfall

Negative edge weights break Dijkstra. The algorithm assumes a settled vertex can never be improved; a negative edge discovered later can improve it. With a settled array the result is simply wrong; with the lazy-deletion heap version it may still be right but can re-settle vertices exponentially many times, and a negative cycle makes it loop forever. Use Bellman–Ford instead.

Key point

Does adding a constant to every edge keep the shortest path? No. Path 0→1→2 with weights 1 + 1 = 2 beats the direct edge 0→2 of weight 3; add 2 to every edge and it becomes 6 against 5. Paths with more edges are penalised more, so the shortest path can change — which is why Johnson's algorithm reweights with vertex potentials rather than a constant.

Bellman–Ford algorithm

Single-source shortest paths that allow negative edge weights and detect negative cycles. Instead of picking vertices cleverly it relaxes every edge, V − 1 times. After pass i, every shortest path that uses at most i edges is final; a shortest path has at most V − 1 edges, so V − 1 passes suffice.

Directed graph with negative edges: 0→1 (−1), 0→2 (4), 1→2 (3), 1→3 (2), 1→4 (2), 3→2 (5), 3→1 (1), 4→3 (−3)
          -1             2
  0 ──────────▶ 1 ──────────▶ 4
  │           ▲ │ ╲           │
4 │         1 │ │  ╲ 2        │ -3
  ▼           │ ▼   ▼         │
  2 ◀─────────┴─────3 ◀───────┘
          5   3
Example

Input: edges above, s = 0, V = 5
Output: 0 -1 2 -2 1
Input: same edges plus 3→4 (−1)
Output: negative-weight cycle

Idea

Shortest paths of one edge are found in pass 1, two edges in pass 2, and so on — each pass extends the frontier of correct distances by one edge. If a V-th pass can still improve something, a path with V edges is shorter than every path with fewer edges, which is only possible by going round a negative cycle.

1
Initialise
dist[s] = 0, every other dist[v] = INF.
2
Relax V − 1 times
For every edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
3
Check for a negative cycle
One more pass over all edges — if any edge can still be relaxed, a negative-weight cycle is reachable from s.
Python
INF = 10 ** 9

def bellman_ford(n, edges, s):            # edges: list of (u, v, w); no adjacency list needed
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[s] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):                # V - 1 passes
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w     # relax u -> v
    for u, v, w in edges:                 # pass V: anything still improving = negative cycle
        if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            return None
    return dist

edges = [(0, 1, -1), (0, 2, 4), (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2), (1, 4, 2), (3, 2, 5), (3, 1, 1), (4, 3, -3)]
d = bellman_ford(5, edges, 0)
print("graph 1:", *d)
d = bellman_ford(5, edges + [(3, 4, -1)], 0)         # 3 -> 4 -> 3 has weight -4
print("graph 2:", "negative-weight cycle" if d is None else " ".join(map(str, d)))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

const int INF = 1e9;
struct Edge { int u, v, w; };

// returns false when a negative-weight cycle is reachable from s
bool bellmanFord(int n, const vector<Edge>& edges, int s, vector<int>& dist) {
    dist.assign(n, INF);
    dist[s] = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)       // V - 1 passes
        for (auto& e : edges)
            if (dist[e.u] != INF && dist[e.u] + e.w < dist[e.v])
                dist[e.v] = dist[e.u] + e.w;          // relax u -> v
    for (auto& e : edges)                 // pass V: anything still improving = negative cycle
        if (dist[e.u] != INF && dist[e.u] + e.w < dist[e.v]) return false;
    return true;
}

void report(const char* name, int n, const vector<Edge>& edges) {
    vector<int> dist;
    cout << name << ":";
    if (!bellmanFord(n, edges, 0, dist)) { cout << " negative-weight cycle\n"; return; }
    for (int d : dist) cout << " " << d;
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    vector<Edge> edges = {{0, 1, -1}, {0, 2, 4}, {1, 2, 3}, {1, 3, 2}, {1, 4, 2}, {3, 2, 5}, {3, 1, 1}, {4, 3, -3}};
    report("graph 1", 5, edges);
    edges.push_back({3, 4, -1});          // 3 -> 4 -> 3 has weight -4
    report("graph 2", 5, edges);
}
Java
import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static final int INF = 1_000_000_000;

    // returns null when a negative-weight cycle is reachable from s
    static int[] bellmanFord(int n, List<int[]> edges, int s) {
        int[] dist = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        dist[s] = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)       // V - 1 passes
            for (int[] e : edges)
                if (dist[e[0]] != INF && dist[e[0]] + e[2] < dist[e[1]])
                    dist[e[1]] = dist[e[0]] + e[2];       // relax u -> v
        for (int[] e : edges)                 // pass V: anything still improving = negative cycle
            if (dist[e[0]] != INF && dist[e[0]] + e[2] < dist[e[1]]) return null;
        return dist;
    }

    static void report(String name, int n, List<int[]> edges) {
        int[] dist = bellmanFord(n, edges, 0);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(name + ":");
        if (dist == null) sb.append(" negative-weight cycle");
        else for (int d : dist) sb.append(' ').append(d);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new int[]{0, 1, -1}, new int[]{0, 2, 4}, new int[]{1, 2, 3},
                new int[]{1, 3, 2}, new int[]{1, 4, 2}, new int[]{3, 2, 5}, new int[]{3, 1, 1}, new int[]{4, 3, -3}));
        report("graph 1", 5, edges);
        edges.add(new int[]{3, 4, -1});       // 3 -> 4 -> 3 has weight -4
        report("graph 2", 5, edges);
    }
}

const INF = 1e9;

function bellmanFord(n, edges, s) {           // edges: [u, v, w]; returns null on a negative cycle
    const dist = new Array(n).fill(INF);
    dist[s] = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)           // V - 1 passes
        for (const [u, v, w] of edges)
            if (dist[u] !== INF && dist[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = dist[u] + w;   // relax u -> v
    for (const [u, v, w] of edges)            // pass V: anything still improving = negative cycle
        if (dist[u] !== INF && dist[u] + w < dist[v]) return null;
    return dist;
}

function report(name, n, edges) {
    const dist = bellmanFord(n, edges, 0);
    console.log(`${name}:`, dist === null ? "negative-weight cycle" : dist.join(" "));
}

const edges = [[0, 1, -1], [0, 2, 4], [1, 2, 3], [1, 3, 2], [1, 4, 2], [3, 2, 5], [3, 1, 1], [4, 3, -3]];
report("graph 1", 5, edges);
report("graph 2", 5, [...edges, [3, 4, -1]]);   // 3 -> 4 -> 3 has weight -4

graph 2: negative-weight cycle

Key point

Stop early when a whole pass changes nothing — on most graphs that happens long before V − 1 passes. SPFA (queue-based Bellman–Ford) only re-relaxes edges out of vertices whose distance changed; same worst case, much faster on average.

Strongly connected components — Kosaraju's algorithm

Strongly connected component (SCC) — a maximal set of vertices in a directed graph in which every vertex can reach every other. Collapsing each SCC to a single vertex turns any digraph into a DAG (the condensation).

The digraph used for both SCC algorithms: 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 1→3, 3→4, 4→5, 5→3, 4→6
0 ───▶ 1 ───▶ 3 ───▶ 4 ───▶ 6
▲      │      ▲      │
│      ▼      │      ▼
└───── 2      └───── 5

SCCs: {0, 1, 2}   {3, 4, 5}   {6}
Example

Input: edges above, V = 7
Output: {0,1,2} {3,4,5} {6} — 3 components

Idea

Reverse every edge and the SCCs stay the same, but the edges between them flip. A DFS on the original graph finishes the “source” SCC last; starting the second DFS there, on the reversed graph, cannot leak into other SCCs (their edges now point towards it), so each DFS of the second pass collects exactly one SCC.

1
DFS and record finish order
Run DFS over the whole graph, pushing each vertex onto a stack as it finishes (the same post-order used for topological sort).
2
Reverse the graph
Build rev with every edge u → v turned into v → u.
3
DFS the reversed graph in stack order
Pop vertices from the stack; for each unvisited one, DFS in rev — every vertex reached is in its SCC.
Python
def build(n, edges, reverse=False):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        if reverse:
            adj[v].append(u)
        else:
            adj[u].append(v)
    return adj

def dfs(adj, u, visited, out):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(adj, v, visited, out)
    out.append(u)                             # post-order

def kosaraju(n, edges):
    adj = build(n, edges)
    visited, finish = [False] * n, []
    for u in range(n):                        # step 1: finish order on the original graph
        if not visited[u]:
            dfs(adj, u, visited, finish)
    rev = build(n, edges, reverse=True)       # step 2: reversed graph
    visited = [False] * n
    sccs = []
    for u in reversed(finish):                # step 3: latest finisher first
        if not visited[u]:
            comp = []
            dfs(rev, u, visited, comp)        # reaches exactly one SCC
            sccs.append(sorted(comp))
    return sccs

edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (1, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3), (4, 6)]
sccs = kosaraju(7, edges)
for comp in sccs:
    print("SCC:", *comp)
print("count:", len(sccs))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> build(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges, bool reverse) {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) {
        if (reverse) adj[v].push_back(u); else adj[u].push_back(v);
    }
    return adj;
}

void dfs(const vector<vector<int>>& adj, int u, vector<bool>& visited, vector<int>& out) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, out);
    out.push_back(u);                             // post-order
}

vector<vector<int>> kosaraju(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    auto adj = build(n, edges, false);
    vector<bool> visited(n, false);
    vector<int> finish;
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)                   // step 1: finish order on the original graph
        if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, finish);
    auto rev = build(n, edges, true);             // step 2: reversed graph
    visited.assign(n, false);
    vector<vector<int>> sccs;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {            // step 3: latest finisher first
        int u = finish[i];
        if (visited[u]) continue;
        vector<int> comp;
        dfs(rev, u, visited, comp);               // reaches exactly one SCC
        sort(comp.begin(), comp.end());
        sccs.push_back(comp);
    }
    return sccs;
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<int,int>> edges = {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 0}, {1, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 5}, {5, 3}, {4, 6}};
    auto sccs = kosaraju(7, edges);
    for (auto& comp : sccs) {
        cout << "SCC:";
        for (int v : comp) cout << " " << v;
        cout << "\n";
    }
    cout << "count: " << sccs.size() << "\n";
}

        for (int[] e : edges) {
            if (reverse) adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]); else adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        }

        visited[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj.get(u))
            if (!visited[v]) dfs(adj, v, visited, out);
        out.add(u);                                   // post-order

        boolean[] visited = new boolean[n];
        List<Integer> finish = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)                   // step 1: finish order on the original graph
            if (!visited[u]) dfs(adj, u, visited, finish);

        visited = new boolean[n];
        List<List<Integer>> sccs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {            // step 3: latest finisher first
            int u = finish.get(i);
            if (visited[u]) continue;
            List<Integer> comp = new ArrayList<>();
            dfs(rev, u, visited, comp);               // reaches exactly one SCC
            Collections.sort(comp);

    }

Key point

Kosaraju emits SCCs in topological order of the condensation (sources first: {0,1,2} before {3,4,5} before {6}); Tarjan's algorithm below emits them in reverse. A digraph is strongly connected exactly when the count is 1.

Strongly connected components — Tarjan's algorithm

One DFS pass instead of two. Every vertex gets a discovery time disc[u] and a low-link low[u]: the smallest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using at most one back edge to a vertex that is still on the stack. A vertex with low[u] == disc[u] is the root of an SCC — everything above it on the stack belongs to that component.

Idea

Keep every vertex on an explicit stack from the moment it is discovered until its SCC is complete. A back edge to a stacked vertex v lowers low[u] to disc[v]; after visiting a child v, low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). If, when u finishes, nothing in its subtree reached anything discovered earlier (low[u] == disc[u]), then u and all vertices stacked after it form one SCC — pop them off.

Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
    return adj

def tarjan(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    disc, low = [-1] * n, [0] * n
    on_stack, stack, sccs = [False] * n, [], []
    timer = [0]

    def dfs(u):
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer[0]
        timer[0] += 1
        stack.append(u)
        on_stack[u] = True
        for v in adj[u]:
            if disc[v] == -1:                 # tree edge
                dfs(v)
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
            elif on_stack[v]:                 # back edge into the current SCC
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])
        if low[u] == disc[u]:                 # u is the root of an SCC
            comp = []
            while True:
                v = stack.pop()
                on_stack[v] = False
                comp.append(v)
                if v == u:
                    break
            sccs.append(sorted(comp))

    for u in range(n):
        if disc[u] == -1:
            dfs(u)
    return sccs

adj = build(7, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (1, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3), (4, 6)])
sccs = tarjan(adj)
for comp in sccs:
    print("SCC:", *comp)
print("count:", len(sccs))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Tarjan {
    const vector<vector<int>>& adj;
    vector<int> disc, low, stack;
    vector<bool> onStack;
    vector<vector<int>> sccs;
    int timer = 0;

    Tarjan(const vector<vector<int>>& g) : adj(g), disc(g.size(), -1), low(g.size(), 0), onStack(g.size(), false) {}

    void dfs(int u) {
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
        stack.push_back(u);
        onStack[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj[u]) {
            if (disc[v] == -1) {                  // tree edge
                dfs(v);
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]);
            } else if (onStack[v]) {              // back edge into the current SCC
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
        if (low[u] == disc[u]) {                  // u is the root of an SCC
            vector<int> comp;
            while (true) {
                int v = stack.back(); stack.pop_back();
                onStack[v] = false;
                comp.push_back(v);
                if (v == u) break;
            }
            sort(comp.begin(), comp.end());
            sccs.push_back(comp);
        }
    }

    vector<vector<int>> run() {
        for (int u = 0; u < (int)adj.size(); u++)
            if (disc[u] == -1) dfs(u);
        return sccs;
    }
};

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(7);
    for (auto [u, v] : vector<pair<int,int>>{{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 0}, {1, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 5}, {5, 3}, {4, 6}})
        adj[u].push_back(v);
    auto sccs = Tarjan(adj).run();
    for (auto& comp : sccs) {
        cout << "SCC:";
        for (int v : comp) cout << " " << v;
        cout << "\n";
    }
    cout << "count: " << sccs.size() << "\n";
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static List<List<Integer>> adj;
    static int[] disc, low;
    static boolean[] onStack;
    static Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    static List<List<Integer>> sccs = new ArrayList<>();
    static int timer = 0;

    static void dfs(int u) {
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
        stack.push(u);
        onStack[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (disc[v] == -1) {                      // tree edge
                dfs(v);
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], low[v]);
            } else if (onStack[v]) {                  // back edge into the current SCC
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
        if (low[u] == disc[u]) {                      // u is the root of an SCC
            List<Integer> comp = new ArrayList<>();
            while (true) {
                int v = stack.pop();
                onStack[v] = false;
                comp.add(v);
                if (v == u) break;
            }
            Collections.sort(comp);
            sccs.add(comp);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 7;
        int[][] edges = {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 0}, {1, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 5}, {5, 3}, {4, 6}};
        adj = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        disc = new int[n]; low = new int[n]; onStack = new boolean[n];
        Arrays.fill(disc, -1);
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            if (disc[u] == -1) dfs(u);
        for (List<Integer> comp : sccs) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("SCC:");
            for (int v : comp) sb.append(' ').append(v);
            System.out.println(sb);
        }
        System.out.println("count: " + sccs.size());
    }
}
JavaScript
function build(n, edges) {
    const adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    for (const [u, v] of edges) adj[u].push(v);
    return adj;
}

function tarjan(adj) {
    const n = adj.length;
    const disc = new Array(n).fill(-1), low = new Array(n).fill(0);
    const onStack = new Array(n).fill(false), stack = [], sccs = [];
    let timer = 0;

    function dfs(u) {
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
        stack.push(u);
        onStack[u] = true;
        for (const v of adj[u]) {
            if (disc[v] === -1) {                     // tree edge
                dfs(v);
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], low[v]);
            } else if (onStack[v]) {                  // back edge into the current SCC
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
        if (low[u] === disc[u]) {                     // u is the root of an SCC
            const comp = [];
            for (;;) {
                const v = stack.pop();
                onStack[v] = false;
                comp.push(v);
                if (v === u) break;
            }
            sccs.push(comp.sort((a, b) => a - b));
        }
    }

    for (let u = 0; u < n; u++)
        if (disc[u] === -1) dfs(u);
    return sccs;
}

Pitfall

For the back-edge case use disc[v], not low[v], and only when v is still on the stack — a visited vertex that has already been popped belongs to a finished SCC and must not lower low[u]. Using low[v] still yields correct SCCs here, but the identical-looking articulation-point algorithm below genuinely breaks with that mistake.

Articulation points (cut vertices)

Articulation point — a vertex of a connected undirected graph whose removal (with its edges) disconnects the graph — the single point of failure in a network. A graph with no articulation point is biconnected.

The graph used for articulation points and bridges: edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4; vertices 1 and 3 are articulation points
0 ───── 1 ───── 3 ───── 4
│     ╱
│   ╱
2 ╱

remove 1 → {0, 2} and {3, 4}    remove 3 → {0, 1, 2} and {4}
remove 0, 2 or 4 → still connected
Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, V = 5
Output: 1 3

Naive solution. Remove every vertex in turn and count the connected components of what is left (skipping the removed vertex). If the count goes above 1, the vertex is an articulation point. One DFS per vertex: O(V · (V + E)).

Python — naive O(V · (V + E))
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def dfs(adj, u, visited):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(adj, v, visited)

def components_without(adj, removed):
    visited = [False] * len(adj)
    visited[removed] = True                   # pretend the vertex is gone
    count = 0
    for u in range(len(adj)):
        if not visited[u]:
            count += 1
            dfs(adj, u, visited)
    return count

def articulation_points_naive(adj):
    return [u for u in range(len(adj)) if components_without(adj, u) > 1]

adj = build(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 4)])
print("articulation points (naive):", *articulation_points_naive(adj))
Output
articulation points (naive): 1 3

First idea (DFS tree, root only). Run a DFS and look at its tree. If the root has two or more DFS children, the root is an articulation point: the subtrees are separate branches that no back edge can connect (an undirected DFS tree has no cross edges, so an edge between two subtrees would have been a tree edge). The rule is only valid for the root — any other vertex can have several children that are still joined through back edges to its ancestors.

Python — the root rule
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def dfs(adj, u, visited):
    visited[u] = True
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not visited[v]:
            dfs(adj, v, visited)

def root_children(adj, root):
    visited = [False] * len(adj)
    visited[root] = True
    children = 0
    for v in adj[root]:
        if not visited[v]:                    # each unvisited neighbour starts a new subtree
            children += 1
            dfs(adj, v, visited)
    return children

adj = build(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 4)])
for root in (0, 3):
    c = root_children(adj, root)
    print(f"root {root}: {c} DFS child(ren) ->", "articulation point" if c >= 2 else "not an articulation point")
Output
root 0: 1 DFS child(ren) -> not an articulation point
root 3: 2 DFS child(ren) -> articulation point

Tarjan's algorithm (low-link values). Give every vertex a discovery time disc[u] (the DFS counter when u is first visited) and a low value low[u]: the smallest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using tree edges plus at most one back edge. A non-root u is an articulation point iff some DFS child v has low[v] ≥ disc[u] — nothing in v's subtree climbs above u, so removing u strands that subtree.

Idea

low[u] starts as disc[u]. A back edge u – v to an already visited vertex (that is not the parent) lowers it to disc[v]; after returning from a child v, low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). The check low[v] >= disc[u] is made right after dfs(v) returns, when low[v] is final.

1
Discover
On entering u: disc[u] = low[u] = timer++, children = 0.
2
Tree edge
For an unvisited neighbour v: children++, dfs(v), then low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). If u is not the root and low[v] >= disc[u], mark u.
3
Back edge
For a visited neighbour v that is not the parent: low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]).
4
Root rule
After the loop: if u is the root and children >= 2, mark u.
Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def articulation_points(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    disc, low, parent = [-1] * n, [0] * n, [-1] * n
    is_ap = [False] * n
    timer = [0]

    def dfs(u):
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer[0]
        timer[0] += 1
        children = 0
        for v in adj[u]:
            if disc[v] == -1:                     # tree edge
                parent[v] = u
                children += 1
                dfs(v)
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
                if parent[u] != -1 and low[v] >= disc[u]:
                    is_ap[u] = True               # v's subtree cannot climb above u
            elif v != parent[u]:                  # back edge
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])
        if parent[u] == -1 and children >= 2:
            is_ap[u] = True                       # root rule

    for u in range(n):
        if disc[u] == -1:
            dfs(u)
    print("disc:", *disc)
    print("low:", *low)
    return [u for u in range(n) if is_ap[u]]

adj = build(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 4)])
print("articulation points:", *articulation_points(adj))

void dfs(const vector<vector<int>>& adj, int u) {

    int children = 0;

            low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]);
        }
    }
    if (parent[u] == -1 && children >= 2) isAp[u] = true;   // root rule
}

        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;

            } else if (v != parent[u]) {              // back edge
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
        if (parent[u] == -1 && children >= 2) isAp[u] = true;   // root rule
    }

Pitfall

Two classic mistakes. (1) Applying the low[v] >= disc[u] test to the root: the root's disc is 0, so every child passes it and the root would always be reported — the root needs the children count instead. (2) Writing low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]) for a back edge: low[v] may already have been lowered through v's own back edges to vertices above u, which makes u look safe when it is not. For a back edge use disc[v].

Key point

The same disc/low arrays answer several questions at once: articulation points (low[v] >= disc[u]), bridges (low[v] > disc[u], next section) and, in a directed graph, strongly connected components (low[u] == disc[u]). Learn the DFS once and remember the three conditions.

Bridges (cut edges)

Bridge — an edge of a connected undirected graph whose removal disconnects the graph. Every bridge lies on no cycle; equivalently, an edge is a bridge exactly when it is not part of any cycle.

Edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4 versus 0-1, 1-2, 2-0, 2-3, 3-4, 4-2
Graph 1                           Graph 2 (two triangles sharing 2)

0 ───── 1 ═════ 3 ═════ 4         0 ───── 1         3 ───── 4
│     ╱                            ╲     ╱           ╲     ╱
│   ╱                               ╲   ╱             ╲   ╱
2 ╱                                   2 ───────────────┘

bridges: 1-3, 3-4                 bridges: none (2 is an articulation point, though)
Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4
Output: 1-3 3-4
Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 2-0, 2-3, 3-4, 4-2
Output: none

Idea

Same DFS, same disc and low, one character different. The tree edge u – v is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u]: nothing in v's subtree reaches u or anything above it, so the tree edge is the only way out. With >= a back edge landing exactly on u would still count as a cycle through u – v, which is why that case is an articulation point but not a bridge. There is no root special case for bridges.

Python
def build(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

def bridges(adj):
    n = len(adj)
    disc, low = [-1] * n, [0] * n
    found = []
    timer = [0]

    def dfs(u, parent):
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer[0]
        timer[0] += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            if disc[v] == -1:                     # tree edge
                dfs(v, u)
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
                if low[v] > disc[u]:              # v's subtree never reaches u or above
                    found.append((min(u, v), max(u, v)))
            elif v != parent:                     # back edge
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])

    for u in range(n):
        if disc[u] == -1:
            dfs(u, -1)
    return sorted(found)

g2 = build(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 2)])
for name, g in (("graph 1", g1), ("graph 2", g2)):
    b = bridges(g)
    print(f"{name}:", " ".join(f"{u}-{v}" for u, v in b) if b else "none")

#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<vector<int>> build(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) { adj[u].push_back(v); adj[v].push_back(u); }
    return adj;
}

struct Bridges {
    const vector<vector<int>>& adj;
    vector<int> disc, low;
    vector<pair<int,int>> found;
    int timer = 0;

    Bridges(const vector<vector<int>>& g) : adj(g), disc(g.size(), -1), low(g.size(), 0) {}

    void dfs(int u, int parent) {
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
        for (int v : adj[u]) {
            if (disc[v] == -1) {                      // tree edge
                dfs(v, u);
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]);
                if (low[v] > disc[u])                 // v's subtree never reaches u or above
                    found.push_back({min(u, v), max(u, v)});
            } else if (v != parent) {                 // back edge
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
    }

    vector<pair<int,int>> run() {
        for (int u = 0; u < (int)adj.size(); u++)
            if (disc[u] == -1) dfs(u, -1);
        sort(found.begin(), found.end());
        return found;
    }
};

void report(const string& name, const vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    auto b = Bridges(g).run();
    cout << name << ":";
    if (b.empty()) cout << " none";
    for (auto [u, v] : b) cout << " " << u << "-" << v;
    cout << "\n";
}

int main() {
    report("graph 1", build(5, {{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {3, 4}}));
    report("graph 2", build(5, {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 0}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 2}}));
}

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    static List<List<Integer>> build(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) { adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]); }
        return adj;
    }

    static List<List<Integer>> adj;
    static int[] disc, low;
    static List<int[]> found;
    static int timer;

    static void dfs(int u, int parent) {
        disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (disc[v] == -1) {                      // tree edge
                dfs(v, u);
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], low[v]);
                if (low[v] > disc[u])                 // v's subtree never reaches u or above
                    found.add(new int[]{Math.min(u, v), Math.max(u, v)});
            } else if (v != parent) {                 // back edge
                low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]);
            }
        }
    }

    static List<int[]> bridges(List<List<Integer>> g) {
        adj = g;
        int n = g.size();
        disc = new int[n]; low = new int[n]; found = new ArrayList<>(); timer = 0;
        Arrays.fill(disc, -1);
        for (int u = 0; u < n; u++)
            if (disc[u] == -1) dfs(u, -1);
        found.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] - b[0] : a[1] - b[1]);
        return found;
    }

    static void report(String name, List<List<Integer>> g) {
        List<int[]> b = bridges(g);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(name + ":");
        if (b.isEmpty()) sb.append(" none");
        for (int[] e : b) sb.append(' ').append(e[0]).append('-').append(e[1]);
        System.out.println(sb);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        report("graph 1", build(5, new int[][]{{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {3, 4}}));
        report("graph 2", build(5, new int[][]{{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 0}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 2}}));
    }
}
