            for (int i = 1; i + len - 1 < n; i++) {
                int j = i + len - 1;
                dp[i][j] = Long.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int k = i; k < j; k++)                  // last split: (i..k)(k+1..j)
                    dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + (long) dims[i - 1] * dims[k] * dims[j]);
            }
        return dp[1][n - 1];
    }

Pitfall

Off-by-one in the dimensions: matrix Ai is dims[i-1] × dims[i], so the final product of (i..k)(k+1..j) costs dims[i-1]·dims[k]·dims[j] — not dims[i]·dims[k]·dims[j]. Check with [2, 1, 3]: one multiplication, 2·1·3 = 6.

Palindrome partitioning
Example

Input: s = "geek"
Output: 2 (g | ee | k)
Input: s = "abbac"
Output: 1 (abba | c)
Input: s = "aab"
Output: 1 (aa | b)

Find the minimum number of cuts so that every piece of the string is a palindrome. A string that is already a palindrome needs 0 cuts.

Idea

Two tables. pal[i][j] says whether s[i..j] is a palindrome — s[i] == s[j] and the inside is a palindrome (any string of length ≤ 2 with equal ends qualifies). cuts[j] = minimum cuts for the prefix s[0..j]: if some s[i..j] is a palindrome, the prefix s[0..i-1] plus one more cut is a candidate; i = 0 means the whole prefix is a palindrome → 0 cuts.

cuts[j] = min over i ≤ j with pal[i][j] of ( 0 if i = 0 else cuts[i−1] + 1 ); pal[i][j] = s[i] = s[j] AND (j − i ≤ 2 OR pal[i+1][j−1])

The straightforward recursion tries every cut position of every substring and recomputes the palindrome checks each time — O(2^n):

Python
def is_pal(s, i, j):
    while i < j:
        if s[i] != s[j]:
            return False
        i += 1; j -= 1
    return True

def min_cuts_rec(s, i, j):
    if is_pal(s, i, j):
        return 0                                   # whole piece is a palindrome
    best = float("inf")
    for k in range(i, j):                          # cut after position k
        best = min(best, 1 + min_cuts_rec(s, i, k) + min_cuts_rec(s, k + 1, j))
    return best

print(min_cuts_rec("geek", 0, 3))
print(min_cuts_rec("abbac", 0, 4))
Output
2
1
Python
def min_cuts(s):
    n = len(s)
    pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    cuts = [0] * n
    for j in range(n):                                  # end of the prefix
        best = float("inf")
        for i in range(j + 1):                          # candidate last piece s[i..j]
            if s[i] == s[j] and (j - i <= 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1]):
                pal[i][j] = True
                best = 0 if i == 0 else min(best, cuts[i - 1] + 1)
        cuts[j] = best
    return cuts[n - 1]

for s in ["geek", "abbac", "aab", "ababbbabbababa"]:
    print(s, "->", min_cuts(s))

#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int minCuts(const string& s) {
    int n = s.size();
    vector<vector<bool>> pal(n, vector<bool>(n, false));
    vector<int> cuts(n, 0);
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {                           // end of the prefix
        int best = 1e9;
        for (int i = 0; i <= j; i++)                        // candidate last piece s[i..j]
            if (s[i] == s[j] && (j - i <= 2 || pal[i + 1][j - 1])) {
                pal[i][j] = true;
                best = i == 0 ? 0 : min(best, cuts[i - 1] + 1);
            }
        cuts[j] = best;
    }
    return cuts[n - 1];
}

Pitfall

Once i == 0 makes the whole prefix a palindrome, best must become 0 and stay 0 — do not min it with later candidates (they can only be ≥ 0 anyway, but writing best = min(best, 0) hides the intent). Also note pal[i+1][j-1] is only read when j - i > 2, so the indices never go out of range.

Allocate minimum pages
Example

Input: pages = [12, 34, 67, 90], students = 2
Output: 113 ([12, 34, 67] | [90])
Input: pages = [10, 20, 30, 40], students = 2
Output: 60 ([10, 20, 30] | [40])

Books are in a fixed order and each student gets a contiguous block of books. Minimise the maximum number of pages any one student reads.

Idea

dp[i][j] = the best (smallest) maximum load when the first j books are split among i students. The last student takes books p+1..j for some p; the first p books go to the other i-1 students. The load of this split is the larger of dp[i-1][p] and pages(p+1..j); take the p that minimises it. With one student, dp[1][j] is just the prefix sum.

dp[i][j] = min over 0 < p < j of max( dp[i−1][p], prefix[j] − prefix[p] ); dp[1][j] = prefix[j]
Python
def min_pages(pages, k):
    n = len(pages)
    prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + pages[i]            # sum of books 0..i-1
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [[INF] * (n + 1) for _ in range(k + 1)]
    for j in range(n + 1):
        dp[1][j] = prefix[j]                             # one student reads everything
    for i in range(2, k + 1):
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            for p in range(1, j):                        # last student takes books p..j-1
                load = max(dp[i - 1][p], prefix[j] - prefix[p])
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], load)
    return dp[k][n]

for pages, k in [([12, 34, 67, 90], 2), ([10, 20, 30, 40], 2), ([12, 34, 67, 90], 3)]:
    print("[" + ", ".join(map(str, pages)) + "] with", k, "students ->", min_pages(pages, k))
C++
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int minPages(const vector<int>& pages, int k) {
    int n = pages.size();
    vector<int> prefix(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + pages[i];   // sum of books 0..i-1
    const int INF = 1e9;
    vector<vector<int>> dp(k + 1, vector<int>(n + 1, INF));
    for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[1][j] = prefix[j];                 // one student reads everything
    for (int i = 2; i <= k; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
            for (int p = 1; p < j; p++)                                  // last student takes books p..j-1
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], max(dp[i - 1][p], prefix[j] - prefix[p]));
    return dp[k][n];
}

void show(const vector<int>& pages, int k) {
    cout << "[";
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)pages.size(); i++) cout << (i ? ", " : "") << pages[i];
    cout << "] with " << k << " students -> " << minPages(pages, k) << "\n";
}

int main() {
    show({12, 34, 67, 90}, 2);
    show({10, 20, 30, 40}, 2);
    show({12, 34, 67, 90}, 3);
}

import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static int minPages(int[] pages, int k) {
        int n = pages.length;
        int[] prefix = new int[n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + pages[i];   // sum of books 0..i-1
        final int INF = 1_000_000_000;
        int[][] dp = new int[k + 1][n + 1];
        for (int[] row : dp) Arrays.fill(row, INF);
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[1][j] = prefix[j];                 // one student reads everything
        for (int i = 2; i <= k; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                for (int p = 1; p < j; p++)                                  // last student takes books p..j-1
                    dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], Math.max(dp[i - 1][p], prefix[j] - prefix[p]));
        return dp[k][n];
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        int[] students = {2, 2, 3};

            System.out.println(Arrays.toString(tests[t]) + " with " + students[t] + " students -> " + minPages(tests[t], students[t]));
    }
}

Key point

The DP is the natural first solution, but the standard interview answer is binary search on the answer (Searching topic): guess a maximum load, check greedily whether k students suffice, and narrow the range — O(n log(sum)). Know both and say why the DP is slower.

Interview Q&A
What is the difference between dynamic programming and divide and conquer?

Both split a problem into subproblems and combine the answers. Divide and conquer (merge sort, quicksort) produces independent subproblems, so nothing is reused. DP applies when the subproblems overlap — the same instance is needed many times — and stores each answer once. Without overlap, memoization adds cost and no benefit.

Memoization or tabulation — which should I use in an interview?

Start with the recursive formulation (it is how you find the recurrence), then add a memo — that is usually enough and hard to get wrong. Switch to tabulation when recursion depth is a risk (Python, n in the 10⁴ range), when you need the whole table (printing the LCS), or when a rolling row can cut space — e.g. knapsack in O(W) instead of O(n·W).

How do you spot that a problem is DP?

Three signs: it asks for an optimum (min/max), a count, or a yes/no over choices (take/skip, cut here/there); a brute-force recursion exists whose calls repeat; and the answer for a bigger input is built from answers for strictly smaller inputs (optimal substructure). Then name the state in words — if you cannot say what dp[i][j] means, you do not have a recurrence yet.

Why is the 0-1 knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial?

Its running time O(n·W) is polynomial in the numeric value of the capacity W, not in the number of bits used to write W. Doubling the number of digits of W squares the running time. Knapsack and subset sum remain NP-complete; the DP is only efficient when the numbers are small.

How do you reconstruct the actual solution, not just its value?

Keep the table and walk back from the final cell, re-deciding at each step which branch produced the stored value — as in “Printing the LCS”. For knapsack, compare dp[i][w] with dp[i-1][w]: if they differ, item i was taken and w shrinks by its weight. Rolling-row space optimisations destroy this information, so keep the full table when you must reconstruct.

What is the role of the order of loops in the 1-D coin change?

With dp[j] += dp[j - coin] and the coins in the outer loop, each coin is introduced once and the array counts combinations ({1, 3} once). With the sums in the outer loop and the coins inside, every ordering of the same coins is counted separately — permutations. For minimum coins the order does not matter because min is idempotent.

Advanced Structures

Trie Data Structure

A trie (prefix tree) stores a set of words as a tree of characters, so that every operation costs time proportional to the length of the word — not to the number of words — and so that words sharing a prefix share a path. It is the structure behind autocomplete, spell-checkers and IP routing tables.

Trie — a rooted tree in which every edge is labelled with a character and every node represents the prefix spelled out by the path from the root. A flag on a node marks that this prefix is a complete word. The root represents the empty string.

Trie for { geeks, geek, bad, bat, cat, cut } — "geek" and "geeks" share one path, "ba" is a prefix of two words
         (root)
  ┌────────┼────────┐
  b        c        g
  │     ┌──┴──┐     │
  a     a     u     e
┌─┴─┐   │     │     │
d*  t*  t*    t*    e
                    │
                    k*          * = isEndOfWord
                    │
                    s*

Tries are the right choice when a dictionary of words must support these operations efficiently:

  1. Search — is this exact word in the dictionary?
  2. Insert — add a word.
  3. Delete — remove a word (without disturbing words that share its prefix).
  4. Prefix search — does any word start with pre? List them all (autocomplete).
  5. Lexicographic ordering — a pre-order traversal visits the words in sorted order for free.
OperationTrieHash table
SearchΘ(word_len)Θ(word_len) average
InsertΘ(word_len)Θ(word_len) average
DeleteΘ(word_len)Θ(word_len) average
Prefix searchΘ(prefix_len)not supported
Lexicographic orderingΘ(output_len)not supported (needs a sort)
Memoryhigh — up to 26 pointers per nodelow
Key point

A hash table matches a trie on exact-match operations, and uses far less memory. Reach for a trie only when you need prefix queries or sorted output — those are the operations a hash table simply cannot do.

Trie representation

For lowercase English words each node holds an array of 26 child pointers (index ch − 'a') and a boolean isEndOfWord. The characters themselves are not stored in the nodes — they are implied by the array index on the way down.

Python
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None] * 26          # child[i] → node for chr(ord('a') + i), or None
        self.is_end_of_word = False       # True ⇔ the path from the root spells a stored word

root = TrieNode()                         # the empty trie: a root with no children
print(sum(c is not None for c in root.child), root.is_end_of_word)
Output
0 False
FieldMeaning
child[26]one slot per letter; None/nullptr means no word continues with that letter
isEndOfWordmarks a complete word — needed because geek must be found while gee must not
Variants

Alphabets larger than 26 letters (Unicode, arbitrary bytes) use a hash map from character to child instead of a fixed array — slower per step, but the memory no longer scales with the alphabet size.

Insert, search and prefix search
Example

Input: insert geeks, geek, bad, bat, cat, cut; search("geek")
Output: true
Input: search("gee")
Output: false (a prefix, not a word)
Input: startsWith("ge")
Output: true

Idea

All three walk the same path. Insert creates the missing child at every step and marks the final node. Search stops with false as soon as a child is missing and, at the end, returns the isEndOfWord flag. Prefix search is search without the final flag check.

1
Start at the root
with the first character of the key.
2
Follow child[ch − 'a']
insert: create the node if it is missing — search: return false if it is missing.
3
At the last character
insert: set isEndOfWord = true — search: return isEndOfWord — startsWith: return true.
Python
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None] * 26
        self.is_end_of_word = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, key):
        node = self.root
        for ch in key:
            i = ord(ch) - ord('a')
            if node.child[i] is None:            # extend the path where it stops
                node.child[i] = TrieNode()
            node = node.child[i]
        node.is_end_of_word = True               # mark the complete word

    def _walk(self, key):                        # node where `key` ends, or None
        node = self.root
        for ch in key:
            node = node.child[ord(ch) - ord('a')]
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def search(self, key):
        node = self._walk(key)
        return node is not None and node.is_end_of_word

    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None

    def words(self):                             # pre-order traversal → lexicographic order
        out = []
        def dfs(node, prefix):
            if node.is_end_of_word:
                out.append(prefix)
            for i, c in enumerate(node.child):
                if c is not None:
                    dfs(c, prefix + chr(ord('a') + i))
        dfs(self.root, "")
        return out

trie = Trie()
for w in ["geeks", "geek", "bad", "bat", "cat", "cut"]:
    trie.insert(w)
for w in ["geek", "gee", "cut", "dog"]:
    print(f"search {w}:", "true" if trie.search(w) else "false")
for pre in ["ge", "do"]:
    print(f"startsWith {pre}:", "true" if trie.starts_with(pre) else "false")
print("words:", " ".join(trie.words()))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct TrieNode {
    TrieNode* child[26] = {};
    bool isEndOfWord = false;
};

class Trie {
    TrieNode* root = new TrieNode();
    TrieNode* walk(const string& key) const {           // node where `key` ends, or nullptr
        TrieNode* node = root;
        for (char ch : key) {
            node = node->child[ch - 'a'];
            if (!node) return nullptr;
        }
        return node;
    }
    void dfs(TrieNode* node, string& prefix, vector<string>& out) const {
        if (node->isEndOfWord) out.push_back(prefix);
        for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++)
            if (node->child[i]) {
                prefix.push_back('a' + i);
                dfs(node->child[i], prefix, out);
                prefix.pop_back();
            }
    }
public:
    void insert(const string& key) {
        TrieNode* node = root;
        for (char ch : key) {
            int i = ch - 'a';
            if (!node->child[i]) node->child[i] = new TrieNode();   // extend the path where it stops
            node = node->child[i];
        }
        node->isEndOfWord = true;                                   // mark the complete word
    }
    bool search(const string& key) const { TrieNode* n = walk(key); return n && n->isEndOfWord; }
    bool startsWith(const string& prefix) const { return walk(prefix) != nullptr; }
    vector<string> words() const { vector<string> out; string p; dfs(root, p, out); return out; }   // sorted
};

int main() {
    Trie trie;
    for (string w : {"geeks", "geek", "bad", "bat", "cat", "cut"}) trie.insert(w);
    for (string w : {"geek", "gee", "cut", "dog"}) cout << "search " << w << ": " << (trie.search(w) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
    for (string p : {"ge", "do"}) cout << "startsWith " << p << ": " << (trie.startsWith(p) ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
    cout << "words:";
    for (const string& w : trie.words()) cout << " " << w;
    cout << "\n";
}
Java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static class TrieNode {
        TrieNode[] child = new TrieNode[26];
        boolean isEndOfWord;
    }

    static class Trie {
        TrieNode root = new TrieNode();

        void insert(String key) {
            TrieNode node = root;
            for (char ch : key.toCharArray()) {
                int i = ch - 'a';
                if (node.child[i] == null) node.child[i] = new TrieNode();   // extend the path where it stops
                node = node.child[i];
            }
            node.isEndOfWord = true;                                          // mark the complete word
        }
        TrieNode walk(String key) {                                           // node where key ends, or null
            TrieNode node = root;
            for (char ch : key.toCharArray()) {
                node = node.child[ch - 'a'];
                if (node == null) return null;
            }
            return node;
        }
        boolean search(String key) { TrieNode n = walk(key); return n != null && n.isEndOfWord; }
        boolean startsWith(String prefix) { return walk(prefix) != null; }
        List<String> words() { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); dfs(root, new StringBuilder(), out); return out; }
        void dfs(TrieNode node, StringBuilder prefix, List<String> out) {     // pre-order → sorted
            if (node.isEndOfWord) out.add(prefix.toString());
            for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++)
                if (node.child[i] != null) {
                    prefix.append((char) ('a' + i));
                    dfs(node.child[i], prefix, out);
                    prefix.setLength(prefix.length() - 1);
                }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Trie trie = new Trie();
        for (String w : new String[]{"geeks", "geek", "bad", "bat", "cat", "cut"}) trie.insert(w);
        for (String w : new String[]{"geek", "gee", "cut", "dog"}) System.out.println("search " + w + ": " + trie.search(w));
        for (String p : new String[]{"ge", "do"}) System.out.println("startsWith " + p + ": " + trie.startsWith(p));
        System.out.println("words: " + String.join(" ", trie.words()));
    }
}

class TrieNode {
    constructor() { this.child = new Array(26).fill(null); this.isEndOfWord = false; }
}

class Trie {
    constructor() { this.root = new TrieNode(); }
    insert(key) {
        let node = this.root;
        for (const ch of key) {
            const i = ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97;
            if (node.child[i] === null) node.child[i] = new TrieNode();   // extend the path where it stops
            node = node.child[i];
        }
        node.isEndOfWord = true;                                           // mark the complete word
    }
    walk(key) {                                                            // node where key ends, or null
        let node = this.root;
        for (const ch of key) {
            node = node.child[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97];
            if (node === null) return null;
        }
        return node;
    }
    search(key) { const n = this.walk(key); return n !== null && n.isEndOfWord; }
    startsWith(prefix) { return this.walk(prefix) !== null; }
    words() {                                                              // pre-order → sorted
        const out = [];
        const dfs = (node, prefix) => {
            if (node.isEndOfWord) out.push(prefix);
            node.child.forEach((c, i) => { if (c !== null) dfs(c, prefix + String.fromCharCode(97 + i)); });
        };
        dfs(this.root, "");
        return out;
    }
}

Pitfall

Returning true from search as soon as the walk succeeds finds "gee" even though only "geek" was inserted. The final isEndOfWord check is what separates search from startsWith.

Delete

Deleting must remove the word without breaking any other word that shares its path. geeks and geek share g-e-e-k; deleting geeks may remove only the s node, and deleting geek must only clear a flag.

Example

Input: insert geeks, geek, bad, bat, cat, cut; delete("geeks")
Output: search("geeks") = false, search("geek") = true
Input: delete("bad")
Output: search("bad") = false, search("bat") = true

Idea

Write a recursive function that walks down to the last character. On the way back up: clear isEndOfWord at the last node; then delete a node only if it is not the end of another word and has no children. Deletion stops at the first node that is still needed.

1
Recurse to the node of the last character
depth == len(key): unmark isEndOfWord.
2
Is this node now useless?
No children and not the end of any word → return null so the parent drops its pointer.
3
Walk back up
Each parent re-checks: if it is not a word end and has no children left, it is removed as well. The first node that still serves another word stops the chain.
The three cases: remove a leaf, stop at a shared node, remove a whole chain
delete("geeks")              delete("bad")                 delete("geek")
g-e-e-k*-s*                  b-a-d*                        g-e-e-k*
         └ unmark s,         a-t*                                  └ unmark k; k is a leaf → remove
           s has no          └ unmark d; d is a leaf        e has no children now → remove
           children →          → remove d; a still has     e → remove, g → remove
           remove s            child t → stop              root stays (it also has b, c)
k keeps its * — geek lives on
Python
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None] * 26
        self.is_end_of_word = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, key):
        node = self.root
        for ch in key:
            i = ord(ch) - ord('a')
            if node.child[i] is None:
                node.child[i] = TrieNode()
            node = node.child[i]
        node.is_end_of_word = True

    def _walk(self, key):
        node = self.root
        for ch in key:
            node = node.child[ord(ch) - ord('a')]
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def search(self, key):
        node = self._walk(key)
        return node is not None and node.is_end_of_word

    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None

    def delete(self, key):
        def _delete(node, depth):                       # returns the node to keep, or None to drop it
            if node is None:
                return None
            if depth == len(key):
                node.is_end_of_word = False             # the word itself is gone …
            else:
                i = ord(key[depth]) - ord('a')
                node.child[i] = _delete(node.child[i], depth + 1)
            if node.is_end_of_word or any(c is not None for c in node.child):
                return node                             # … but this node still serves other words
            return None                                 # useless node: unlink it
        self.root = _delete(self.root, 0) or TrieNode()

    def words(self):
        out = []
        def dfs(node, prefix):
            if node.is_end_of_word:
                out.append(prefix)
            for i, c in enumerate(node.child):
                if c is not None:
                    dfs(c, prefix + chr(ord('a') + i))
        dfs(self.root, "")
        return out

print("words:", " ".join(t.words()))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct TrieNode {
    TrieNode* child[26] = {};
    bool isEndOfWord = false;
    bool hasChild() const { for (TrieNode* c : child) if (c) return true; return false; }
};

class Trie {
    TrieNode* root = new TrieNode();
    TrieNode* walk(const string& key) const {
        TrieNode* node = root;
        for (char ch : key) { node = node->child[ch - 'a']; if (!node) return nullptr; }
        return node;
    }
    static TrieNode* remove(TrieNode* node, const string& key, size_t depth) {   // node to keep, or nullptr
        if (!node) return nullptr;
        if (depth == key.size()) {
            node->isEndOfWord = false;                              // the word itself is gone …
        } else {
            int i = key[depth] - 'a';
            node->child[i] = remove(node->child[i], key, depth + 1);
        }
        if (node->isEndOfWord || node->hasChild()) return node;     // … but this node still serves other words
        delete node;                                                // useless node: unlink it
        return nullptr;
    }
    void dfs(TrieNode* node, string& prefix, vector<string>& out) const {
        if (node->isEndOfWord) out.push_back(prefix);
        for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++)
            if (node->child[i]) { prefix.push_back('a' + i); dfs(node->child[i], prefix, out); prefix.pop_back(); }
    }
public:
    void insert(const string& key) {
        TrieNode* node = root;
        for (char ch : key) {
            int i = ch - 'a';
            if (!node->child[i]) node->child[i] = new TrieNode();
            node = node->child[i];
        }
        node->isEndOfWord = true;
    }
    bool search(const string& key) const { TrieNode* n = walk(key); return n && n->isEndOfWord; }
    bool startsWith(const string& p) const { return walk(p) != nullptr; }
    void erase(const string& key) { root = remove(root, key, 0); if (!root) root = new TrieNode(); }
    vector<string> words() const { vector<string> out; string p; dfs(root, p, out); return out; }
};

const char* b(bool v) { return v ? "true" : "false"; }

int main() {
    Trie t;
    for (string w : {"geeks", "geek", "bad", "bat", "cat", "cut"}) t.insert(w);
    t.erase("geeks"); cout << "after delete(geeks): geeks=" << b(t.search("geeks")) << " geek=" << b(t.search("geek")) << "\n";
    t.erase("bad");   cout << "after delete(bad): bad=" << b(t.search("bad")) << " bat=" << b(t.search("bat")) << "\n";
    t.erase("geek");  cout << "after delete(geek): geek=" << b(t.search("geek")) << " startsWith(ge)=" << b(t.startsWith("ge")) << "\n";
    cout << "words:";
    for (const string& w : t.words()) cout << " " << w;
    cout << "\n";
}

import java.util.ArrayList;

public class Main {

        TrieNode[] child = new TrieNode[26];
        boolean isEndOfWord;
        boolean hasChild() { for (TrieNode c : child) if (c != null) return true; return false; }
    }

    static class Trie {
        TrieNode root = new TrieNode();

        void insert(String key) {
            TrieNode node = root;
            for (char ch : key.toCharArray()) {
                int i = ch - 'a';
                if (node.child[i] == null) node.child[i] = new TrieNode();
                node = node.child[i];
            }
            node.isEndOfWord = true;
        }
        TrieNode walk(String key) {
            TrieNode node = root;
            for (char ch : key.toCharArray()) { node = node.child[ch - 'a']; if (node == null) return null; }
            return node;
        }
        boolean search(String key) { TrieNode n = walk(key); return n != null && n.isEndOfWord; }
        boolean startsWith(String p) { return walk(p) != null; }

        void delete(String key) { root = delete(root, key, 0); if (root == null) root = new TrieNode(); }
        TrieNode delete(TrieNode node, String key, int depth) {           // node to keep, or null to drop it
            if (node == null) return null;
            if (depth == key.length()) {
                node.isEndOfWord = false;                                 // the word itself is gone …
            } else {
                int i = key.charAt(depth) - 'a';
                node.child[i] = delete(node.child[i], key, depth + 1);
            }
            if (node.isEndOfWord || node.hasChild()) return node;         // … but this node still serves other words
            return null;                                                  // useless node: unlink it
        }

                if (node.child[i] != null) {
                    prefix.append((char) ('a' + i)); dfs(node.child[i], prefix, out); prefix.setLength(prefix.length() - 1);
                }
        }
    }

class Trie {
    constructor() { this.root = new TrieNode(); }
    insert(key) {
        let node = this.root;
        for (const ch of key) {
            const i = ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97;
            if (node.child[i] === null) node.child[i] = new TrieNode();
            node = node.child[i];
        }
        node.isEndOfWord = true;
    }
    walk(key) {
        let node = this.root;
        for (const ch of key) { node = node.child[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97]; if (node === null) return null; }
        return node;
    }
    search(key) { const n = this.walk(key); return n !== null && n.isEndOfWord; }
    startsWith(p) { return this.walk(p) !== null; }

    delete(key) {
        const rec = (node, depth) => {                              // node to keep, or null to drop it
            if (node === null) return null;
            if (depth === key.length) {
                node.isEndOfWord = false;                           // the word itself is gone …
            } else {

                node.child[i] = rec(node.child[i], depth + 1);
            }
            if (node.isEndOfWord || node.hasChild()) return node;   // … but this node still serves other words
            return null;                                            // useless node: unlink it
        };
        this.root = rec(this.root, 0) ?? new TrieNode();
    }
    words() {

        const dfs = (node, prefix) => {
            if (node.isEndOfWord) out.push(prefix);
            node.child.forEach((c, i) => { if (c !== null) dfs(c, prefix + String.fromCharCode(97 + i)); });
        };
        dfs(this.root, "");
        return out;
    }
}

Pitfall

Only clearing isEndOfWord ("lazy delete") keeps search correct but leaves dead branches in memory and makes startsWith("ge") wrongly return true after every ge… word is gone. Deleting a node that is still a word end or still has children breaks other words — check both conditions before unlinking.

Count distinct rows in a binary matrix

Given a binary matrix (every entry 0 or 1), count how many distinct rows it has.

Example

Input: matrix = [[1,0,0], [1,1,1], [1,0,0], [1,1,1]]
Output: 2

Naive: for every row, compare it with every earlier row; count it if it matches none. R rows, each compared with up to R others, C entries per comparison.

Python
def count_distinct_rows(matrix):
    res = 0
    for i, row in enumerate(matrix):
        if all(row != matrix[j] for j in range(i)):     # matches no earlier row → new
            res += 1
    return res

print(count_distinct_rows([[1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]))
Output
2
Time O(R² · C)Space O(1)
Idea

Treat every row as a word over the alphabet {0, 1} and insert it into a binary trie (two children per node). Insertion of a row that is already present ends at a node that is already marked — so insert can report whether the row was new. Every row is inserted once: O(R · C) in total.

A binary trie of the rows: equal rows walk the same path and hit the same leaf
rows: 1 0 0 / 1 1 1 / 1 0 0 / 1 1 1

         (root)
           │ 1
           ●
      0 ┌──┴──┐ 1
        ●     ●
      0 │     │ 1
        ●*    ●*          two marked leaves → 2 distinct rows
Python
class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None, None]          # child[0] for a 0, child[1] for a 1
        self.is_end = False

def insert_row(root, row):                 # True if the row was not present before
    node = root
    for bit in row:
        if node.child[bit] is None:
            node.child[bit] = Node()
        node = node.child[bit]
    if node.is_end:
        return False                       # an identical row ended here already
    node.is_end = True
    return True

def count_distinct_rows(matrix):
    root = Node()
    return sum(1 for row in matrix if insert_row(root, row))

matrix = [[1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]]
print("distinct rows:", count_distinct_rows(matrix))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Node {
    Node* child[2] = {nullptr, nullptr};   // child[0] for a 0, child[1] for a 1
    bool isEnd = false;
};

bool insertRow(Node* root, const vector<int>& row) {   // true if the row was not present before
    Node* node = root;
    for (int bit : row) {
        if (!node->child[bit]) node->child[bit] = new Node();
        node = node->child[bit];
    }
    if (node->isEnd) return false;                     // an identical row ended here already
    node->isEnd = true;
    return true;
}

int countDistinctRows(const vector<vector<int>>& matrix) {
    Node* root = new Node();
    int res = 0;
    for (const auto& row : matrix)
        if (insertRow(root, row)) res++;
    return res;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> matrix = {{1, 0, 0}, {1, 1, 1}, {1, 0, 0}, {1, 1, 1}};
    cout << "distinct rows: " << countDistinctRows(matrix) << "\n";
}

Alternative

A hash set of rows (as tuples / strings) also solves this in O(R · C) expected time and is shorter to write. The trie answers two things the set cannot: it can list the distinct rows in sorted order, and its memory is shared across rows with equal prefixes.

Interview Q&A
When would you choose a trie over a hash map?

When the workload needs prefix operations — autocomplete, "does any key start with…", longest-prefix match (IP routing) — or sorted enumeration of the keys. For pure exact-match lookups a hash map is faster and uses far less memory.

What is the space complexity of a trie, and how can it be reduced?

Worst case O(N · L · A) for N words of length L over an alphabet of size A, because every node reserves A child slots. Reduce it with a hash map or sorted list of children per node (only the children that exist), with a compressed trie / radix tree that merges chains of single-child nodes, or with a ternary search tree.

How do you implement autocomplete with a trie?

Walk down the prefix (O(P)); if the walk fails there are no completions. Otherwise do a DFS from that node, appending characters, and emit every node with isEndOfWord. The DFS visits the children in alphabetical order, so the suggestions come out sorted. Store a count or top-k list in each node to rank suggestions without a full traversal.

Why does a trie give lexicographic order for free?

A pre-order traversal that visits the children in index order (a before b before c…) reaches every word end in dictionary order, because a shorter word is a prefix of the longer ones below it and siblings are visited alphabetically. This is also why words() above prints bad bat cat cut geek geeks.

What goes wrong if delete just clears the end-of-word flag?

Searches stay correct, but memory for dead branches is never reclaimed, and startsWith returns true for prefixes that no longer lead to any word. Proper deletion removes nodes bottom-up while they are unmarked and childless, stopping at the first node another word still uses.

Advanced Structures

Disjoint Set

A disjoint-set (union–find) structure keeps track of a collection of elements partitioned into non-overlapping groups, and answers two questions almost instantly: which group is x in? and merge the groups of x and y. It is the engine behind Kruskal's MST, cycle detection and dynamic connectivity.

Disjoint set (union–find) — a data structure over elements 0 … n-1 that maintains a partition into disjoint sets, each identified by one representative element, supporting find(x) → representative of x's set, and union(x, y) → merge the two sets containing x and y.

The problem: dynamic connectivity

n people are initially strangers. Two operations arrive in any order: makeFriends(x, y) — now x and y are in the same friend circle (friendship is transitive) — and areFriends(x, y) — are they in the same circle? Answer the queries as they come, with no knowledge of future operations.

Example

Input: n = 4; makeFriends(0, 1), makeFriends(1, 3), areFriends(0, 2), areFriends(0, 1), areFriends(0, 3)
Output: No Yes Yes

ApproachmakeFriendsareFriendsProblem
Adjacency list + DFS/BFSO(1)O(n + m) — traverse the grapha query must explore the whole component
Adjacency matrix + DFS/BFSO(1)O(n²)same, and n² memory
Store the component id of every nodeΘ(n) — relabel one whole componentΘ(1)every merge rewrites up to n labels
Disjoint set≈ O(1) amortised≈ O(1) amortised—
Idea

Represent every set as a tree: each element stores its parent, the root is the set's representative. find(x) climbs to the root. union(x, y) makes one root the parent of the other. Two elements are in the same set exactly when they climb to the same root.

Each set is a tree stored in a parent array; a root is its own parent
initially                 makeFriends(0, 1)        makeFriends(1, 3)
parent: 0 1 2 3           parent: 0 0 2 3          parent: 0 0 2 0

(0) (1) (2) (3)            (0)   (2) (3)              (0)    (2)
                            │                         / \
                           (1)                      (1) (3)

areFriends(0, 2): find(0)=0, find(2)=2 → No
areFriends(0, 3): find(0)=0, find(3)=0 → Yes
Basic implementation: parent array
1
make_set
parent[i] = i for every element — n singleton sets.
2
find(x)
Follow parent links until reaching an element that is its own parent; that root is the representative.
3
union(x, y)
rx = find(x), ry = find(y); if they differ, parent[ry] = rx.
4
areFriends(x, y)
find(x) == find(y).
Python
class DisjointSet:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))       # every element starts as its own set

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:         # climb to the root
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, x, y):
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx != ry:
            self.parent[ry] = rx           # hang one tree under the other root

    def are_friends(self, x, y):
        return self.find(x) == self.find(y)

ds = DisjointSet(4)
ds.union(0, 1)                             # makeFriends
ds.union(1, 3)
for x, y in [(0, 2), (0, 1), (0, 3)]:
    print(f"areFriends({x}, {y}):", "Yes" if ds.are_friends(x, y) else "No")
print("parent:", " ".join(map(str, ds.parent)))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class DisjointSet {
    vector<int> parent;
public:
    DisjointSet(int n) : parent(n) {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;      // every element starts as its own set
    }
    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) x = parent[x];          // climb to the root
        return x;
    }
    void unite(int x, int y) {                         // "union" is a C++ keyword
        int rx = find(x), ry = find(y);
        if (rx != ry) parent[ry] = rx;                 // hang one tree under the other root
    }
    bool areFriends(int x, int y) { return find(x) == find(y); }
    const vector<int>& parents() const { return parent; }
};

int main() {
    DisjointSet ds(4);
    ds.unite(0, 1);                                    // makeFriends
    ds.unite(1, 3);
    int queries[3][2] = {{0, 2}, {0, 1}, {0, 3}};
    for (auto& q : queries)
        cout << "areFriends(" << q[0] << ", " << q[1] << "): " << (ds.areFriends(q[0], q[1]) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    cout << "parent:";
    for (int p : ds.parents()) cout << " " << p;
    cout << "\n";
}

Time O(n) worst case per operation — the tree can degenerate into a chainSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Naive union can build a tree that is a straight line: union(1,0), union(2,1), union(3,2), … makes find(0) walk n steps. The two optimisations below exist to keep every tree shallow.

Union by rank (or by size)

Keep an extra array rank that stores an upper bound on the height of each root's tree. When uniting two roots, make the root of the shorter tree a child of the taller one — the height does not grow. Only when both have equal rank does the merged tree get one level taller.

Attach the shallower tree under the deeper root — height grows only on a tie
rank[rx] < rank[ry]          rank[rx] > rank[ry]          rank[rx] == rank[ry]
parent[rx] = ry              parent[ry] = rx              parent[ry] = rx; rank[rx] += 1

    (ry)                         (rx)                         (rx)  rank+1
   /  │  \                      /  │  \                      /  │  \
 ...  ... (rx)                ...  ... (ry)                 ...  ... (ry)
VariantWhat is comparedGuarantee
Union by rankheight bound of the two treesheight ≤ log₂ n → find is O(log n)
Union by sizenumber of elements in the two trees (attach smaller under larger)same O(log n) bound; the size array is useful in its own right (component sizes)
Why log n

With union by rank alone, a tree of height h must contain at least 2^h elements (each rank increase doubles the minimum size), so no tree is deeper than log₂ n.

Path compression

find(x) already visits every node on the path from x to the root. While it is there, re-point each of them directly at the root — the next find on any of them is a single step. The parent array is only ever changed in a way that keeps the same sets.

Path compression flattens the path that find() walks
before find(6)                      after find(6)

     (0)                               (0)
     / \                             / | \
   (1) (2)                         (1)(2)(4)        6 and 4 now point straight at 0;
         │                              │   \       5 still points at 4 (it was not on the path)
        (4)                            (3)  (6) …
       /   \
     (5)   (6)
Example

Input: n = 7; union(0,1) union(2,3) union(4,5) union(1,3) union(5,6) union(3,5); then find(6)
Output: parent array before / after shows the compression; connected(2, 5) = Yes

Python
class DisjointSet:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n                    # upper bound on the height of each root's tree
        self.components = n

    def find(self, x):
        if self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])   # path compression: point straight at the root
        return self.parent[x]

    def union(self, x, y):
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return False                       # already in the same set
        if self.rank[rx] < self.rank[ry]:      # union by rank: shallower tree goes under the deeper root
            rx, ry = ry, rx
        self.parent[ry] = rx
        if self.rank[rx] == self.rank[ry]:
            self.rank[rx] += 1                 # only a tie makes the tree taller
        self.components -= 1
        return True

    def connected(self, x, y):
        return self.find(x) == self.find(y)

ds = DisjointSet(7)
for x, y in [(0, 1), (2, 3), (4, 5), (1, 3), (5, 6), (3, 5)]:
    ds.union(x, y)
print("parent after unions:", " ".join(map(str, ds.parent)))
print("find(6) =", ds.find(6))
print("parent after find(6):", " ".join(map(str, ds.parent)))
print("connected(2, 5):", "Yes" if ds.connected(2, 5) else "No")
print("connected(3, 6):", "Yes" if ds.connected(3, 6) else "No")
print("components:", ds.components)
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class DisjointSet {
    vector<int> parent, rnk;                      // rnk = upper bound on the height of each root's tree
public:
    int components;
    DisjointSet(int n) : parent(n), rnk(n, 0), components(n) {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
    }
    int find(int x) {
        if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);   // path compression: point straight at the root
        return parent[x];
    }
    bool unite(int x, int y) {
        int rx = find(x), ry = find(y);
        if (rx == ry) return false;               // already in the same set
        if (rnk[rx] < rnk[ry]) swap(rx, ry);      // union by rank: shallower tree goes under the deeper root
        parent[ry] = rx;
        if (rnk[rx] == rnk[ry]) rnk[rx]++;        // only a tie makes the tree taller
        components--;
        return true;
    }
    bool connected(int x, int y) { return find(x) == find(y); }
    void printParents(const string& label) {
        cout << label << ":";
        for (int p : parent) cout << " " << p;
        cout << "\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    DisjointSet ds(7);
    int edges[6][2] = {{0, 1}, {2, 3}, {4, 5}, {1, 3}, {5, 6}, {3, 5}};
    for (auto& e : edges) ds.unite(e[0], e[1]);
    ds.printParents("parent after unions");
    cout << "find(6) = " << ds.find(6) << "\n";
    ds.printParents("parent after find(6)");
    cout << "connected(2, 5): " << (ds.connected(2, 5) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    cout << "connected(3, 6): " << (ds.connected(3, 6) ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
    cout << "components: " << ds.components << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static class DisjointSet {
        int[] parent, rank;                           // rank = upper bound on the height of each root's tree
        int components;
        DisjointSet(int n) {
            parent = new int[n]; rank = new int[n]; components = n;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
        }
        int find(int x) {
            if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);   // path compression: point straight at the root
            return parent[x];
        }
        boolean union(int x, int y) {
            int rx = find(x), ry = find(y);
            if (rx == ry) return false;               // already in the same set
            if (rank[rx] < rank[ry]) { int t = rx; rx = ry; ry = t; }   // union by rank: shallower under deeper
            parent[ry] = rx;
            if (rank[rx] == rank[ry]) rank[rx]++;     // only a tie makes the tree taller
            components--;
            return true;
        }
        boolean connected(int x, int y) { return find(x) == find(y); }
        String parents() {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int p : parent) sb.append(' ').append(p);

Time O(α(n)) amortised per operation — effectively constantSpace O(n)
Optimisations usedAmortised cost per operation
noneO(n)
union by rank onlyO(log n)

bothO(α(n)) — the inverse Ackermann function, ≤ 4 for every n that fits in the universe
Rank ≠ height

After path compression the rank values are no longer exact heights — they are only upper bounds. That is fine: the proof of the log n bound only needs ranks to be upper bounds, and leaving them untouched keeps find simple.

Pitfall

The recursive find compresses the path but recurses once per level. Python's recursion limit (1000) can be hit on adversarial inputs before the first compression; an iterative two-pass version (first find the root, then re-point every node on the path) avoids that.

Detect a cycle in an undirected graph

Process the edges one by one. For edge (u, v): if u and v are already in the same set, this edge closes a cycle; otherwise unite them. This is also exactly the test Kruskal's algorithm uses to decide whether an edge may join the spanning tree.

Example

Input: n = 4, edges = (0,1) (1,2) (2,3) (3,1)
Output: cycle found at edge 3-1

Idea

An edge between two vertices that are already connected creates a second path between them — a cycle. Union–find answers "already connected?" in near-constant time, so the whole scan is O(E · α(V)).

Python
class DisjointSet:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n

    def find(self, x):
        if self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])
        return self.parent[x]

    def union(self, x, y):
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return False
        if self.rank[rx] < self.rank[ry]:
            rx, ry = ry, rx
        self.parent[ry] = rx
        if self.rank[rx] == self.rank[ry]:
            self.rank[rx] += 1
        return True

def has_cycle(n, edges):
    ds = DisjointSet(n)
    for u, v in edges:
        if ds.find(u) == ds.find(v):                 # already connected → this edge closes a cycle
            print(f"edge {u}-{v}: already connected → cycle")
            return True
        ds.union(u, v)
        print(f"edge {u}-{v}: joined")
    return False

edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)]
print("graph has a cycle:", "Yes" if has_cycle(4, edges) else "No")

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct DisjointSet {
    vector<int> parent, rnk;
    DisjointSet(int n) : parent(n), rnk(n, 0) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i; }
    int find(int x) { return parent[x] == x ? x : parent[x] = find(parent[x]); }
    bool unite(int x, int y) {
        int rx = find(x), ry = find(y);
        if (rx == ry) return false;
        if (rnk[rx] < rnk[ry]) swap(rx, ry);
        parent[ry] = rx;
        if (rnk[rx] == rnk[ry]) rnk[rx]++;
        return true;
    }
};

bool hasCycle(int n, const vector<pair<int,int>>& edges) {
    DisjointSet ds(n);
    for (auto [u, v] : edges) {
        if (ds.find(u) == ds.find(v)) {              // already connected → this edge closes a cycle
            cout << "edge " << u << "-" << v << ": already connected → cycle\n";
            return true;
        }
        ds.unite(u, v);
        cout << "edge " << u << "-" << v << ": joined\n";
    }
    return false;
}

int main() {
    vector<pair<int,int>> edges = {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}};
    bool cyc = hasCycle(4, edges);
    cout << "graph has a cycle: " << (cyc ? "Yes" : "No") << "\n";
}

Time O(E · α(V))Space O(V)
Pitfall

This test is for undirected graphs only. In a directed graph the edges a → b and c → b put a, b, c in one set without any cycle; directed cycle detection needs DFS with colours (see Graphs).

Where disjoint sets are used

Kruskal's MST

Sort edges by weight; add an edge iff its endpoints are in different sets.

Connected components

Union every edge; the number of roots is the number of components — components above.

Cycle detection

An edge inside one set closes a cycle (above).

Dynamic connectivity

Answer "are x and y connected?" while edges keep arriving — the friends problem.

Image / grid regions

Flood-fill alternatives: unite neighbouring pixels of the same colour (number of islands).

Percolation, LCA (Tarjan), equivalence classes

Any problem that merges groups and never splits them.

Watch out

Union–find supports merge only — there is no efficient split. If sets must be separated again, it is the wrong structure (use offline processing in reverse, or a link-cut tree).

Interview Q&A
What is the amortised complexity of union–find with both optimisations, and what does α(n) mean?

O(α(n)) per operation amortised, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — it grows so slowly that α(n) ≤ 4 for any n below 2^65536. In practice every operation is constant time. Tarjan proved this bound is tight for the structure.

Union by rank vs union by size — any difference?

Both guarantee O(log n) tree height and O(α(n)) with path compression. Size is more useful when you also need component sizes (e.g. "size of the largest group"); rank is a smaller number to store. Never attach arbitrarily — that is what allows O(n) chains.

How does path compression work and why doesn't it break the sets?

During find(x), every node on the path to the root gets parent[node] = root. Membership is defined by which root you reach, not by the exact path, so re-pointing nodes at the same root changes nothing about the sets while making future finds shorter.

How would you detect a cycle in an undirected graph with union–find?

Process the edges; for (u, v) check find(u) == find(v). Equal → the edge connects two already-connected vertices → cycle. Otherwise union(u, v). Total O(E · α(V)). It also counts components: V − (number of successful unions).

Why does Kruskal's algorithm rely on union–find?

Kruskal adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. The cycle test on each of E sorted edges would cost O(V) with DFS; union–find makes it near constant, giving O(E log E) total dominated by the sort.

Advanced Structures

Segment Tree

A segment tree answers range queries (sum, min, max, …) over an array and updates single elements, both in O(log n). It is the structure to use when both operations are frequent, because a plain array makes queries slow and a prefix-sum array makes updates slow.

Segment tree — a binary tree over a fixed-size array in which every node stores an aggregate (e.g. the sum) of one contiguous segment: the root covers the whole array, each child covers one half of its parent's segment, and the leaves are the individual elements.

Segment tree of sums over [10, 20, 30, 40], stored in an array like a heap
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]            index:  0   1   2   3

                [0..3] = 100                 tree[0]
               /            \
      [0..1] = 30          [2..3] = 70        tree[1]  tree[2]
      /       \            /       \
[0]=10     [1]=20    [2]=30     [3]=40        tree[3] tree[4] tree[5] tree[6]

tree array:  100  30  70  10  20  30  40
              0    1   2   3   4   5   6        children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; getSum(0, 2); getSum(1, 3); update(1, 60); getSum(0, 2)
Output: 60, 90, then 100

Why not a plain array or prefix sums?

Suppose x operations arrive, of which a quarter are range-sum queries and three quarters are updates. With a plain array queries cost O(n) and updates O(1), so the average is (x/4 · O(n) + 3x/4 · O(1)) / x = O(n). With a prefix-sum array it is the reverse — queries O(1), updates O(n) — and the average is again O(n). A segment tree makes both O(log n).

StructureRange sumPoint updatePreprocessingSpace
Plain arrayO(n)O(1)—O(n)
Prefix-sum arrayO(1)O(n)O(n)O(n)
Segment treeO(log n)O(log n)O(n)O(n) (≈ 4n slots)
Binary indexed treeO(log n)O(log n)O(n log n) (O(n) possible)O(n) (n + 1 slots)
Key point

Segment trees work for any associative aggregate: sum, min, max, gcd, XOR, number of zeros, … Replace the + in the three functions below and nothing else changes. They also extend to range updates with lazy propagation — the binary indexed tree does not handle min/max.

Size of the tree array

Children of node i live at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so the tree is stored in a plain array with no pointers. How large must it be?

  • If n is a power of two the tree is perfect: 2n − 1 nodes.
  • Otherwise let x be the smallest power of two greater than n; the tree needs at most 2x − 1 slots (some stay unused).
  • In practice allocate 4n — it is always enough (2x − 1 < 4n) and saves computing x.
size = 2 · 2^⌈log₂ n⌉ − 1 (≤ 4n)
Example

n = 5 → x = 8 → at most 15 slots; n = 4 → exactly 7 slots, all used.

Constructing the segment tree
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]
Output: tree = [100, 30, 70, 10, 20, 30, 40]

Idea

Build recursively: if the segment is a single element store it; otherwise build the left half and the right half, then store their sum. Every node is written exactly once — O(n).

1
build(ss, se, si)
ss/se = segment start/end in arr, si = index of this node in tree.
2
Leaf
ss == se → tree[si] = arr[ss].
3
Internal node
mid = (ss + se) / 2; tree[si] = build(ss, mid, 2si+1) + build(mid+1, se, 2si+2).
Python
def build(arr, tree, ss, se, si):
    if ss == se:                                        # leaf: a single element
        tree[si] = arr[ss]
        return tree[si]
    mid = (ss + se) // 2
    tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2)
    return tree[si]                                     # parent = left sum + right sum

def tree_size(n):
    x = 1
    while x < n:                                        # smallest power of two ≥ n
        x *= 2
    return 2 * x - 1

arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]
tree = [0] * tree_size(len(arr))
build(arr, tree, 0, len(arr) - 1, 0)
print("tree:", " ".join(map(str, tree)))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int build(const vector<int>& arr, vector<int>& tree, int ss, int se, int si) {
    if (ss == se) return tree[si] = arr[ss];            // leaf: a single element
    int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
    return tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1)
                    + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);   // parent = left sum + right sum
}

int treeSize(int n) {
    int x = 1;
    while (x < n) x *= 2;                                // smallest power of two ≥ n
    return 2 * x - 1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {10, 20, 30, 40};
    int n = arr.size();
    vector<int> tree(treeSize(n), 0);
    build(arr, tree, 0, n - 1, 0);
    cout << "tree:";
    for (int v : tree) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
}

        int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
        return tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1)
                        + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);   // parent = left sum + right sum
    }

    static int treeSize(int n) {
        int x = 1;
        while (x < n) x *= 2;                            // smallest power of two ≥ n
        return 2 * x - 1;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

Range query
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]; getSum(0, 2)
Output: 60
Input: getSum(1, 3)
Output: 90

Idea

Walk down from the root. A node's segment relates to the query range [qs, qe] in one of three ways: completely inside → return its stored sum without going deeper; completely outside → contribute 0; partially overlapping → recurse into both children and add.

The three cases — at most two nodes per level are partially overlapped, so the query touches O(log n) nodes
getSum(1, 2) on [10, 20, 30, 40]

         [0..3]  partial overlap → recurse
        /      \
  [0..1] partial  [2..3] partial
  /    \          /    \
[0]    [1]      [2]    [3]
outside inside  inside outside
  0     20       30      0        → 20 + 30 = 50
Python
def build(arr, tree, ss, se, si):
    if ss == se:
        tree[si] = arr[ss]
        return tree[si]
    mid = (ss + se) // 2
    tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2)
    return tree[si]

def get_sum_rec(tree, qs, qe, ss, se, si):
    if qe < ss or qs > se:                              # segment completely outside the query
        return 0
    if qs <= ss and se <= qe:                           # segment completely inside the query
        return tree[si]
    mid = (ss + se) // 2                                # partial overlap: ask both children
    return get_sum_rec(tree, qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + get_sum_rec(tree, qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2)

def get_sum(tree, n, qs, qe):
    if qs < 0 or qe > n - 1 or qs > qe:
        raise ValueError("invalid range")
    return get_sum_rec(tree, qs, qe, 0, n - 1, 0)

arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]
n = len(arr)
x = 1
while x < n:
    x *= 2
tree = [0] * (2 * x - 1)
build(arr, tree, 0, n - 1, 0)
print("tree:", " ".join(map(str, tree)))
for qs, qe in [(0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 2)]:
    print(f"sum({qs}, {qe}):", get_sum(tree, n, qs, qe))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <stdexcept>
using namespace std;

int build(const vector<int>& arr, vector<int>& tree, int ss, int se, int si) {
    if (ss == se) return tree[si] = arr[ss];
    int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
    return tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
}

int getSumRec(const vector<int>& tree, int qs, int qe, int ss, int se, int si) {
    if (qe < ss || qs > se) return 0;                   // segment completely outside the query
    if (qs <= ss && se <= qe) return tree[si];          // segment completely inside the query
    int mid = (ss + se) / 2;                             // partial overlap: ask both children
    return getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
}

int getSum(const vector<int>& tree, int n, int qs, int qe) {
    if (qs < 0 || qe > n - 1 || qs > qe) throw invalid_argument("invalid range");
    return getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, 0, n - 1, 0);
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {10, 20, 30, 40};
    int n = arr.size(), x = 1;
    while (x < n) x *= 2;
    vector<int> tree(2 * x - 1, 0);
    build(arr, tree, 0, n - 1, 0);
    cout << "tree:";
    for (int v : tree) cout << " " << v;
    cout << "\n";
    int queries[3][2] = {{0, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 2}};
    for (auto& q : queries) cout << "sum(" << q[0] << ", " << q[1] << "): " << getSum(tree, n, q[0], q[1]) << "\n";
}

public class Main {
    static int build(int[] arr, int[] tree, int ss, int se, int si) {
        if (ss == se) return tree[si] = arr[ss];
        int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
        return tree[si] = build(arr, tree, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(arr, tree, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
    }

    static int getSumRec(int[] tree, int qs, int qe, int ss, int se, int si) {
        if (qe < ss || qs > se) return 0;               // segment completely outside the query
        if (qs <= ss && se <= qe) return tree[si];      // segment completely inside the query
        int mid = (ss + se) / 2;                         // partial overlap: ask both children
        return getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
    }

    static int getSum(int[] tree, int n, int qs, int qe) {
        if (qs < 0 || qe > n - 1 || qs > qe) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid range");
        return getSumRec(tree, qs, qe, 0, n - 1, 0);
    }

Pitfall

The order of the two base cases matters: test completely outside before completely inside. For a single-element segment both qe < ss and qs <= ss && se <= qe can be evaluated — the outside test must win when the leaf is not in the range.

Point update
Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]; update(1, 60); getSum(0, 2)
Output: 100 (the tree becomes 140 70 70 10 60 30 40)

Idea

Only the nodes whose segment contains index i — one per level, root to leaf — are affected. Compute diff = newValue − arr[i], then walk down from the root adding diff to every node on the path to leaf i and ignoring the subtrees that do not contain i.

1
Compute the difference
diff = new_val − arr[i]; also store arr[i] = new_val so later updates compute the right difference.
2
update(ss, se, i, si, diff)
If i is outside [ss, se] → return (this subtree is untouched).
3
Add and descend
tree[si] += diff; if the segment has more than one element, recurse into both children (only the one containing i does any work).
Exactly one node per level changes
update(1, 60) on [10, 20, 30, 40]: diff = 60 − 20 = +40

         [0..3] 100 → 140            ← contains index 1: += 40
        /            \
  [0..1] 30 → 70      [2..3] 70       ← index 1 not in [2..3]: skip
  /       \
[0] 10    [1] 20 → 60                 ← the leaf itself
Python
class SegmentTree:
    def __init__(self, arr):
        self.arr = arr[:]
        self.n = len(arr)
        x = 1
        while x < self.n:
            x *= 2
        self.tree = [0] * (2 * x - 1)
        self._build(0, self.n - 1, 0)

    def _build(self, ss, se, si):
        if ss == se:
            self.tree[si] = self.arr[ss]
            return self.tree[si]
        mid = (ss + se) // 2
        self.tree[si] = self._build(ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + self._build(mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2)
        return self.tree[si]

    def get_sum(self, qs, qe, ss=0, se=None, si=0):
        if se is None:
            se = self.n - 1
        if qe < ss or qs > se:
            return 0
        if qs <= ss and se <= qe:
            return self.tree[si]
        mid = (ss + se) // 2
        return self.get_sum(qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + self.get_sum(qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2)

    def update(self, i, new_val):
        diff = new_val - self.arr[i]                    # how much every ancestor must change
        self.arr[i] = new_val
        self._update(0, self.n - 1, i, 0, diff)

    def _update(self, ss, se, i, si, diff):
        if i < ss or i > se:                            # index not in this segment
            return
        self.tree[si] += diff                           # this node's segment contains i
        if ss < se:
            mid = (ss + se) // 2
            self._update(ss, mid, i, 2 * si + 1, diff)
            self._update(mid + 1, se, i, 2 * si + 2, diff)

st = SegmentTree([10, 20, 30, 40])
print("tree:", " ".join(map(str, st.tree)))
print("sum(0, 2):", st.get_sum(0, 2))
print("update(1, 60)")
st.update(1, 60)
print("tree:", " ".join(map(str, st.tree)))
print("sum(0, 2):", st.get_sum(0, 2))
print("sum(1, 3):", st.get_sum(1, 3))
C++
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class SegmentTree {
    vector<int> arr, tree;
    int n;
    int build(int ss, int se, int si) {
        if (ss == se) return tree[si] = arr[ss];
        int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
        return tree[si] = build(ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
    }
    int getSum(int qs, int qe, int ss, int se, int si) const {
        if (qe < ss || qs > se) return 0;
        if (qs <= ss && se <= qe) return tree[si];
        int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
        return getSum(qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + getSum(qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
    }
    void update(int ss, int se, int i, int si, int diff) {
        if (i < ss || i > se) return;                   // index not in this segment
        tree[si] += diff;                               // this node's segment contains i
        if (ss < se) {
            int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
            update(ss, mid, i, 2 * si + 1, diff);
            update(mid + 1, se, i, 2 * si + 2, diff);
        }
    }
public:
    SegmentTree(const vector<int>& a) : arr(a), n(a.size()) {
        int x = 1;
        while (x < n) x *= 2;
        tree.assign(2 * x - 1, 0);
        build(0, n - 1, 0);
    }
    int getSum(int qs, int qe) const { return getSum(qs, qe, 0, n - 1, 0); }
    void update(int i, int newVal) {
        int diff = newVal - arr[i];                     // how much every ancestor must change
        arr[i] = newVal;
        update(0, n - 1, i, 0, diff);
    }
    void print() const { cout << "tree:"; for (int v : tree) cout << " " << v; cout << "\n"; }
};

int main() {
    SegmentTree st({10, 20, 30, 40});
    st.print();
    cout << "sum(0, 2): " << st.getSum(0, 2) << "\n";
    cout << "update(1, 60)\n";
    st.update(1, 60);
    st.print();
    cout << "sum(0, 2): " << st.getSum(0, 2) << "\n";
    cout << "sum(1, 3): " << st.getSum(1, 3) << "\n";
}
Java
public class Main {
    static class SegmentTree {
        int[] arr, tree;
        int n;
        SegmentTree(int[] a) {
            arr = a.clone(); n = a.length;
            int x = 1;
            while (x < n) x *= 2;
            tree = new int[2 * x - 1];
            build(0, n - 1, 0);
        }
        int build(int ss, int se, int si) {
            if (ss == se) return tree[si] = arr[ss];
            int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
            return tree[si] = build(ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + build(mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
        }
        int getSum(int qs, int qe) { return getSum(qs, qe, 0, n - 1, 0); }
        int getSum(int qs, int qe, int ss, int se, int si) {
            if (qe < ss || qs > se) return 0;
            if (qs <= ss && se <= qe) return tree[si];
            int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
            return getSum(qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + getSum(qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
        }
        void update(int i, int newVal) {
            int diff = newVal - arr[i];                 // how much every ancestor must change
            arr[i] = newVal;
            update(0, n - 1, i, 0, diff);
        }
        void update(int ss, int se, int i, int si, int diff) {
            if (i < ss || i > se) return;               // index not in this segment
            tree[si] += diff;                           // this node's segment contains i
            if (ss < se) {
                int mid = (ss + se) / 2;
                update(ss, mid, i, 2 * si + 1, diff);
                update(mid + 1, se, i, 2 * si + 2, diff);
            }
        }
        String dump() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("tree:"); for (int v : tree) sb.append(' ').append(v); return sb.toString(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SegmentTree st = new SegmentTree(new int[]{10, 20, 30, 40});
        System.out.println(st.dump());
        System.out.println("sum(0, 2): " + st.getSum(0, 2));
        System.out.println("update(1, 60)");
        st.update(1, 60);
        System.out.println(st.dump());
        System.out.println("sum(0, 2): " + st.getSum(0, 2));
        System.out.println("sum(1, 3): " + st.getSum(1, 3));
    }
}
JavaScript
class SegmentTree {
    constructor(a) {
        this.arr = [...a]; this.n = a.length;
        let x = 1;
        while (x < this.n) x *= 2;
        this.tree = new Array(2 * x - 1).fill(0);
        this.build(0, this.n - 1, 0);
    }
    build(ss, se, si) {
        if (ss === se) return (this.tree[si] = this.arr[ss]);
        const mid = Math.floor((ss + se) / 2);
        return (this.tree[si] = this.build(ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + this.build(mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2));
    }
    getSum(qs, qe, ss = 0, se = this.n - 1, si = 0) {
        if (qe < ss || qs > se) return 0;
        if (qs <= ss && se <= qe) return this.tree[si];
        const mid = Math.floor((ss + se) / 2);
        return this.getSum(qs, qe, ss, mid, 2 * si + 1) + this.getSum(qs, qe, mid + 1, se, 2 * si + 2);
    }
    update(i, newVal) {
        const diff = newVal - this.arr[i];              // how much every ancestor must change
        this.arr[i] = newVal;
        this.updateRec(0, this.n - 1, i, 0, diff);
    }
    updateRec(ss, se, i, si, diff) {
        if (i < ss || i > se) return;                   // index not in this segment
        this.tree[si] += diff;                          // this node's segment contains i
        if (ss < se) {
            const mid = Math.floor((ss + se) / 2);
            this.updateRec(ss, mid, i, 2 * si + 1, diff);
            this.updateRec(mid + 1, se, i, 2 * si + 2, diff);
        }
    }
}

Min / max trees

For aggregates where a difference makes no sense (min, max, gcd) do not propagate diff; instead descend to the leaf, overwrite it, and on the way back up recompute each ancestor as combine(tree[2si+1], tree[2si+2]). That version works for every aggregate, including sum.

Pitfall

Forgetting to write arr[i] = new_val makes the second update of the same index compute a wrong diff — the tree then silently drifts away from the array.

Interview Q&A
Segment tree vs binary indexed tree — which one and why?

Both give O(log n) point update and range query over a fixed-size array. A BIT is shorter to code and uses n + 1 slots, but only works for invertible operations (sum, XOR) where prefix(r) − prefix(l−1) makes sense. A segment tree handles any associative operation (min, max, gcd), range updates with lazy propagation, and is easier to extend — at the cost of ≈ 4n memory and more code.

Why is a range query O(log n) when it may recurse into both children?

At every level at most two nodes are partially overlapped by the query (the ones containing its left and right boundaries); every other visited node is either fully inside or fully outside and returns immediately. So the recursion touches at most 4 nodes per level × log n levels.

How much memory does a segment tree need and why 4n?

Exactly 2n − 1 nodes when n is a power of two; otherwise at most 2x − 1 where x is the next power of two above n. Since x < 2n, 2x − 1 < 4n, which is why 4n is the usual safe allocation. The iterative bottom-up segment tree needs only 2n.

How would you support range updates (add v to every element in [l, r])?

With lazy propagation: store a pending add value in each node; a range update marks the fully covered nodes lazily instead of descending to every leaf, and the pending value is pushed down to the children only when a later query or update needs to look inside. Both operations stay O(log n).

Can a segment tree be built for an array that grows?

Not directly — the structure assumes a fixed size. Either allocate for the maximum size up front (unused leaves hold the identity element, 0 for sums), or use a dynamic / implicit segment tree that creates nodes on demand.

Advanced Structures

Binary Indexed Tree

A binary indexed tree (Fenwick tree) supports prefix queries and point updates over a fixed-size array in O(log n) each, using a single array of n + 1 integers and a handful of lines of code. It is the lightweight alternative to a segment tree for sums, counts and XORs.

Binary indexed tree (BIT, Fenwick tree) — an array BIT[1..n] in which BIT[i] stores the sum of the i & −i elements of the input ending at position i (1-based). Prefix sums and updates both walk O(log n) entries by repeatedly clearing or adding the lowest set bit of the index.

It is used for a fixed input array with many operations of two kinds: a prefix operation — sum, product, XOR, OR, count — and updating a value. It is stored as a plain array, but the idea behind the indices is a tree. It needs O(n log n) preprocessing (O(n) with a trick) and Θ(n) auxiliary space.

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]; getSum(2); getSum(4)
Output: 60 150
Input: update(2, 35); getSum(2); getSum(4)
Output: 65 155

rangeSum(i, j) = prefixSum(j) − prefixSum(i − 1)
Three approaches to prefix sum + update

getSum(i) returns arr[0] + … + arr[i]; update(i, x) sets arr[i] = x. Both operations are frequent and interleaved.

MethodgetSum(i)update(i, x)SpaceCode
1 — simple: loop from 0 to iO(n)O(1) — arr[i] = xO(1)trivial
2 — prefix-sum array: pre[i]O(1)O(n) — add diff to pre[i..n−1]O(n)trivial
3 — segment treeO(log n)O(log n)≈ 4nthree recursive functions
Binary indexed treeO(log n)O(log n)n + 1two short loops

Methods 1 and 2 each make one operation linear; with a mixed workload the average cost is O(n) per operation. The segment tree fixes that but is a comparatively heavy piece of code. The BIT gets the same O(log n) for both operations with less memory and about ten lines.

Limitation

Unlike a segment tree, a BIT works only for operations that have an inverse: rangeSum(i, j) = getSum(j) − getSum(i−1) needs subtraction. Prefix min or max cannot be undone, so range-min queries need a segment tree.

The idea: every prefix is a sum of powers of two

Any positive integer is a sum of distinct powers of two: 14 = 8 + 4 + 2. So a prefix of length 14 can be split into three blocks of lengths 8, 4 and 2, and if the sum of each block is pre-computed, getSum needs three additions instead of fourteen. The BIT stores exactly these blocks: entry i (1-based) is responsible for the last i & −i elements ending at i.

Each BIT entry covers a block whose length is the lowest set bit of its index; a query adds up the blocks on the path to the root
arr (0-based):  10   20   30   40   50   60
BIT index i  :   1    2    3    4    5    6
i & -i       :   1    2    1    4    1    2
covers       :  [1] [1,2] [3] [1..4] [5] [5,6]
BIT[i]       :  10   30   30   100   50  110

              0 (virtual root)
        ┌─────┼──────────┐
        1     2          4           parent of i for queries = i − (i & −i)
              │        ┌─┴─┐
              3        5   6

getSum(4) → arr[0..4] → i = 5:  BIT[5] + BIT[4] = 50 + 100 = 150
The i & -i trick: isolating the lowest set bit

−i in two's complement is ~i + 1: flip every bit, then add one. Flipping turns the trailing zeros of i into ones and the lowest 1 into 0; adding one carries through those ones and stops exactly at that position. The result shares only that one bit with i, so i & −i is the lowest set bit as a power of two.

i & −i for i = 6 and i = 12
 i = 6  :  0 1 1 0
~i      :  1 0 0 1
-i = ~i+1: 1 0 1 0
 i & -i :  0 0 1 0   = 2        6 → block of length 2 ([5, 6]);  6 − 2 = 4 is the next block

 i = 12 :  1 1 0 0
-i      :  0 1 0 0
 i & -i :  0 1 0 0   = 4        12 → block of length 4 ([9..12]); 12 − 4 = 8 is the next block
Python
for i in range(1, 9):
    print(f"{i}  {i:04b}  lowest set bit = {i & -i}")
